##### Chapter 12 — Quantum Information Theory (lines 333–348)

- **Staleness:** The reconciliation explicitly says channels/CPTP/Kraus/operator-sum moved to Chapter 10 and delivered
  Chapter 12 became Shannon→von Neumann→Holevo→trace distance/fidelity→capacities→LOCC/resource theories. Thus the first
  four sections and numbering here are obsolete, and capacities/LOCC are missing.
- **Original redundancy:** §§12.1–12.4 are essentially one mathematical topic: channels are CPTP maps represented (not
  uniquely) by Kraus/operator-sum forms. Splitting them into four sequential sections encourages synonym confusion;
  introduce definitions, representations, dilations and examples as one arc.
- **Channel precision:** CPTP applies to deterministic quantum channels on density operators including complete positivity
  for extensions; conditional branches are trace-nonincreasing, measurements are instruments/classical-quantum channels,
  and initial correlations can complicate reduced maps. Kraus decompositions are nonunique.
- **Metric ordering:** Trace distance and fidelity should precede channel diamond norm, with explicit convention for
  squared versus unsquared fidelity. Cover operational discrimination meanings, monotonicity, Fuchs–van de Graaf bounds
  and estimation limitations.
- **Diamond norm:** Technically demanding and easy to misuse; distinguish channel distance with ancillary extension,
  worst-case operational meaning and normalization factors. If later engineering metrics do not use it, mark deep dive.
- **Entropy arc:** Delivered Shannon→von Neumann ordering is much better. Define log base/units, spectra, pure/mixed limits,
  subadditivity/conditional entropy and why quantum conditional entropy can be negative; do not call entropy ignorance
  without qualification.
- **Mutual information:** Quantum mutual information measures total correlations and equals a relative entropy; it is not
  an entanglement measure. Include data processing and classical-register examples.
- **Holevo:** State ensemble/classical-quantum setup, accessible-information upper bound and asymptotic/measurement context.
  It does not mean “one qubit carries only one bit” unconditionally—entanglement-assisted dense coding and prior resources
  require careful accounting.
- **Entanglement measures:** Repeating Chapter 7 should deepen into LOCC monotones, pure versus mixed operational measures,
  cost/distillable/bound entanglement and multipartite limitations. One scalar does not universally rank states.
- **Capacities:** Delivered channel capacities require classical/private/quantum/entanglement-assisted distinctions,
  regularization/additivity subtleties and coding asymptotics. Avoid implying a single “capacity” or easy computability.
- **LOCC/resource theory:** Define free operations/states, resource conversion, monotones and task dependence. This
  framework corrects the book’s repeated unqualified “entanglement is a resource” slogan.
- **Pedagogical load:** This is among the mathematically densest chapters. Use classical binary/channel examples,
  qubit-state calculations and operational questions before theorem catalogs; declare proof depth and prerequisites.
- **Reader entertainment: 3.5/5.** Dense distances/entropies can feel abstract, but state discrimination, compression and
  resource-conversion puzzles offer strong payoff. The obsolete outline looks more like a terminology stack than a story.
- **Unit completion:** Lines 333–348 inspected in full, including all 11 planned sections, every moved/missing delivered
  topic, channel/metric/entropy/resource precision, ordering, and divider.

##### Part VI / Chapter 13 — Quantum Algorithms Mindset (lines 349–360)

- **Role:** A pattern-language chapter before named algorithms is excellent for transfer learning, provided it uses small
  circuits and cost models rather than mystical slogans. It overlaps Chapter 10’s interference/phase kickback and should
  absorb or reference that material.
- **§13.1:** “Amplitude manipulation” needs unitarity/normalization constraints, indirect control through gates and limited
  readout. Algorithms shape distributions/observables; they cannot arbitrarily set amplitudes or read the whole vector.
- **§13.2:** Phase kickback repeats §10.6. Here connect controlled eigenvalue phases to Fourier/phase estimation with one
  derivation and resource assumptions; merge duplicate exposition.
- **§13.3:** Define oracle encoding, query versus gate/time complexity, coherent/reversible implementation, garbage
  uncomputation and controlled/power access. Oracle cost cannot be hidden when judging practical advantage.
- **§13.4:** “Transform-domain” is DSP-friendly but can mislead QFT=fast readable FFT. Cover basis changes/Fourier sampling,
  inaccessible amplitude output, structure-dependent measurement and alternative transforms/block encodings.
- **§13.5:** Hidden subgroup/period/linear structure are important families, but “extraction” requires repeated samples and
  classical postprocessing. Not all applications contain discoverable hidden structure and no generic quantum pattern
  detector exists.
- **§13.6:** State success probability, amplification/repetition, independence, confidence, verification and expected cost.
  Quantum amplitude amplification is not the same as rerunning; postselection can have exponential cost.
- **§13.7:** Complexity framing should be earlier enough to qualify every claimed speedup: decision/function/sampling,
  exact/bounded error, query/gate/depth/space, input/output encoding, promise problems, uniformity and best classical
  comparator. Chapter 17 later should deepen, not retroactively repair claims.
- **Missing patterns:** State preparation/data access, Hamiltonian/block encoding, phase estimation, amplitude estimation,
  quantum walks, variational/hybrid loops, measurement/observable design and verification are central modern mindsets;
  explicitly choose scope or the chapter overfits early oracle algorithms.
- **Anti-hype exit:** Require readers to answer: where does data enter, what coherent operation is assumed, what is
  measured, how many repetitions, what classical work remains, what error precision, and what baseline is beaten.
- **Reader entertainment: 4/5.** Pattern recognition suits experienced developers and can make later algorithms feel
  composed rather than magical. Abstract gerunds without worked failures/successes would feel like motivational jargon.
- **Unit completion:** Lines 349–360 inspected in full, including Part/Chapter headings, all seven mindset sections,
  overlaps, missing patterns, complexity/access requirements, and proposed exit checklist.

##### Chapter 14 — Foundational Algorithms (lines 361–372)

- **Progression:** Toy oracle algorithms→Simon→QFT/QPE→amplitude primitives→hidden subgroup is intellectually coherent,
  but QFT/QPE are prerequisites/mechanisms and hidden subgroup contextualizes Simon/Shor; consider concept-first ordering
  or explicit dependency graph.
- **§14.1:** Deutsch’s one-bit promise problem should demonstrate phase oracle/interference, with exact deterministic and
  randomized classical comparators. Avoid presenting it as useful speedup; it is a minimal mechanism exercise.
- **§14.2:** State constant/balanced promise and one exact quantum query versus worst-case exact deterministic
  \(2^{n-1}+1\); bounded-error randomized classical sampling uses constant queries, so practical/exponential rhetoric must
  be constrained.
- **§14.3:** Define \(f_s(x)=s\cdot x\bmod2\), one versus \(n\) deterministic queries and why a phase oracle exposes bits.
  The separation is linear/query-specific; implementation cost and classical randomized variants matter.
- **§14.4:** Include two-to-one XOR-period promise, sampling orthogonal vectors, repeated linear solves, success probability
  and exponential randomized query separation. Connect to Shor without the false claim that it is the same reduction.
- **§14.5:** QFT is a unitary on amplitudes, not an FFT returning all coefficients. Fix endianness/bit reversal/sign/
  normalization, exact/approximate circuits and measurement use; classical postprocessing/readout is fundamental.
- **§14.6:** QPE requires eigenstate overlap and controlled powers/evolution, with precision/success/depth tradeoffs.
  Iterative/semiclassical variants, inverse QFT and energy/period applications should distinguish primitive from a free
  oracle.
- **§14.7:** Amplitude amplification generalizes Grover given state preparation and good-state phase marking plus inverses;
  cover known/unknown success amplitude, query bounds and oracle construction. It is not generic optimizer magic.
- **§14.8:** Classical Monte Carlo \(O(1/\epsilon^2)\) versus ideal quantum query \(O(1/\epsilon)\) needs assumptions,
  coherent access, confidence, variants, depth/noise and end-to-end costs. “Amplitude estimation” now names multiple
  algorithms with distinct resources.
- **§14.9:** Abelian HSP unifies Simon/order finding under group/function promises; nonabelian HSP remains hard in important
  cases. Do not imply a solved universal framework; state representation/oracle and postprocessing requirements.
- **Verification:** Every algorithm should include promise validator, hand calculation, simulator test with seeded shots,
  resource count and failure-mode example. Oracle circuits must be reversible and clean garbage.
- **Reader entertainment: 4.5/5.** Small exact algorithms and phase-estimation reveals provide repeated “aha” moments.
  Nine algorithms/primitives can blur unless a comparison/dependency map keeps the story visible.
- **Unit completion:** Lines 361–372 inspected in full, including all nine entries, exact comparator/promise/access details,
  ordering, verification requirements, and chapter narrative.

##### Chapter 15 — Landmark Quantum Algorithms (lines 373–385)

- **Taxonomy:** The chapter mixes concrete algorithms (Grover/Shor/HHL), problem applications (factoring/discrete log),
  paradigms (walks/variational), subalgorithms (VQE/QAOA) and a whole field (QML). Use one level of abstraction and avoid
  duplicating Shor with two following problem sections.
- **§15.1:** Grover follows amplitude amplification and should focus on oracle construction, multiple solutions, iteration
  count/overshoot, unknown count, lower bound, verification and real database caveat. State bounded-error query advantage,
  not generic quadratic runtime.
- **§§15.2–15.4:** Teach Shor as order finding plus classical reduction, then separate factoring/discrete-log arithmetic
  only if each is worked. Include random bases, gcd, even period/nontrivial square root, success repetition, modular
  exponentiation, QFT approximation and fault-tolerant resource estimates. Distinguish RSA from DH/ECC and no proved
  classical lower bound.
- **§15.5:** HHL outputs a quantum state proportional to a solution under sparsity/access, conditioning, normalization,
  precision and state-preparation assumptions; it does not print an \(N\)-entry vector exponentially fast. Observable
  extraction and classical dequantization/input models are essential.
- **§15.6:** Discrete/continuous-time walks, hitting/search algorithms and graph/oracle access differ. Give one actual
  speedup and limitations rather than a survey label.
- **§15.7:** Variational algorithms are hybrid optimization frameworks, not one algorithm. Define ansatz, estimator,
  optimizer, shot/noise cost, trainability/barren plateaus, expressibility, verification and classical baseline; useful
  advantage remains unsettled for many proposed applications.
- **§15.8:** VQE targets energies/observables under Hamiltonian decomposition and ansatz assumptions; cover measurement
  grouping, optimizer bias, excited states, error mitigation and classical chemistry baselines. It is not guaranteed to
  reach the ground state.
- **§15.9:** QAOA is an alternating variational ansatz; approximation guarantees depend on problem/depth and classical
  optimization. Do not expand acronym as “Approximate” (it is “Approximate Optimization”) incorrectly or imply broad
  industrial superiority.
- **§15.10:** QML overview duplicates Chapter 30 and is too broad. If retained, use it to explain data-loading/output/
  dequantization caveats and taxonomy, then defer algorithms; otherwise it becomes ungrounded hype at the landmark climax.
- **“Landmark” criterion:** Recent/heuristic VQE/QAOA/QML are influential but not established speedup landmarks comparable
  to Shor/Grover. Separate theoretically established algorithms from NISQ-era research programmes and label evidence.
- **Missing simulation:** Quantum simulation is historically/core algorithmic family and more naturally landmark than a
  generic QML overview. Its absence conflicts with Chapter 13’s developer bridge and Feynman narrative.
- **Reader entertainment: 4/5.** Grover/Shor provide a high-energy center; the abrupt shift into acronym-heavy NISQ/QML
  survey dilutes climax. One end-to-end resource reality check would be gripping.
- **Unit completion:** Lines 373–385 inspected in full, including all ten entries, taxonomy/duplication, every algorithm’s
  assumptions/output/comparator, missing simulation, evidence-tiering, and chapter title claim.

##### Chapter 16 — Modern Algorithmic Frontier (lines 386–398)

- **Temporal label:** “Modern/frontier” ages quickly. Add a snapshot date, selection criteria and update policy; much of
  this framework is now established core theory rather than a transient frontier.
- **Dependency arc:** Hamiltonian simulation→product formulas→LCU/block encodings→qubitization/QSP/QSVT is coherent, but
  terminology and prerequisites are exceptionally dense. Provide a map of encoded object, primitive, polynomial
  transformation, output and cost at each step.
- **§16.1:** Define simulation goal \(e^{-iHt}\), Hamiltonian input/access model (local/sparse/linear combination/block
  encoding), time/error norm, state preparation and observable output. No-fast-forwarding and structure requirements
  prevent “quantum systems simulate nature efficiently” generalization.
- **§16.2:** Product-formula order/error/commutator bounds, step count, negative coefficients, gate synthesis and practical
  constants matter. “Trotter–Suzuki decompositions” are algorithms/approximations, not an exact generic decomposition;
  compare with newer methods fairly.
- **§16.3:** LCU needs coefficient normalization, PREPARE/SELECT oracles, ancillas, postselection/amplitude amplification
  and success cost. Query complexity hides implementation cost; use one small Hamiltonian example.
- **§16.4:** A block encoding embeds a scaled operator in a larger unitary with normalization/error/oracle costs. It is an
  access assumption/construction, not a free conversion from arbitrary classical matrix data.
- **§16.5:** Qubitization builds invariant subspaces/walk operators from block encodings and enables near-optimal
  simulation under assumptions. Explain terminology distinct from “turning something into qubits” and resource overhead.
- **§16.6:** QSP applies phase sequences to enact constrained polynomial transformations on singular/eigenvalue variables;
  phase-factor synthesis, parity/boundedness conditions and convention variants make it unsuitable for slogan-only
  coverage.
- **§16.7:** QSVT generalizes polynomial singular-value transformation given a block encoding, enabling many algorithms.
  It does not automatically make all linear algebra exponentially faster; data access, condition number, precision and
  output bottlenecks remain.
- **§16.8:** “Modern view” should synthesize evidence classes: query versus end-to-end, structure/access, polynomial degree,
  condition/precision, input/output, fault-tolerant costs, dequantization and best classical algorithms. Avoid a triumphal
  capstone.
- **Prerequisites:** Polynomial approximation, singular values/SVD, functional calculus, oracles, ancillas and amplitude
  amplification must be established. The reconciliation’s SVD addition to Chapter 4 supports this; link it explicitly.
- **Examples/entertainment:** One problem carried from Trotter to QSVT with resource comparison is preferable to seven
  independent derivations. Visual polynomial-filter intuition can be engaging if normalization/access costs stay visible.
- **Reader entertainment: 3.5/5.** The unifying progression can deliver a deep “many algorithms are one pattern” insight.
  Acronym/abstraction density will be forbidding without a running example and optional proof layers.
- **Unit completion:** Lines 386–398 inspected in full, including all eight sections, access/error/resource assumptions,
  temporal governance, prerequisite links, synthesis criteria, and divider.

##### Part VII / Chapter 17 — Complexity Theory (lines 399–418)

- **Placement:** A dedicated complexity chapter after algorithms can formalize examples, but earlier Chapters 1/13–16
  already make speedup claims. Supply a minimal complexity toolkit earlier and use Chapter 17 for deeper relationships;
  qualifications cannot arrive retroactively.
- **§17.1:** Define decision languages, polynomial-time uniformity, deterministic/nondeterministic/randomized bounded error,
  reductions and completeness. Factoring is not known NP-complete and is a function problem; do not use it as standard
  NP-complete example.
- **§17.2:** BQP requires uniform polynomial-size quantum circuits/TM and bounded error, with \(P\subseteq BPP\subseteq BQP
  \subseteq PP\subseteq PSPACE\) known containments as appropriate. BPP versus BQP and NP versus BQP are unresolved.
- **§17.3:** QMA versus QCMA differ by quantum versus classical witnesses to quantum verification; define completeness/
  soundness amplification and canonical problems. Avoid the lazy “quantum NP” equivalence without caveats.
- **§17.4:** QIP concerns interactive proof systems and QIP=PSPACE, a deep result that may be peripheral to experienced
  developers. Explain learning payoff or mark optional; distinguish proof complexity from implementable quantum
  algorithms.
- **§17.5:** PH/PSPACE relations are nuanced and oracle/conditional evidence matters. Cover Toda-like context only as
  needed; do not draw an unsupported Venn diagram implying unknown strict containments.
- **§§17.6–17.7:** Query models must specify oracle encoding/access and ignore internal cost deliberately. Oracle
  separations are evidence/relative-world results, not unconditional class separation; controlled oracle access may add
  assumptions.
- **§§17.8–17.10:** Define polynomial/quadratic/exponential/superpolynomial, query versus gate/time/depth/sample/end-to-end
  speedup, input size versus dimension, approximation/error and hardware parallelism. “Exponential” often evaporates when
  data loading/output or a logarithmic encoding is mishandled.
- **§17.11:** Lower bounds need a model; Grover optimality is query-specific, no-fast-forwarding and black-box bounds do not
  rule out structured algorithms. Complexity assumptions are not proofs of physical infeasibility.
- **§17.12:** Dequantization covers classical algorithms matching quantum-inspired claims under comparable data-access/
  sampling assumptions. Define term carefully and use dated primary papers; it is not “turning a quantum algorithm
  classical” uniformly.
- **§17.13:** Stabilizer/Gottesman–Knill, low-entanglement tensor networks, matchgates/free fermions, low magic,
  near-Clifford and restricted circuits show simulability depends on structure/output/error. Entanglement/dimension alone
  does not decide hardness.
- **Missing sampling/functional classes:** Many quantum tasks are sampling, relation or function problems, not decision
  languages. Include FBQP/SampBQP-style distinctions at the level needed for Shor/RCS; otherwise class-centric treatment
  mismatches applications.
- **Visual caution:** Complexity containment diagrams should mark known inclusion, equality, believed strictness and
  incomparability/open status distinctly, with date/source and accessible text.
- **Reader entertainment: 3.5/5.** Lower-bound surprises and dequantization can be intellectually bracing. A 13-section
  alphabet-soup march will lose most developers unless every class answers a previously encountered algorithmic question.
- **Unit completion:** Lines 399–418 inspected in full, including Part/Chapter headings, all 13 sections, class definitions/
  containments, oracle/speedup/model caveats, missing task types, placement and visualization concerns.

##### Part VIII / Chapter 18 — Noise, Decoherence, and Errors (lines 419–450)

- **Staleness:** Reconciliation says delivered Chapter 18 consolidated individual channel sections and expanded RB
  variants, spectral-density/non-Markovian models, GST, error budgets and practitioner workflow. This 18-section plan is
  therefore obsolete and materially underrepresents current structure.
- **Taxonomy:** Sources, observables/times, phenomenological channels, error mechanisms, characterization metrics/methods
  and mitigation are intermixed. Organize physical source→mathematical model→measurement/estimation→system impact→response,
  and distinguish error from uncertainty/drift.
- **§18.1:** Sources depend on platform: environment, control electronics, materials/defects, loss, temperature, laser/
  microwave phase/amplitude, fabrication, cosmic/burst events and classical controller. Avoid one superconducting-centric
  list while claiming generality.
- **§18.2:** \(T_1\) energy relaxation and \(T_2\) coherence decay need definitions/protocols, \(T_2\le2T_1\) under standard
  assumptions, \(T_2^*\)/echo distinction, nonexponential/time-dependent behavior and why ratios do not equal gate error.
- **§18.3:** Dephasing overlaps T2/phase-flip but real noise may be continuous/non-Markovian rather than an independent
  Pauli flip. Connect phase-damping channel, spectra/filter functions and basis dependence.
- **§§18.4–18.6:** Gate/readout/preparation errors are effective categories with SPAM identifiability and context
  dependence. Separate coherent miscalibration, stochastic noise, leakage, crosstalk and sampling estimator; reported
  “fidelity” depends on protocol/model.
- **§§18.7–18.9:** Crosstalk, leakage and thermal population require multi-level/system models. Leakage is outside qubit
  subspace and can persist/spread; thermal noise is not a single channel and detailed-balance/effective temperature matter.
- **§§18.10–18.13:** Bit/phase/depolarizing/amplitude-damping are useful toy channels, not exhaustive physical truth.
  Define Kraus/Pauli-transfer/Lindblad representations, fixed points and compositional limitations; amplitude damping is
  nonunital, depolarizing convention differs by dimension/probability.
- **§18.14:** Coherent/incoherent is not a complete dichotomy; coherent systematic errors can randomize under twirling,
  drift/non-Markovian/correlated errors complicate classification. Diamond/worst-case and average metrics respond very
  differently.
- **§18.15:** “Noise Models” after thirteen model/mechanism sections is backwards. Introduce channel/process assumptions,
  Markovianity, locality/correlation, time stationarity, context and model validation early, then classify examples.
- **§18.16:** Fidelity/error rate is not one scalar. Specify state/process/average/entanglement fidelity, infidelity,
  diamond distance, Pauli error, leakage/readout metrics and confidence; incomparable vendor metrics must not be ranked.
- **§18.17:** RB estimates average error under assumptions and variants address leakage/simultaneous/interleaved/cycle;
  XEB is distribution/circuit benchmark with modeling assumptions; GST is self-consistent but costly/model-sensitive.
  Define what each identifies and does not.
- **§18.18:** ZNE/PEC/CDR/readout mitigation have distinct assumptions, sampling overhead/bias and failure modes. Expand
  acronyms, separate readout calibration, and distinguish mitigation from QEC/fault tolerance; no method magically
  recovers deep-circuit truth.
- **Missing delivered topics:** Spectral density/filter functions, correlated/non-Markovian processes, drift monitoring,
  error budgets, characterization workflow, uncertainty and reproducible data belong. Link from diagnosis to code/
  compiler/control decisions.
- **Reader entertainment: 3.5/5.** Noise sleuthing and real diagnostic traces can feel like systems debugging. Eighteen
  category headings plus acronym bullets look like a catalog unless unified by one failing circuit investigation.
- **Unit completion:** Lines 419–450 inspected in full, including Part/Chapter headings, all 18 sections, every nested
  benchmark/mitigation method, delivered reorganization, taxonomy, metrics and workflow omissions.

##### Chapter 19 — Quantum Error Correction and Fault Tolerance (lines 451–478)

- **Scale:** Twenty-three sections span an entire advanced textbook, from repetition code to qLDPC/magic factories/
  surgery. Define core versus deep dive and use a dependency map; otherwise breadth guarantees shallow theorem and
  architecture treatment.
- **§§19.1–19.3:** Avoid “classical copying easy/quantum impossible” caricature. Classical codes also use indirect parity;
  quantum codes encode subspaces, must handle phase/coherent errors, cannot directly learn logical amplitudes, and face
  noisy extraction/fault propagation. Explain what “naive” scheme fails and why.
- **§§19.4–19.5:** Three-qubit bit/phase-flip codes are pedagogical and related by Hadamards, but neither corrects arbitrary
  single-qubit errors alone. Show stabilizers, syndromes, logical operators and why continuous errors reduce to Pauli basis
  under QEC conditions.
- **§§19.6–19.7:** Shor nine-qubit and Steane seven-qubit CSS codes should be worked examples with distance [[9,1,3]]/
  [[7,1,3]], degeneracy/transversal properties and historical caveats. Avoid calling one simply better; resource/fault
  models differ.
- **§§19.8–19.11:** Stabilizers, syndrome, decoding and CSS form one formal arc. Define abelian Pauli subgroup excluding
  \(-I\), code space/logicals/normalizer, degeneracy, noisy repeated syndrome, decoder inference and classical-code pair
  commutation conditions. Syndrome does not uniquely identify exact fault.
- **§19.10:** Decoding is a real-time classical probabilistic inference problem; compare lookup, matching, union-find,
  belief propagation/neural methods only with latency/accuracy/training/generalization caveats. A decoder can create
  logical failure from ambiguous/noisy syndrome.
- **§§19.12–19.14:** Surface codes are topological codes, so separate headings overlap. Explain planar/toric variants,
  boundaries/defects, stabilizer cycles and code distance; color codes trade checks/connectivity/transversal gates. Do not
  conflate topological code with topological hardware qubit.
- **§19.15:** qLDPC is fast-moving and heterogeneous; define sparse checks, rate/distance, connectivity/check weight,
  syndrome circuits/decoding and difference between asymptotic promise and hardware realization. Date all “low overhead”
  comparisons.
- **§§19.16–19.18:** Logical qubit/distance/overhead should precede code families or be introduced immediately. Distance
  \(d\) corrects up to \(\lfloor(d-1)/2\rfloor\) arbitrary faults only under suitable model; overhead is space–time,
  factories/routing/decoder/control, not qubits alone.
- **§19.19:** Threshold theorems require explicit local/stochastic/correlation/preparation/measurement/classical-control
  assumptions and target computation. Threshold is code/circuit/decoder/noise dependent; below it, increasing code size
  can suppress logical failure with overhead, not guarantee engineering feasibility.
- **§§19.20/19.23:** Fault-tolerant gates and logical implementation duplicate. Organize by propagation criteria,
  transversal gates, code deformation/surgery, teleportation, gauge fixing and Eastin–Knill constraint; physical
  correction may be Pauli-frame tracking.
- **§19.21:** Magic-state distillation/injection supplies non-Clifford resources in many architectures and can dominate
  cost. Cover factory protocols/error/output, Clifford assumptions and alternatives; “magic” must be formally defined as
  nonstabilizer resource, not mystique.
- **§19.22:** Lattice surgery performs joint logical parity measurements/patch operations with boundaries and code-cycle
  space–time cost. It is not a universal synonym for logical operations and depends on surface-code layouts/decoder.
- **Missing operations:** State preparation, repeated syndrome circuits, logical measurement, reset, leakage handling,
  erasures/loss, correlated bursts, verification and memory experiment metrics are necessary. QEC versus mitigation should
  be explicit.
- **Reader entertainment: 4/5.** The protect-without-copying puzzle and growing encoded architecture are compelling.
  Twenty-three headings risk turning the resolution into taxonomy overload; one logical qubit carried through noise,
  decode and gate would sustain narrative.
- **Unit completion:** Lines 451–478 inspected in full, including all 23 sections, code-family overlaps, theorem/decoder/
  overhead assumptions, missing operational pieces, taxonomy/ordering, and divider.

##### Part IX / Chapter 20 — Quantum Hardware Platforms (lines 479–495)

- **Taxonomy:** Platform families, subtypes, defects/centers and computational models are mixed. Superconducting is split
  into transmon/fluxonium while trapped ions/photonic/neutral/spin remain broad; choose consistent encoding-level
  taxonomy and explain hybrids/modularity.
- **Temporal governance:** Hardware state, fidelities, scale and claims change quickly. Use dated primary peer-reviewed
  evidence, invariant operating principles and no vendor leaderboard; separate demonstrated, projected and contested.
- **§§20.1–20.3:** “Superconducting qubits” should introduce circuit quantization/Josephson nonlinearity, then transmon/
  fluxonium tradeoffs (anharmonicity, charge/flux sensitivity, coherence, gates/readout) without treating architectures
  as homogeneous. Include cryogenics, fabrication/yield, wiring, crosstalk and leakage.
- **§20.4:** Trapped ions require species/encoding, laser/microwave control, shared motion, gate speed/fidelity,
  connectivity, heating, readout, vacuum and modular photonic links. “All-to-all” is finite-chain/context-dependent.
- **§20.5:** Neutral atoms span Rydberg gates/analog simulation, reconfigurable arrays, loading/loss, blockade, laser
  control and measurement. Large atom count is not equivalent to universal high-fidelity logical compute.
- **§20.6:** Photonic encodings/models (dual rail, time/frequency, continuous variable, fusion/MBQC) have different
  sources/detectors/loss/gate tradeoffs. “Room temperature” or communication-friendly claims need whole-system caveats.
- **§20.7:** Silicon spin qubits include single/electron/nuclear/donor/exchange variants, cryogenic control, valley/disorder,
  variability, readout/connectivity and semiconductor fabrication promise. Density is not automatically scalable yield.
- **§20.8:** NV centers are one color-center family with sensing/networking strengths and optical/material limitations;
  “other solid-state” is too broad. Separate quantum compute from sensing/network nodes and include defects only by use
  case.
- **§20.9:** Topological qubits/non-Abelian anyons remain experimentally uncertain; distinguish them sharply from surface/
  topological codes already used on conventional hardware. Majorana claims require dated independent evidence and
  controversy disclosure.
- **§20.10:** Analog simulators emulate specific Hamiltonians and differ from universal digital simulation in control,
  verification/error models and computational claims. Define programmability and validation; analog is not “less
  quantum” or automatically efficient.
- **§20.11:** Annealing versus gate model needs Hamiltonian schedule, open-system/stoquastic distinctions, optimization
  mapping/embedding, fair classical baselines and lack of generic demonstrated speedup. Vendor-specific D-Wave discussion
  should be dated/neutral.
- **§20.12:** Cross-platform metrics are rarely apples-to-apples: fidelity protocol, operation set, connectivity, speed,
  coherence, parallelism, measurement/reset, leakage, uptime, calibration, yield, logical error and total application
  success. Use a dimensional framework, not one score.
- **Missing platform dimensions:** Control stack, operating environment, native gate set, error bias/correlation, QEC
  compatibility, modular networking, manufacturing, energy/footprint and classical co-processing should appear in every
  platform template.
- **Reader entertainment: 4/5.** Contrasting physical embodiments is naturally fascinating. Twelve modality sections risk
  a spec-sheet parade; following one logical operation across three platforms would make tradeoffs memorable.
- **Unit completion:** Lines 479–495 inspected in full, including Part/Chapter headings, all 12 platform/model/metric
  sections, taxonomy symmetry, per-platform caveats, temporal evidence and comparison methodology.

##### Chapter 21 — Quantum Control and Electronics (lines 496–512)

- **Platform bias:** Microwave/RF, DAC/ADC, cryogenic electronics and FPGA stack strongly fit superconducting/spin systems
  but not photonic/ion/neutral platforms with lasers, optics, cameras/detectors and vacuum. Declare a superconducting case-
  study scope or add platform-specific control paths.
- **§21.1:** Pulse shaping should connect Hamiltonian/control objectives, envelopes/quadratures, bandwidth, DRAG/composite/
  optimal control, leakage/crosstalk and hardware transfer functions. Ideal waveform simulations do not equal delivered
  device fields.
- **§21.2:** Define carriers, IQ mixing, phase noise, frequency reference, up/downconversion, filtering, crosstalk and
  calibration. RF/microwave safety/hardware specifics should stay conceptual unless maintained/tested.
- **§21.3:** Pulse-level programming is backend/API dependent and increasingly restricted; date examples and avoid tying
  core learning to one vendor. Explain compiler-to-schedule-to-waveform abstraction and calibration portability limits.
- **§21.4:** Control architecture needs clocks/synchronization, trigger distribution, waveform memory/generation, readout
  chain, low-latency compute, networking, error handling and observability. Separate control plane from data/readout path.
- **§21.5:** DAC/ADC specs (sample rate, resolution/ENOB, jitter, latency, bandwidth, SFDR) trade off and do not map directly
  to gate fidelity. Include mixers/amplifiers/filters and calibrated transfer functions.
- **§21.6:** Signal integrity spans impedance/reflections, attenuation, dispersion, isolation, grounding, EMI, thermal noise
  and line-to-line coupling. Avoid importing deterministic digital-SI intuition without cryogenic/analog context.
- **§21.7:** Cryogenic electronics can reduce wiring/latency but adds power/heat/noise/process constraints. Distinguish
  cryo-CMOS, amplifiers, multiplexing and room-temperature controllers; not every platform is cryogenic.
- **§§21.8–21.9:** Real-time feedback/mid-circuit loops overlap. Define measurement integration, discrimination, transport,
  branching, reset/correction, deterministic latency/jitter and coherence budget; QEC decoder loops are more demanding
  than simple active reset.
- **§21.10:** Calibration is continuous system identification/optimization under drift, context and hysteresis; cover
  scheduling, versioning, rollback, uncertainty, interdependence, automation and when calibration invalidates experiments.
- **§21.11:** “Control-plane engineering” risks repeating architecture/feedback/calibration. Use it for APIs, scheduling,
  resource arbitration, telemetry, safety/interlocks, provenance and multi-user operations, or merge.
- **§21.12:** FPGA/HDL can provide deterministic streaming/feedback but is not the only implementation; include CPU/GPU/
  ASIC/SoC and verification/timing/resource constraints. HDL examples need simulation/tests and should not imply software
  logic is faultless.
- **§21.13:** Packaging/interconnect determines thermal load, loss, modes, crosstalk, density, yield and serviceability.
  Cover optical/fiber/vacuum variants if chapter remains cross-platform.
- **§21.14:** Gate speed and readout fidelity are two metrics, not one section’s whole objective. Faster gates can worsen
  leakage/crosstalk; readout fidelity depends on states/protocol/time and trades against demolition/heating. Include total
  cycle/feedback performance and uncertainty.
- **Missing software engineering:** Configuration/calibration schemas, reproducibility, CI/hardware-in-loop testing,
  observability, fault injection, security/isolation and data provenance are especially relevant to experienced developers.
- **Reader entertainment: 4/5.** This rare full-stack material can be one of the book’s distinctive strengths. A 14-section
  electronics inventory will overwhelm unless organized around a pulse’s round trip through the stack.
- **Unit completion:** Lines 496–512 inspected in full, including all 14 sections, cross-platform bias, each control-stack
  layer, metric tradeoffs, missing software practices, and chapter narrative opportunity.

##### Chapter 22 — Hardware Engineering Metrics (lines 513–525)

- **Staleness:** Reconciliation says delivered Chapter 22 has 14 sections, replaces “Scalability Constraints,” and adds
  XEB, mid-circuit/reset/feedforward latency, calibration drift and a 2024–26 benchmark survey. This ten-section plan is
  noncanonical and its current/commercial metric names require timestamping.
- **Metric philosophy:** No scalar ranks platforms. Define target workload, operation set, confidence/method, calibration
  context, date and end-to-end success; distinguish component, layer, logical and application metrics and resist vendor-
  selected leaderboards.
- **§22.1:** Raw physical qubit count omits yield/active/calibrated qubits, connectivity, errors, parallelism, uptime and
  logical overhead. State exactly which qubits are counted and whether usable simultaneously.
- **§22.2:** Connectivity includes graph degree/direction, dynamic/reconfigurable links, routing cost, crosstalk and module
  networks; all-to-all within a small ion chain is not system-wide free connectivity.
- **§22.3:** Gate fidelity depends on gate, context, simultaneous operation and protocol/model; average fidelity can hide
  coherent/worst-case/leakage/correlated faults. Include uncertainty and RB/GST/process distinctions.
- **§22.4:** T1/T2/T2*/echo times are not standalone computational quality and may vary over time/qubits. Compare coherence
  to operation/cycle times only with full error channels.
- **§22.5:** Gate duration trades with control error, leakage, crosstalk and scheduling; distinguish physical pulse,
  logical gate and fault-tolerant cycle latency. Faster is not automatically better.
- **§22.6:** Readout assignment fidelity/confusion matrix varies by state, qubit, multiplexing/context and integration time;
  include QND character, reset, leakage, correlated errors and latency.
- **§22.7:** Quantum Volume combines width/depth under a specific random-circuit/heavy-output test; compilation, confidence
  and implementation choices matter. It is a useful system benchmark, not application performance or universal scale.
- **§22.8:** CLOPS measures circuit-layer throughput under a defined workload and includes parts of classical interaction;
  it is vendor-originated/versioned and says little about fidelity/utility alone. Expand acronym and cite specification.
- **§22.9:** “Algorithmic qubits” is provider-defined and methodology-dependent, not equivalent to error-corrected logical
  qubits. Use quotation/attribution, version/date and avoid cross-platform comparison without common protocol.
- **§22.10:** Scalability is multidimensional: fabrication/yield, wiring/thermal load, calibration complexity, control/

##### Chapter 24 — Classical Simulation (lines 561–580)

- **Staleness:** Reconciliation says delivered Chapter 24 replaced planned Trotterization/many-body/numerical-stability/
  connections sections with near-Clifford/magic, Schrödinger–Feynman path sums, GPU/distributed, noise simulators,
  advantage frontier and choosing-a-simulator guide. This 15-section outline is deeply noncanonical.
- **§24.1:** Motivate algorithm development/testing, compiler verification, hardware validation, scientific simulation and
  classical baselines. Classical simulation is not merely a fallback before quantum hardware; it remains essential and
  often wins for structured tasks.
- **§24.2:** Generic statevector memory scales \(O(2^n)\), but “barrier” depends on target output, circuit/state structure,
  approximation, entanglement, sparsity, gate class and hardware. Avoid deriving hardness from dimension alone.
- **§24.3:** Statevector methods need memory/layout, gate kernels, endianness, sampling/expectation output, batching,
  parallelism and precision. Exact full state is unnecessary for some queries; disk/distributed/GPU costs matter.
- **§24.4:** Density matrices scale \(O(4^n)\) and represent mixed/channel evolution but quantum trajectories/Monte Carlo
  may be cheaper under assumptions. Kraus/superoperator integration and positivity/trace numerical errors need care.
- **§24.5:** Stabilizer simulation is efficient for Clifford states/circuits/Pauli measurements under Gottesman–Knill
  conditions; adding non-Clifford magic changes cost. It does not show Clifford quantum systems are physically classical.
- **§§24.6–24.9:** Tensor networks exploit graph/entanglement/treewidth structure; MPS is one topology, DMRG a ground-state
  variational algorithm, not merely simulator backend. Bond dimension/truncation error/canonicalization and failure under
  volume-law entanglement are central; “variational tensor methods” is too broad.
- **§24.10:** Product-formula simulation can be classical or quantum; specify what object is evolved, local tensor/MPS or
  full vector, discretization/commutator error and stability. Its removal in delivered taxonomy should say where the
  relevant concept moved.
- **§24.11:** “Many-body systems” is domain, not method, and spans equilibrium/dynamics, fermions/bosons, lattice/
  continuum, sign problem and observables. Too broad for one catch-all section.
- **§24.12:** Removing numerical stability is questionable: normalization, cancellation, SVD truncation, floating-point,
  stochastic error, time-step/conditioning and reproducibility materially affect simulations. Preserve it in a
  practitioner workflow even if not a standalone section.
- **§§24.13–24.15:** Signal-processing/numerical/tomography “connections” are vague and duplicate prerequisites/Chapter 11.
  Only retain specific algorithms or diagnostic payoffs; tomography estimates physical states from data, whereas
  simulation predicts under a model.
- **Delivered additions:** Near-Clifford/magic rank/extent methods, path-sum Schrödinger–Feynman splitting, GPU/distributed
  communication, noise simulators and method selection materially improve coverage. Each needs cost/error/output criteria
  and honest benchmark reproducibility.
- **Advantage frontier:** Any quantum-classical boundary is task/fidelity/hardware/algorithm/date dependent. Sycamore-style
  estimates evolve with classical algorithms; use dated matched criteria and never a raw-qubit frontier.
- **Choosing guide:** This is the most developer-useful close: input circuit/state/noise, desired output/accuracy,
  entanglement/non-Clifford structure, memory/compute, available hardware and validation. Provide a decision table and
  cross-check two methods where feasible.
- **Reader entertainment: 4/5.** Classical techniques puncture simplistic quantum-hardness stories and offer hands-on
  performance puzzles. The original MPS/DMRG-heavy middle may feel specialist; the delivered method-choice arc sounds
  more useful if numerics are retained.
- **Unit completion:** Lines 561–580 inspected in full, including all 15 planned sections, every delivered replacement,
  method assumptions/scaling/errors, removed-topic risk, frontier governance, and divider.

##### Part X / Chapter 25 — NISQ and Early Fault-Tolerant Era (lines 581–591)

- **Part title:** “Practice and Era” is vague and grammatically uneven. “Current Practice and Transitional Systems” would

  plateaus, reproducibility, error mitigation, scaling and best classical comparator. Do not use NISQ availability as

- **§25.5:** Progress cannot be one line chart: raw qubits/fidelity/QV/XEB/logical suppression/application success are
  incomparable. Use dated metric definitions and uncertainty, show benchmark gaming/selection risk and prioritize

  measurement, decoder/control, magic/resource overhead and an application-level error budget. “Early FTQC” should not be

- **Temporal snapshot:** The prior archive draft used June 2026; this original plan is dated May 2026 in its reconciliation

- **Reader entertainment: 4/5.** A candid progress-versus-definition chapter can be gripping and epistemically useful.

##### Chapter 26 — Practical Access and Hands-On Work (lines 592–608)

- **Placement:** Hands-on access arriving after 25 chapters is far too late for developer engagement. Establish a
  simulator-first runnable path in early chapters; use Chapter 26 for production experiment practice and hardware
  variability rather than the first execution.
- **§26.1:** Simulators and hardware answer different questions. Compare ideal/noisy/model-limited simulation, exact versus
  shots, structure/scaling, reproducibility, queue/cost, drift, unknown errors and validation; real hardware is not
  automatically ground truth for an ideal algorithm.
- **§26.2:** IBM/AWS/Azure/other is a cloud-provider list that ages and risks endorsement. Use dated official docs, access/
  region/cost/credential/privacy terms and a provider-neutral job abstraction; include local/emulator and direct lab
  access conceptually.
- **Provider taxonomy:** AWS/Azure are aggregators exposing multiple backends, while IBM is also a hardware/provider
  ecosystem; categories are asymmetric. “Other Platforms” is unhelpful and will hide meaningful alternatives. Generate a
  dated appendix rather than canonical prose.
- **§26.3:** Choose an SDK by learning goal, language, simulator, IR/standards, hardware support, maintenance/governance,
  license, docs, testing and lock-in—not popularity. Recommend one book-tested baseline with pinned version and explain
  portability limits.
- **§26.4:** Hardware target selection needs gate set/connectivity, qubit calibration, queue/cost, required shots/depth,
  dynamic features, reproducibility and data/security constraints. “First target” should often be a small simulator,
  followed by the simplest device matched to learning outcome.
- **§26.5:** Experiment design should specify hypothesis, circuit ensemble, baseline/control, preregistered metric, sample/
  shot allocation, randomized ordering, calibration snapshots, seeds, uncertainty/multiple comparisons and stopping rule.
  Avoid post-hoc cherry-picking best device/run.
- **§26.6:** Record code/commit, environment/lockfile, SDK/backend/version, transpilation seed/config, circuit and QASM/IR,
  calibration/time/job IDs, raw counts, metadata, analysis script and costs. Hardware drift means exact repeatability may
  be impossible; aim for provenance and statistical reproducibility.
- **§26.7:** “Without drowning” is empathetic. Teach claim→assumption→access model→metric→baseline→evidence→limitations,
  distinguish preprint/peer review/vendor report, inspect appendices/resource estimates, and reproduce toy cases. Include
  literature-search/update methods and citation hygiene.
- **Missing safety/operations:** Credentials/secrets, terms/licensing, data export/privacy, budget limits, job cancellation,
  accessibility and responsible use belong in practical access. Avoid instructions that depend on live paid services
  without fallback.
- **Example inventory:** The current repo contains five tracked example programs while README says four; this chapter’s
  hands-on catalog must be generated from tests/manifest to prevent similar drift.
- **Reader entertainment: 4.5/5.** Real jobs, noisy outcomes and paper detective work can be highly engaging. Provider

##### Part XI / Chapter 27 — Cryptography and Security (lines 609–619)

- **Staleness:** Reconciliation says delivered Chapter 27 adds hash functions, NIST PQC timeline, harvest-now-decrypt-
  later and BB84/E91/B92/decoy states. This six-section plan is incomplete and all standards/threat timelines require a
  dated legal/organizational context.
- **§27.1:** Shor factors integers in polynomial quantum time under fault-tolerant resource assumptions; RSA impact depends
  on modulus size, algorithm/circuit implementation, logical/physical errors and migration. Do not say RSA is currently
  broken by existing quantum hardware.
- **§27.2:** Shor’s discrete-log algorithm threatens ECC as well as finite-field DH/DSA. ECC may require fewer logical
  resources than RSA at comparable classical security but exact comparisons are evolving; cite dated resource estimates
  and distinguish signatures/key agreement.
- **§27.3:** Grover gives ideal black-box square-root search, effectively reducing brute-force security exponents under
  large coherent/depth/oracle costs and parallelization tradeoffs. Symmetric ciphers/hashes are not simply “key length
  halved”; circuit cost, preimage/collision distinctions and quantum query models matter.
- **§27.4:** PQC is classical cryptography designed against quantum/classical attacks, distinct from QKD. Official NIST
  sources verified in this review that FIPS 203/204/205 were finalized 13 August 2024, FIPS 206/FN-DSA remained in
  development, and HQC was selected in March 2025; use individual standards and an explicit access date, not a timeless
  algorithm list.
- **Migration:** Cover crypto inventory/agility, protocols/certificates/PKI, hybrid transition, interoperability,
  implementation side channels, performance, long-lived data and standards/compliance schedules. “Quantum resistant” is
  confidence under current cryptanalysis, not proof.
- **§27.5:** QKD establishes keys using quantum plus authenticated classical channels under protocol/device assumptions;
  it does not replace encryption/authentication or secure endpoints. Include sifting, parameter estimation, reconciliation,
  privacy amplification, finite-key/composable security and practical sources/detectors/side channels.
- **Protocol expansion:** BB84/E91/B92/decoy-state concepts differ: E91 links entanglement/Bell, B92 uses two nonorthogonal
  states, decoy states address photon-number-splitting in weak-pulse implementations. Do not list them as interchangeable
  “quantum-safe” products.
- **§27.6:** “Realistic timelines” is impossible as a confident forecast. Use scenario/risk management: data confidentiality
  lifetime + migration lead time + uncertain cryptanalytic machine arrival, with dated authoritative guidance and no
  vendor roadmaps as evidence.
- **Harvest-now risk:** Explain adversary collection now/decryption later, which data/signatures are affected, and why
  migration urgency can precede a machine. Avoid fear rhetoric or universal claim that all encrypted traffic is stored.
- **Security breadth:** Add authentication, signatures, protocol downgrade, random-number generation, side-channel/
  implementation security, supply chain and quantum-system attack surfaces. Algorithm replacement alone is not a security
  programme.
- **High-stakes sourcing:** This chapter needs primary standards/agencies and peer-reviewed cryptanalysis, explicit
  jurisdiction/snapshot, threat-model language and professional-security disclaimer; factual currency should be tested in
  CI or scheduled review.
- **Reader entertainment: 4/5.** Concrete “what breaks/what changes” stakes are compelling. Timeline speculation and
  acronym catalogs can become alarmist; migration case studies provide more useful tension.
- **Unit completion:** Lines 609–619 inspected in full, including Part/Chapter headings, all six planned sections,
  delivered additions, algorithm/resource/security qualifications, current NIST facts already externally verified, and
  threat-governance requirements.

##### Chapter 28 — Scientific Computing and Physical Simulation (lines 620–630)

- **Taxonomy overlap:** Materials, many-body and condensed matter overlap; Hamiltonian simulation is a method used across
  them; high-energy and lattice gauge likewise overlap; PDEs are mathematical problems across domains. Organize by task/
  encoding/observable or use domain case studies with a common evidence template.
- **§28.1:** Quantum chemistry needs basis/second quantization/mapping, Hamiltonian construction, state preparation,
  ground/excited/dynamics observables, precision and classical coupled-cluster/DMRG/Monte Carlo baselines. “Chemical
  accuracy” and end-to-end resource estimates must be defined, not marketed.
- **§28.2:** Materials applications span electronic structure, dynamics, defects/catalysis and models. Identify a task
  where quantum algorithm/input/output is specified; broad “materials science” claims often outrun evidence.
- **§§28.3–28.4:** Many-body/condensed-matter quantum systems may be classically tractable under low entanglement,
  integrability, sign-free Monte Carlo or finite dimensions. Explain sign problem, phases/dynamics and observable
  extraction; quantum advantage is structure-dependent.
- **§28.5:** This duplicates Chapter 16; here apply simulation algorithms/resource estimates to a physical model rather
  than reteach Trotter/LCU/QSP. Include state preparation and measurement, often dominant, plus verification against small
  classical regimes.
- **§§28.6–28.7:** High-energy/lattice-gauge simulation has gauge constraints, fermions/bosons, truncation, real-time
  dynamics and continuum/extrapolation demands. Early demonstrations are not proof of scale advantage; separate analog/
  digital proposals and date status.
- **§28.8:** Quantum linear/PDE algorithms often output encoded states or functionals under sparsity/oracle/condition/
  smoothness/precision assumptions; data loading and full-field readout can remove exponential claims. Compare best
  classical solvers/preconditioners and dequantized methods.
- **Evidence ladder:** For each domain distinguish mathematical speedup, fault-tolerant resource estimate, small hardware
  demonstration, validated scientific result and practical utility. Do not treat a proposed algorithm as an application.
- **Validation:** Scientific use needs uncertainty budgets, model/discretization error, quantum algorithm error, hardware
  error, observable statistics and classical/experimental validation. A quantum answer is not self-verifying.
- **Missing classical/HPC integration:** State preparation from classical data, Hamiltonian generation, optimization,
  decoding/analysis and HPC workflows dominate end to end. Include hybrid workflow and total time/energy/cost.
- **Reader entertainment: 4/5.** Simulating nature closes Feynman’s historical loop and offers real scientific stakes.
  Eight broad fields read like grant categories; one molecule/lattice problem carried end to end would be more gripping.
- **Unit completion:** Lines 620–630 inspected in full, including all eight sections, taxonomy overlaps, per-domain
  assumptions/baselines, evidence/validation ladder, missing workflow integration, and chapter role.

##### Chapter 29 — Optimization, Finance, and Industrial Use Cases (lines 631–639)

- **Bundling:** Optimization methods, finance risk calculations, logistics and scheduling are not one coherent technical
  domain; logistics/scheduling are optimization applications, while sampling/Monte Carlo crosses finance/science. Center
  problem formulations/evidence and use industry cases only as scoped examples.
- **§29.1:** Define exact/approximate objective, constraint encoding, NP-hardness versus typical instances, QAOA/annealing/
  Grover alternatives, mapping/penalty/qubit overhead and fair classical heuristics. Quantum mechanics does not make
  NP-complete problems generically polynomial.
- **§29.2:** Sampling may target quantum distributions, Gibbs/posterior distributions or Monte Carlo estimates with very
  different hardness/access/output. Specify metric/accuracy and classical sampler; “sampling advantage” can be hard to
  verify.
- **§29.3:** Amplitude estimation offers ideal quadratic query scaling for expected values under coherent state/oracle
  access; loading financial distributions/payoffs, precision, fault-tolerant depth and readout determine end-to-end value.
  Financial advice/high-stakes claims require dated sources and must not imply investment returns.
- **§29.4:** Vehicle routing/network/logistics mappings can require many binary variables, constraints and dense
  connectivity; toy instances do not beat mature operations-research solvers. Include data integration, reoptimization,
  robustness and solution feasibility.
- **§29.5:** Scheduling overlaps logistics and combinatorial optimization. Compare mixed-integer programming, CP-SAT,
  heuristics/metaheuristics and hybrid decomposition on identical instances/hardware/time budgets; avoid cherry-picked
  synthetic cases.
- **§29.6:** This realism section should govern every prior claim rather than clean up afterward. Use evidence ladder:
  proposal→simulation→hardware demo→matched classical comparison→scaling/resource estimate→operational deployment→
  audited value, with uncertainty and negative results.
- **Near-term temporal risk:** “Near-term” is moving and historically overpromised. State literature cutoff, target
  hardware/error model, data scale and no known practical advantage where applicable; distinguish research exploration
  from procurement recommendation.
- **Industrial evidence:** Vendor/customer case studies may be marketing, unpublished or confounded. Prefer peer-reviewed
  reproducible data, disclose affiliations, define KPIs and total cost/energy/latency, and include classical improvement
  over the same period.
- **Responsible scope:** Finance/logistics decisions affect people and resources; discuss robustness, explainability,
  privacy/security, regulatory/audit requirements and harm from infeasible/stochastic outputs.
- **Reader entertainment: 3.5/5.** Real operational constraints can be compelling. A familiar use-case list risks brochure
  tone; forensic teardown of one claimed advantage would be far more engaging and trustworthy.
- **Unit completion:** Lines 631–639 inspected in full, including all six sections, domain/taxonomy overlap, algorithm/
  baseline assumptions, high-stakes/evidence safeguards, near-term governance, and chapter narrative.

##### Chapter 30 — Quantum Machine Learning (lines 640–649)

- **Staleness/taxonomy:** Reconciliation says delivered Chapter 30 is reorganized around three QML categories, so this
  model-name list is obsolete. A taxonomy by data/model/task—classical data on quantum models, quantum data learning,
  quantum-enhanced subroutines—better exposes access/output assumptions.
- **§30.1:** “Quantum neural network” is not one architecture and neural terminology can be metaphorical. Define
  parameterized circuit, input encoding, observable/loss, optimizer and hypothesis class; expressivity does not imply
  trainability/generalization or neural equivalence.
- **§30.2:** Quantum SVM claims often rely on QRAM/state access, kernel estimation precision and favorable matrix
  condition/rank. Classical kernel approximation/dequantization and full training/inference cost are mandatory
  comparators.
- **§30.3:** Quantum GANs mix quantum/classical generator/discriminator/data variants; training stability, measurement
  cost, mode collapse, verification and any advantage are unsettled. This fashionable label may deserve demotion unless
  tied to quantum-data tasks.
- **§30.4:** Hybrid loops are implementation patterns, not evidence of benefit. Include gradient estimators/assumptions,
  shot noise, barren plateaus, latency/batching, optimizer bias, reproducibility and hardware drift.
- **§30.5:** Data loading should come first and distinguish basis/amplitude/angle/kernel encodings, preparation circuit/
  QRAM assumptions and repeated-copy cost. Exponential vector encoding is not useful if loading/readout is exponential.
- **§30.6:** Classify claimed speedup as query/sample/training/inference/end-to-end, proved versus conditional, quantum
  versus classical data and accuracy/generalization. Match input models and include dequantized/quantum-inspired classical
  methods; no cherry-picked baseline.
- **§30.7:** Limitations should not be a disclaimer after hype; integrate them per method. Cover trainability, noise,
  scaling, data/output, verification, classical compute, reproducibility, benchmark leakage and absence of demonstrated
  practical advantage for many classical-data tasks.
- **Missing learning science:** Generalization bounds, data splits, hyperparameter search, baselines/ablations, confidence,
  multiple trials, fairness/privacy/security and model evaluation matter more than circuit novelty. Tiny datasets and
  parameter-matched classical models need careful treatment.
- **Promising distinction:** Learning properties of quantum states/processes can avoid classical data-loading bottlenecks
  and may be the most native use case. Ensure delivered three-category structure highlights this rather than centering
  quantum versions of familiar ML brands.
- **Temporal/evidence policy:** QML is fast-moving and hype-prone; date literature, disclose preprint/vendor status, require
  code/data/resources and separate theoretical possibility from hardware demonstration and downstream utility.
- **Reader entertainment: 3.5/5.** ML familiarity offers an easy hook, but an acronym parade feels trend-chasing. A
  controlled experiment where a flashy claim disappears under a fair baseline could be unusually instructive and fun.
- **Unit completion:** Lines 640–649 inspected in full, including all seven sections, delivered taxonomy change, each model/

##### Chapter 31 — Sensing, Metrology, and Tomography (lines 650–660)

- **Scope coherence:** Sensing/metrology estimate physical parameters; tomography reconstructs states/processes and was
  reportedly moved/expanded in Chapter 11. “Computational tomography” is ambiguous. Clarify why these belong in
  Applications and prevent duplication with measurement theory.
- **§31.1:** Define sensor/probe interaction, resource count, estimator and classical/quantum baseline. Quantum enhancement
  may use squeezing/entanglement/coherence but losses/decoherence/control/readout can remove advantage; include real
  technologies only with dated evidence.
- **§31.2:** Distinguish standard quantum limit versus Heisenberg scaling under equal resources, local/global estimation,
  Fisher/quantum Fisher information and Cramér–Rao conditions. Count time, particles, energy, passes and prior knowledge
  consistently; “Heisenberg limit” is not universal.
- **§31.3:** State tomography needs informationally complete measurements, many copies, physical reconstruction and
  uncertainty; generic \(n\)-qubit parameter/sample cost is exponential. Compare full, compressed, local and shadow
  methods by assumptions/output rather than promise free scaling.
- **§31.4:** Process tomography scales worse and conflates SPAM unless methods address it; define channel representation,
  complete positivity/trace preservation, gate-set tomography and randomized alternatives. A reconstructed model is only
  as valid as stationarity/Markov assumptions.
- **§31.5:** “Computational tomography” could mean medical CT, computational imaging, classical reconstruction algorithms
  or quantum algorithms for tomography. Rename and define exact relationship; without this, the heading is fog rather
  than cross-disciplinary insight.
- **§31.6:** “Cross-disciplinary connections” is empty scope. Select concrete links—signal processing/system
  identification, inverse problems, experimental design, control/benchmarking—and state which concepts transfer and where
  quantum measurement changes assumptions.
- **Chapter 11 duplication:** Delivered Chapter 11 reportedly includes tomography/classical shadows. Keep formal methods
  there; Chapter 31 should apply them to sensing/device characterization with case studies, or remove tomography from this
  title.
- **Missing practical issues:** Calibration, nuisance parameters, drift, adaptive design, Bayesian/frequentist uncertainty,
  identifiability, multiple parameters, robustness and end-to-end sensor utility are essential.
