## Second-pass review: `factcheck/part-08-noise-and-qec/19-quantum-error-correction-and-fault-tolerance.md`

### Lines 1–6 — Mirror identity, open status, and separator

- The mirror target is explicit. QEC hardware/status claims will need a dated cutoff and source revision; neither is recorded.
- “Claims identified” should say whether exhaustive. A 494-line mirror can still omit derivations, definitions, or rapidly changing experimental milestones.
- Horizontal separators improve record boundaries but add substantial vertical bulk.
- Verdict: **clear structural metadata; revision/coverage provenance missing**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 3/5.** Functional and orderly.

### Lines 8–16 — Quantum Hamming and Singleton bounds

- Quantum codes have Hamming/sphere-packing and Singleton analogues. For an ([[n,k,d]]_q) code, the quantum Singleton bound is (n-k\ge2(d-1)), while the familiar binary nondegenerate quantum Hamming bound is (2^k\sum_{j=0}^{t}3^j\binom nj\le2^n) for (t=\lfloor(d-1)/2\rfloor).
- **Important qualification:** The standard quantum Hamming counting argument directly applies to nondegenerate/pure codes because distinct correctable Pauli errors produce orthogonal subspaces. Degenerate codes require more careful statements and can evade naive sphere counting in some regimes/formulations.
- The classical sentence says the bounds “cap how many errors any code ... can correct,” which oversimplifies their different hypotheses and parameter tradeoffs. Singleton is not merely an error-sphere count.
- “Direct quantum analogs” is acceptable, but notation should distinguish binary bits (n,k) from qubits/logical qubits and general (q)-ary codes.
- Verdict: **broad claim verified; quantum Hamming bound needs its nondegeneracy caveat and both formulas should be stated**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4/5.** Counting error spheres is intuitive; the loophole of degeneracy adds an especially quantum twist.

### Lines 18–26 — Shor code date and priority

- Shor’s 1995 code is conventionally recognized as the first quantum error-correcting code capable of correcting an arbitrary single-qubit error.
- “Proposed” should link to the exact 1995 paper/version. Historical priority language benefits from “widely regarded as” if simultaneous unpublished developments are not surveyed.
- The code works by combining repetition-code protection against bit and phase flips; linearity/Pauli expansion then extends correction to arbitrary single-qubit errors.
- Do not imply it corrects an arbitrary-strength error on an unknown number of qubits; support must be confined to one physical qubit.
- Verdict: **verified at standard historical resolution**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 5/5.** Nesting two classical repetition intuitions to defeat arbitrary quantum errors is a superb conceptual reveal.

### Lines 28–36 — Shor code ([[9,1,3]]) parameters

- Eight independent stabilizer generators on nine qubits leave a (2^{9-8}=2)-dimensional codespace, hence one logical qubit.
- Weight-three representatives (\bar X=Z_1Z_4Z_7) and (\bar Z=X_1X_2X_3) are consistent with the usual Shor-code basis despite the visually counterintuitive physical-Pauli swap.
- Exhibiting weight-three logical operators gives (d\le3); proving correction/detection of every weight-one Pauli (and absence of weight-one/two nontrivial normalizer elements) supplies (d\ge3). The mirror comment should state both directions.
- Logical representatives are nonunique up to stabilizers, so apparent differences across sources are not contradictions.
- Verdict: **verified; make the two-sided distance proof explicit**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4.5/5.** The physical (Z) string acting as logical (X) nicely demonstrates encoded observables’ nonlocality.

### Lines 38–45 — Steane-code attribution and capability

- Andrew Steane’s seven-qubit CSS code appeared in the 1995/1996 publication period and has parameters ([[7,1,3]]), so it corrects any single-qubit error.
- Resolve whether 1996 denotes journal publication and whether an earlier preprint/submission should be mentioned; dates should follow the project’s consistent convention.
- Its construction from the classical ([7,4,3]) Hamming code/dual is the key intellectual attribution, not merely a smaller qubit count.
- “Corrects any single-qubit error” again means an arbitrary operator supported on one qubit under ideal syndrome/recovery.
- Verdict: **verified; normalize preprint/publication chronology**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4.5/5.** A perfect classical Hamming structure reappearing as a symmetric quantum code is highly satisfying.

### Lines 46–56 — Steane code from the classical ([7,4,3]) Hamming code

- The binary ([7,4,3]) Hamming code contains its ([7,3,4]) dual, enabling the symmetric CSS construction with one encoded qubit.
- The parity-check matrix rows generate the dual code and become (X)- and (Z)-type stabilizers; showing this makes “borrows directly” exact.
- Classical distance three alone is not the full quantum-distance proof; identify which classical codewords lie outside the dual and yield weight-three logical operators.
- Matrix row/column ordering changes stabilizer labels but not the code; avoid treating one Hamming matrix convention as canonical.
- Verdict: **verified by the cited construction**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4.5/5.** Seeing one parity-check matrix do double duty for bit and phase errors is elegant.

### Lines 58–66 — Transversal Clifford gates on the Steane code

- The Steane code supports transversal implementations of logical Clifford generators: bitwise CNOT between blocks, bitwise Hadamard, and an appropriate transversal phase gate (often (S) or (S^\dagger) depending on logical/stabilizer convention), plus Pauli operations.
- “The entire Clifford group is transversal” can be misread as every Clifford being one depth-one tensor product. More precisely, the Clifford group is generated by gates each admitting transversal implementations; a general Clifford is a circuit of such transversal layers.
- Logical phases and whether physical (S^{\otimes7}) realizes logical (S) or (S^\dagger) should be explicitly verified against the manuscript’s codeword convention.
- Transversal CNOT acts between corresponding qubits of code blocks and requires architecture/routing assumptions not captured by abstract transversality.
- Verdict: **verified at generator level; revise “entire group” wording and check the phase convention**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4.5/5.** A whole fault-tolerant gate family emerging from bitwise operations is one of Steane code’s chief attractions.

### Lines 68–76 — Dual-containing classical code to symmetric CSS code

- For a binary linear ([n,k,d]) code (C) with (C^\perp\subseteq C), the symmetric CSS construction has (n-2\dim C^\perp=2k-n) logical qubits.
- Its quantum distance is (d_Q=\min\{\operatorname{wt}(c):c\in C\setminus C^\perp\}) in the symmetric case (with the analogous (X/Z) minimum), not automatically exactly the classical (d); it is at least (d) when the classical minimum-weight words relevant to (C) set that bound, and degeneracy/purity needs care.
- The condition is “dual-containing,” not “self-dual-containing”; a genuinely self-dual binary code has (k=n/2) and this symmetric construction would encode zero logical qubits unless terminology is carefully distinguished.
- State binary/Euclidean dual assumptions; nonbinary and Hermitian-dual CSS variants differ.
- Verdict: **dimension formula verified; terminology and (d_Q) definition need precision**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4/5.** The simple (2k-n) count makes the classical-to-quantum conversion gratifyingly concrete.

### Lines 78–86 — Attribution of the stabilizer formalism

- Daniel Gottesman’s papers/thesis systematized the stabilizer formalism and its use for codes, Clifford operations, and fault tolerance; the attribution is standard.
- Historical context also includes Calderbank–Shor–Steane/additive-code and earlier Pauli-group ideas. “Due to” is acceptable for systematization but should not erase the closely parallel code-formalism lineage.
- Cite the exact Gottesman thesis/paper and year rather than leave the well-known attribution TBD.
- Explain the payoff immediately: exponentially large codespaces become binary symplectic linear algebra.
- Verdict: **verified at normal historical resolution; broaden lineage if making a priority claim**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4/5.** Turning Pauli commutation into binary linear algebra is a powerful simplification.

### Lines 88–96 — Gottesman–Knill simulation complexity

- Clifford evolution of stabilizer states and computational-basis/Pauli measurements is classically simulable by tableau updates; the Gottesman–Knill claim is correct.
- A maximal stabilizer group specifies a state, while a smaller group specifies a codespace (C(S)). The anchor’s “stabilizer states (states in (C(S)) for some (S))” is too broad because every state lies in the codespace of a trivial stabilizer.
- In standard tableaux, Clifford gate updates can be (O(n)) or better per local gate, while a measurement update may cost (O(n^2)); (O(n^2)) per operation is therefore a safe coarse upper bound, not a tight uniform cost.
- Aaronson–Gottesman provides improved canonical simulation algorithms; later bit-packed implementations change practical scaling.
- Specify the output task as sampling/updating stabilizers, not emitting a full amplitude vector.
- Verdict: **simulability and safe bound verified; fix the definition of stabilizer state and label bound as coarse**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4.5/5.** Highly entangled states remaining tractable through generators is a crucial conceptual surprise.

### Lines 98–105 — Unrotated planar surface-code parameters

- A common unrotated planar distance-(d) surface-code patch has (d^2+(d-1)^2=2d^2-2d+1) data qubits, encodes one logical qubit, and has distance (d).
- The rotated planar patch instead uses (d^2) data qubits. **Internal contradiction:** the heading/anchor say unrotated, while the comment says the parameters follow from “rotated-surface-code geometry.” Correct the comment or source section.
- The restriction to odd (d) is common in layouts/experiments but the parameter formula is not intrinsically meaningful only for odd distances; explain why the manuscript imposes odd (d).
- Clarify whether the count includes data qubits only or also syndrome ancillas. Hardware-qubit totals roughly double under common measurement layouts.

### Lines 106–116 — MWPM attribution lineage

- Edmonds’s blossom algorithm is foundational for polynomial-time matching; minimum-weight perfect matching became a standard decoder for toric/surface-code syndrome defects.
- Dennis, Kitaev, Landahl, and Preskill’s 2002 work is a canonical surface-code/threshold source linking spacetime error chains to matching, but “adapted to QEC by” may overassign sole priority given earlier decoding/topological-code work.
- Separate the generic optimization algorithm, construction of a decoding graph, edge weights from a noise model, and use of matching to infer a recovery.

- Exact citations for Edmonds and Dennis et al. should replace TBD.
- Verdict: **broad attribution verified; avoid an exclusive adaptation-priority claim**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4/5.** Pairing spacetime defects by cheapest paths gives decoding a satisfying geometric/combinatorial form.

### Lines 118–126 — Claimed cubic MWPM decoding time

- A generic dense blossom implementation can have a coarse cubic complexity in the number (V) of graph vertices; if (V=O(nT)), (O((nT)^3)) is a safe naive upper-bound template.
- Here (n) is undefined. If it means physical qubits, detection events can be (O(nT)); if it means code distance, there are (O(n^2T)) syndrome locations and the exponent changes dramatically.
- Practical surface-code matching uses sparse/local graphs, precomputed weights, windowing, parallelism, and specialized implementations with much better typical scaling/latency.
- MWPM finds a minimum-weight matching under assigned edge weights, not necessarily the globally most likely **logical equivalence class**; degeneracy and correlated noise can make minimum-energy differ from maximum-probability decoding.
- Complexity must include graph construction/all-pairs path weights and streaming latency, not only blossom.
- Verdict: **coarse generic bound possible after defining (n); phrasing as the decoder’s operative complexity and “most likely” solution is misleading**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 3.5/5.** Cubic notation is abstract; decoder latency per syndrome round is the more gripping engineering constraint.

### Lines 128–136 — Union-find decoder complexity and performance

- Delfosse and Nickerson introduced a union-find decoder with near-linear/almost-linear runtime for topological codes under standard implementations/graph models.
- State the precise bound—typically involving inverse-Ackermann factors—and which stages (cluster growth, peeling) it includes.
- “Competitive with MWPM at threshold” is vague. Threshold values can be relatively close in selected phenomenological/code-capacity noise models, while subthreshold logical error rates and circuit-level performance may differ materially.
- Noise bias, erasures, boundaries, correlated faults, and weighted graphs alter relative performance. Later union-find variants should not be credited to the original paper without distinction.
- Hardware relevance also depends on constant factors, parallel architecture, memory, and worst-case latency, not asymptotics alone.
- Verdict: **attribution and near-linear scaling verified broadly; competitive-performance claim needs a named noise model and numbers**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4/5.** Growing and merging defect clusters is visually intuitive and contrasts nicely with global matching.

### Lines 138–146 — CSS construction attribution and content

- Calderbank–Shor and Steane independently/developingly established the CSS family, which combines two classical linear codes subject to a dual-orthogonality condition to correct (X)- and (Z)-type errors separately.
- “Pairs of classical linear codes” is correct but incomplete: for one common convention (C_Z^\perp\subseteq C_X), ensuring (X)- and (Z)-stabilizers commute.
- Distances (d_X,d_Z) can differ, making asymmetric CSS codes useful for biased noise; a single (d) can hide this.
- Normalize original-paper dates/priority language and then let the acronym carry the attribution.
- Verdict: **verified; include the commutation/dual-containing condition**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4.5/5.** Splitting arbitrary errors into two classical decoding problems is one of QEC’s cleanest structural ideas.

### Lines 148–156 — Surface-code historical lineage and “leading candidate” status

- Kitaev’s toric-code/topological-code work is the foundational ancestor; Bravyi–Kitaev developed planar/boundary encodings, Dennis et al. developed decoding/threshold analysis, and Fowler et al. systematized practical surface-code architectures.

- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4.5/5.** The journey from topology to manufacturable checkerboards is a strong historical arc.

### Lines 228–236 — Per-logical-operation error budget

- **Definite arithmetic contradiction:** For (N=10^{10}) independent/union-bounded failure opportunities and target total failure at most (10^{-6}), the simple requirement is (p_L\lesssim10^{-16}), not (10^{-11}).

### Lines 258–266 — Google Willow distance-3/5/7 suppression factor

- The primary *Nature* result uses Google’s 105-qubit Willow processor generation and culminates in a 101-qubit distance-7 surface-code memory; device capacity and qubits used in the largest code should be distinguished.
- It reports (\Lambda=2.14\pm0.02) suppression when increasing code distance by **two** (3→5 or 5→7), not per unit increase in (d). The anchor’s “per increase in (d)” is ambiguous and can imply a factor per (d\mapsto d+1).
- The distance-7 logical error was about 0.143% per error-correction cycle in the reported setting, useful context for how far it remained from large-algorithm targets.
- Suppression depends on decoder, basis, rounds, leakage handling, and error metric; it is not an intrinsic property of the chip alone.
- The paper was received/preprinted in 2024 and published in the late-2024/2025 issue cycle; use consistent chronology.
- Verdict: **verified after specifying factor per distance increment of two and 101-qubit largest patch**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 5/5.** Errors falling as the code grows is the threshold theorem becoming visible in hardware.

### Lines 268–275 — Relationship to Google’s earlier distance-3/5 result and “first” status

- Google’s earlier distance-3/5 experiment reported a modest logical-error reduction when scaling from distance 3 to 5, but the later distance-7 result supplied a much clearer consistent exponential trend and was framed as below-threshold surface-code memory.
- Saying the 2024 work “extends below-threshold scaling already reported” risks retroactively overstating the earlier evidence. Describe the earlier modest suppression and the later stronger sequence separately.
- “First below-threshold demonstration” requires scope: first repeated surface-code distance scaling through (d=7), first error-corrected memory of a particular architecture, or first logical break-even are different priority claims, with ions, bosonic codes, and other experiments supplying competing milestones.
- The current primary paper calls its result below-threshold and beyond break-even; reproduce its exact claim rather than a broader universal “first.”
- Verdict: **historical sequence broadly right; priority/scope and strength of the 2023 result need cautious wording**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4.5/5.** Showing the tentative 3→5 hint mature into a 3→5→7 trend creates a strong scientific narrative.

### Lines 276–286 — Surface-code overhead of 1,000–10,000 physical qubits per logical qubit

- Thousand-scale physical qubits per logical patch is plausible for cryptographic logical-error targets under surface-code distances in the 20s–60s, especially after syndrome ancillas/routing are included.
- A tenfold range without physical error, threshold ratio, decoder, logical-failure target, code geometry, operation type, and factory allocation is not a fact so much as a scenario envelope.
- “Per logical qubit” can mean memory patch, active data block with routing space, or whole-computer physical qubits divided by algorithmic logical qubits. Factory-dominated machines make the last ratio workload-dependent.
- “Cryptographically useful workloads” includes RSA factoring, elliptic-curve attacks, and symmetric-key search with very different depth/T rates and parallelization.
- Source the endpoints to representative published architectures and present assumptions in a table.
- Verdict: **plausible synthesis range, not independently verified or portable without scenario definitions**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4/5.** The overhead range conveys scale, but decomposing it into patch, routing, and factory portions would be far more revealing.

### Lines 288–296 — Claimed 20%–30% qubit savings from better decoders

- Better noise-aware decoders can lower logical error at fixed (d,p), allowing a smaller code distance for a target (p_L) and hence roughly quadratic patch-area savings.
- A 20%–30% physical-qubit reduction is plausible when an improved suppression factor permits dropping distance by several units, but it is not a universal property of neural, belief-propagation, or parallel-MWPM decoders.
- Parallelization primarily improves latency; it does not automatically improve decoding accuracy. Neural and BP methods also vary widely and can perform worse off-distribution.
- Include decoder training cost, hardware/classical latency, memory, calibration drift, and correlated-noise robustness; a more accurate decoder that misses the real-time deadline is not a free qubit saving.
- **Anchor formatting defect:** “better decoders**” has unmatched bold markup.
- Verdict: **mechanism sound; numerical savings and grouped decoder attribution need a specific matched study**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4/5.** Software buying back physical qubits is a compelling hardware–algorithm co-design lesson.

### Lines 298–306 — Google/IBM two-qubit errors near (10^{-3})

- Selected superconducting two-qubit couplings/gates have reached approximately (10^{-3}) error in 2024–2025-era benchmarking, and IBM officially described Heron rates “approaching 0.1%.”
- The claim overstates fleet/device-wide performance. IBM’s own 2025 system material reports layered error around (3\times10^{-3}) with best two-qubit error (10^{-3}), while later Heron revisions have subsets of couplings below (10^{-3}).
- Available Willow specifications show mean simultaneous CZ error closer to (3.3\times10^{-3}) for one device (with another gate/device around (1.4\times10^{-3})); “Google reaching (10^{-3})” may describe a best pair or rounded frontier, not average QEC hardware.
- RB/Pauli error, CZ infidelity excluding leakage/stray interaction, simultaneous layered error, and circuit error are different. State the exact metric.
- Vendor names do not substitute for processor revision, gate, sample size, and distribution across couplers.
- Verdict: **verified only for selected best couplings/metrics; misleading as broad Google/IBM device performance**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4/5.** The thousandth-error frontier matters, but distributions across a chip tell the real scaling story.

### Lines 308–316 — IBM bivariate-bicycle code’s tenfold overhead claim

- IBM-associated 2024 work introduced/analyzed bivariate-bicycle codes including ([[144,12,12]]), and the primary *Nature* abstract explicitly claims roughly a tenfold encoding-overhead reduction relative to surface-code memory at comparable regimes.
- “Encoding rate” is (k/n=12/144=1/12) for data qubits in that code; the comparison to twelve separate distance-12 surface patches gives an order-12 rate improvement under a data-qubit count, consistent with “~10×.”
- The fair physical comparison must include check ancillas and the BB code’s degree-six/nonlocal connectivity, routing/couplers, syndrome circuit, decoder, and target logical error. The paper’s threshold/performance model supplies more than bare ([[n,k,d]]) arithmetic.
- Surface-code distances are often chosen odd in common rotated patches, so “surface code at distance 12” should explain the comparison convention rather than imply one canonical patch.
- This was a theoretical/architectural result, not a 2024 hardware implementation of the full code.
- Verdict: **headline reduction verified in the cited model; call it encoding overhead, not a universal installed-qubit saving**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4.5/5.** Twelve logical qubits in one 144-qubit block makes the qLDPC promise wonderfully concrete.

### Lines 318–326 — Bundled RSA-2048 physical-qubit, cycle, and runtime estimate

- The range does not match one clearly identified published scenario. Gidney–Ekerå 2019/2021 gives about 20 million noisy qubits and eight hours under specified hardware assumptions; Gidney 2025 gives below one million and below one week with a different time–space tradeoff.
- “(10^6) to (10^7) qubits, (10^{10}) cycles, around a day” may interpolate incompatible estimates rather than quote a real design point.
- At a 1 μs surface-code cycle, (10^{10}) cycles are about 2.8 hours, not one day; classical reaction latency/serial measurement depth can change wall time, but then the conversion must be shown.
- Physical error (p=10^{-3}) is insufficient to reproduce the estimate: connectivity, code-cycle duration, reaction time, code distances, decoder, logical algorithm, factories, and target failure probability are essential.
- The comment that this estimate has been “stable ... for nearly a decade” is contradicted by the project’s own 20× qubit-count change between 2019 and 2025.
- Verdict: **unsupported synthetic estimate with internal cycle/time tension; replace by separate dated published design points**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4/5.** A resource table across years would vividly show progress; a blended number hides it.

### Lines 328–336 — Concatenated-code suppression recurrence

- **Definite algebraic error:** If (p_{j+1}=C p_j^2) and (p_0=p), then (p_1=Cp^2), (p_2=C^3p^4), and generally (p_\ell=C^{2^\ell-1}p^{2^\ell}=(Cp)^{2^\ell}/C).
- The anchor’s final (p^{2^\ell}/C^{2^\ell-1}) puts (C) in the denominator and contradicts its own first two levels.
- Doubly exponential suppression in concatenation level holds only below threshold (Cp<1) in this toy malignant-pair recurrence and under appropriate local stochastic/independence assumptions.
- A distance-three gadget fails from pairs only if one-fault tolerance is established; the constant (C) counts malignant pairs and changes by location/gadget/noise model.
- Polylogarithmic overhead should be derived separately: each level expands a location by a constant factor while (\ell=O(\log\log(L/\epsilon))), yielding polylog overhead under threshold-theorem assumptions.
- Verdict: **concept correct, general formula wrong by inversion of the (C) exponent**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 5/5.** Doubly exponential suppression is thrilling, and the recurrence is simple enough that readers can verify every exponent themselves.

### Lines 338–346 — Surface-code threshold under realistic noise

- Around 1% is associated with selected balanced circuit-level stochastic depolarizing models and matched decoding, but there is no single “standard” model implementation.
- Correlated errors, persistent leakage, coherent crosstalk, biased measurement/idles, and decoder mismatch can lower effective thresholds or create logical-error floors.
- “Sometimes by 2× or more” is plausible for particular studies but requires exact correlation/leakage model and decoder. It cannot be generalized as the realism penalty.
- Some realistic structure can **raise** a tailored threshold: known erasures, strong bias with adapted codes, or correlated-noise-aware decoding may help. “More realistic” is not synonymous with “strictly worse.”
- Threshold may cease to be a useful scalar under long-range/time-correlated faults; logical scaling curves are more informative.
- Verdict: **qualitative warning verified; universal twofold degradation unsupported and one-directional framing misleading**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4/5.** The idealized 1% number meeting messy hardware is a useful reality check.

### Lines 348–356 — Historical claim about crossing below threshold in 2023–2024

- Surface-code experiments in 2023 showed a modest improvement from distance 3 to 5, and Google’s 2024 result gave a much clearer 3/5/7 below-threshold scaling sequence.
- “Crossed the line decisively” should be scoped to repeated circuit-level surface-code memory scaling. Earlier bosonic, repetition, trapped-ion, error-detection, and break-even logical-memory experiments reached different threshold-like milestones.
- “Three decades” is reasonable when counted from mid-1990s threshold/QEC theory, but identify the starting theorem/milestone rather than use dramatic round-number history.
- Below-threshold **memory** is not yet below-threshold universal logical computation with state preparation, lattice surgery/gates, magic states, real-time decoding, and long algorithms.
- Priority language should cite multiple platforms and define the criterion (logical error decreases with (d), beats constituent physical memory, or full fault-tolerant gadget).
- Verdict: **broad surface-code timeline defensible; “decisively” and universal practical threshold crossing need narrower scope**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4.5/5.** A thirty-year theorem-to-hardware arc is powerful when milestone definitions remain honest.

### Lines 358–366 — Eastin–Knill theorem

- Eastin and Knill proved that a finite-dimensional quantum code capable of correcting the relevant local errors cannot possess a universal set of transversal logical gates.
- “Non-trivial code space” alone is too weak a hypothesis; state the error-detection/correction and subsystem/transversality assumptions from the theorem.
- The theorem forbids universality **within one fixed transversal gate set/code**, not universal fault tolerance altogether. Magic-state injection, code switching, gauge fixing, pieceable FT, and nontransversal gadgets evade the restriction.
- Approximate/covariant codes obey quantitative tradeoffs rather than the exact theorem in identical form; finite-dimensional and exact-correction assumptions matter.
- Define transversal as each physical subsystem in a block interacting with at most the corresponding subsystem of another block, preventing one fault from spreading within a block.
- Verdict: **core no-go theorem verified; hypotheses and escape routes should be explicit**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 5/5.** A theorem forcing every architecture to pay for universality is a perfect setup for magic states.

### Lines 368–376 — Origin and code behind 15-to-1 distillation

- Bravyi and Kitaev’s 2005 magic-state-distillation work contains the canonical 15-to-1 protocol.
- The protocol is based on the ([[15,1,3]]) punctured quantum Reed–Muller/triorthogonal structure, **not the seven-qubit Steane code**. The later comment’s “Steane-code error-detection post-selection” is a definite factual error.
- “Introduced” is fair for this canonical protocol, while earlier state purification/distillation ideas provide broader context.
- Specify input state/noise twirling, Clifford-operation assumptions, acceptance/postselection, and output T-type convention.
- Verdict: **attribution verified; associated-code description must be corrected from Steane to 15-qubit Reed–Muller**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4.5/5.** Fifteen noisy resources collapsing to one much cleaner non-Clifford state is an intuitively dramatic factory process.

### Lines 378–386 — (35p^3+O(p^4)) 15-to-1 output error

- Under independent identically distributed, appropriately twirled input magic-state errors and ideal Clifford/check operations, the 15-to-1 protocol suppresses leading output error to (35p^3+O(p^4)).
- The coefficient counts undetected weight-three error patterns that induce a logical fault; showing that combinatorial origin makes the result memorable.
- Output error should be conditioned on acceptance. Acceptance probability is below one and contributes to expected input/factory cost.
- Correlated input errors, imperfect Clifford operations, measurement faults, and logical errors in an encoded factory add terms that can dominate the ideal cubic expression.
- Again, the derivation must reference the 15-qubit Reed–Muller code, not Steane.
- Verdict: **verified under the stated iid-twirled ideal-operation model; source comment contains a code error**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4.5/5.** Cubic suppression with a visible coefficient gives readers a satisfying quantitative payoff.

### Lines 388–396 — Claimed physical-qubit-cycle cost of one T gate at (d=17)

- “Physical-qubit-cycles” should mean the integral of simultaneously occupied physical qubits over surface-code rounds. The range cannot be checked without factory layout, protocol, number of distillation levels, logical patch convention, injection error, target output error, acceptance, and throughput.
- A distance-17 patch alone contains hundreds of physical qubits, and a 15-to-1 factory occupies multiple patches for multiple rounds; (5{,}000)–(20{,}000) physical-qubit-cycles appears potentially too small unless a nonstandard normalized unit is intended.
- A factory produces a stream of states; amortized cost per accepted state differs from latency and footprint×cycle volume.
- Code distances may be heterogeneous across factory levels; setting every component to (d=17) is rarely optimal.
- Cite an explicit AutoCCZ/lattice-surgery/cultivation factory table and reproduce its assumptions/unit.
- Verdict: **unverified and dimensionally suspicious; exact resource design required**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4/5.** A factory bill per T gate is valuable, but only a transparent floorplan/timeline makes the number meaningful.

### Lines 398–405 — T-to-Clifford cost ratio

- Non-Clifford T operations often dominate fault-tolerant resources because they require injection/distillation/cultivation, while many Clifford operations are transversal, lattice-surgical, tracked in software, or otherwise cheaper.
- There is no universal 50×–200× ratio. A Pauli-frame update is nearly free, a logical CNOT can occupy patches for (O(d)) rounds, and a factory’s amortized T cost depends on throughput/utilization and target fidelity.
- Code families with transversal T, bosonic native gates, code switching, catalysis, or cultivation change the ratio radically.
- Compare one named resource metric—spacetime volume, T-depth latency, physical qubits, or energy—not an undefined “cost.”
- The text anchor says “tens to hundreds,” while the comment invents the more specific 50–200 range; remove stale precision unless sourced.
- Verdict: **qualitative dominance verified in common surface-code architectures; numerical ratio unsupported/design-specific**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4/5.** The asymmetric price list explains why compilers obsess over T gates, but a concrete architecture is indispensable.

### Lines 406–416 — Magic-state cultivation/block-code overhead reductions

- Higher-throughput block-code distillation and newer magic-state cultivation protocols can substantially reduce non-Clifford factory overhead relative to older uniform-distance 15-to-1 baselines.
- “Magic state cultivation introduced 2024” needs version chronology: the key work circulated in the 2024 period, while publication/revisions may carry later dates. Cite exact authors/title.
- A 5–10× reduction is baseline- and target-dependent: physical error, target output fidelity, patch layout, throughput, acceptance, correlated errors, and whether comparing footprint, volume, or runtime all matter.
- The heading mentions “T-state recycling,” but the anchor mentions block codes and cultivation, not recycling. This is an internal scope mismatch.
- Cultivation is not simply a better distillation polynomial; it grows/detects a logical magic state through code expansion and has different failure/restart/resource accounting.
- Verdict: **qualitative improvement credible; date, mechanism grouping, and 5–10× figure require exact resource tables**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4.5/5.** Growing a magic state while growing its code is a fresh and vivid alternative to a factory assembly line.

### Lines 418–426 — Lattice-surgery origin

- Horsman, Fowler, Devitt, and Van Meter’s *Surface code quantum computing by lattice surgery* is the canonical source, with preprint/publication chronology around 2011/2012.
- Lattice surgery performs joint logical parity measurements by merging and splitting patch boundaries, reducing the need for transversal braiding/motion.
- If the manuscript says “introduced in 2012,” use journal publication year and optionally note earlier preprint circulation.
- Later optimized surgery/layout protocols should be credited separately.
- Verdict: **verified; normalize preprint/publication date**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4.5/5.** Sewing patches together to measure logical parity is excellent spatial intuition.

### Lines 428–436 — Litinski’s *A Game of Surface Codes*

- Daniel Litinski’s *A Game of Surface Codes: Large-Scale Quantum Computing with Lattice Surgery* appeared in *Quantum* in 2019 and is a standard architecture/resource reference.
- The work’s tile/game abstractions are a planning model with defined time/space units, not a literal hardware blueprint. Preserve its assumptions when importing resource ratios.
- Exact journal/volume/article number and DOI can replace TBD.
- The quotation marks/title casing should be standardized with bibliography style.
- Verdict: **verified**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 5/5.** The board-game abstraction is unusually effective at making enormous fault-tolerant layouts approachable.

### Lines 438–446 — Solovay–Kitaev and gridsynth as a Clifford+T compilation recipe

- **Markup defect:** The anchor begins “Compile**” with an unmatched closing bold marker.
- Solovay–Kitaev establishes generic polylogarithmic approximation over suitable finite universal gate sets, but is rarely the preferred practical Clifford+T synthesis method for rotations.
- Gridsynth/Ross–Selinger-style methods target efficient approximation of single-qubit (Z)-rotations (and related synthesis), not compilation of an arbitrary algorithm by themselves.
- Separate high-level decomposition, reversible arithmetic, arbitrary rotation synthesis, Clifford optimization, T-count/T-depth reduction, logical layout, and QEC scheduling.
- The earlier Chapter 14 error incorrectly used Solovay–Kitaev to justify linear-log synthesis; ensure §8.11 does not repeat that confusion.
- Verdict: **directionally valid as two synthesis references; misleading as one interchangeable end-to-end compiler step**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 3.5/5.** Compilation becomes interesting when readers see successive IR/resource transformations, not a slash-separated tool name.

### Lines 448–456 — Misclassified fault-tolerant software stacks

- **Category defect:** Stim is a stabilizer/QEC circuit simulator and detector-error-model generator; PyMatching is a minimum-weight-matching decoder library. Neither is an end-to-end fault-tolerant compiler.
- Stim was created by Craig Gidney at Google, but PyMatching is an open-source project led by Oscar Higgott and collaborators; current documentation thanks Google Quantum AI for supporting v2, which does not make it simply “Google’s tool.”
- “IBM Qiskit FT toolbox” is not a sufficiently exact current product/package name. Identify repository/module/version and actual capabilities.
- OpenSurgery and “LSL” require full names, links, maintainers, publication dates, and current activity. LSL may mean a lattice-surgery language/library, but the acronym is not self-verifying.
- A useful taxonomy would separate circuit synthesis, logical compilation, layout/surgery scheduling, QEC simulation, decoding, and resource estimation.
- Verdict: **substantially inaccurate grouping and maintainership; rebuild the tool list from current primary documentation**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 3/5.** Tool lists are useful only when readers know what job each tool actually performs.

### Lines 458–466 — Microsoft Resource Estimator and alleged Quantinuum “tket FT”

- Microsoft’s Quantum Resource Estimator is current and officially documented as an open-source component of the Python Quantum Development Kit, accepting several input representations and configurable hardware/QEC models.
- Product naming has evolved from “Azure Quantum Resource Estimator” toward “Microsoft Quantum resource estimator”; date/version the name used in the manuscript.
- Targeted official search did not locate a Quantinuum product formally named “tket FT.” TKET/pytket is a real Quantinuum compiler ecosystem, but a fault-tolerant resource-estimation package needs an exact repository/product citation.
- A compiler that reports logical gates is not automatically an end-to-end physical resource estimator.
- State whether tools are maintained, research prototypes, cloud services, or installable libraries, and list supported codes/hardware assumptions.
- Verdict: **Microsoft tool verified; Quantinuum tool name/function unverified and likely misnamed**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 3.5/5.** Letting readers vary physical assumptions interactively can be engaging; vendor-name inventory alone is not.

### Lines 468–476 — Repeated “typical” RSA-2048 estimate

- This repeats the unsupported blended estimate from lines 318–326. Known published design points span about 20 million qubits/eight hours (2019/2021) and below one million/below one week (2025), under similar headline physical assumptions but different architectures.
- Calling (10^6)–(10^7) qubits and day–week “typical output” excludes or blurs those very reference points and suggests unwarranted consensus across tools.
- (p=10^{-3}) alone cannot determine output; cycle/reaction time, connectivity, algorithm, code/factory choice, target failure, and decoder are required.
- A resource estimator produces scenario-dependent results, not a canonical oracle answer. Show at least two named configurations.
- Verdict: **unsupported and duplicative; replace with dated scenario table**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 3.5/5.** Repetition of a broad range dulls the quantitative narrative; contrasting real estimates would restore it.

### Lines 478–486 — Willow logical lifetime and suppression claims

- The Willow distance-7 experiment used a 101-qubit patch on a 105-qubit processor and reported logical error suppression factor (2.14\pm0.02) per distance increase of two.
- From (d=3) to (d=7), two such steps yield roughly (2.14^2\approx4.6), **not an order of magnitude**. The anchor’s suppression magnitude is wrong unless it refers to a different baseline/metric.
- The paper reports the distance-7 memory beyond break-even, exceeding its best physical-qubit lifetime/error benchmark by roughly (2.4\pm0.3), not merely a context-free comparison to “underlying physical (T_1).” State the exact physical-memory comparator.
- **False priority overreach:** It was not the first encoded qubit ever to outlive raw hardware; bosonic and other logical-memory break-even demonstrations predate it. Scope any “first” to the paper’s claimed scalable below-threshold surface-code setting.
- Device-wide capacity and patch qubits should again be distinguished.
- Verdict: **below-threshold/break-even result verified; order-of-magnitude and universal-first claims are wrong**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 5/5.** A logical memory beating its best constituent is historic enough without inflating the factor or priority.

### Lines 488–494 — “Comparable” IBM, Quantinuum, and academic demonstrations

- IBM, Quantinuum, and academic teams have published significant logical-memory, fault-tolerant logical-gate, code-switching, and QEC experiments across superconducting and trapped-ion platforms.
- “Comparable distance-scaling” is too vague and may be false apples-to-apples. Quantinuum’s transversal/logical-gate demonstrations on small CSS/color-code blocks are not the same experiment as surface-code (d=3,5,7) scaling; IBM’s 2024 BB-code result was primarily theoretical/architectural rather than a full hardware distance series.
- Name representative experiments and compare code, distance, qubit count, rounds, physical/logical error metric, decoder, and whether memory or gates were tested.
- “Several academic groups” is not a citation and makes comprehensive verification impossible.
- Avoid vendor league tables unless metrics are normalized.
- Verdict: **broad activity verified; claimed comparability and distance-scaling survey remain unsubstantiated**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4/5.** Multiple architectures reaching distinct logical milestones is exciting when presented as a map rather than a horse race.

### Second-pass file verdict — `factcheck/part-08-noise-and-qec/19-quantum-error-correction-and-fault-tolerance.md`

- **Coverage:** Reviewed all 494 lines and every extracted record sequentially, using current official/primary sources for IBM roadmaps/tools, BB codes, and Google Willow.
- **Strong mathematical defects:** The concatenation recurrence incorrectly divides by (C^{2^\ell-1}) instead of multiplying; the RSA union-bound example misses its stated global failure target by five orders of magnitude; and 15-to-1 distillation is wrongly tied to the Steane code.
- **Strong empirical defects:** The repeated RSA resource range blends incompatible design points; Willow’s (d=3\to7) improvement is ~4.6× rather than an order of magnitude; and the “first encoded qubit to outlive raw hardware” claim is historically false without narrow scope.
- **Tooling defects:** Simulators/decoders are mislabeled as compilers, PyMatching is misowned, several tool names are unverifiable, and gridsynth/Solovay–Kitaev are presented as interchangeable end-to-end compilation.
- **Recurring qualification need:** Thresholds, decoder savings, physical-qubit ratios, magic-state costs, and hardware error rates must identify code/noise/decoder/resource metrics. “Typical,” “leading,” and “comparable” repeatedly outrun evidence.
- **Editorial opportunity:** Preserve a complete dependency chain: algorithm locations and failure budget → target logical error per code cycle/gadget → decoder/noise-specific distance → patch/factory layout → physical qubits, cycles, and wall time. Most quantitative contradictions arise when a link is skipped.
- **Overall reader entertainment/readability: 4.6/5.** QEC is full of beautiful ideas—encoded observables, decoding geometry, threshold scaling, surgery, and magic factories. Auditable arithmetic would make this one of the book’s strongest chapters.

## Second-pass review: `factcheck/part-09-hardware-and-software/20-quantum-hardware-platforms.md`

### Lines 1–4 — Mirror identity and hardware-snapshot provenance

- The target chapter and extraction month are explicit. Hardware values and vendor designs change quickly, so a literature cutoff, exact manuscript revision, and “representative versus record” policy are essential and absent.
- Every range should name platform subtype, sample/device scale, metric definition, and source date; “typical” otherwise becomes unmaintainable.
- Verdict: **clear structure, inadequate snapshot methodology for perishable hardware facts**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 3/5.** Functional; a compact “data as of” box would add trust.

### Lines 6–13 — Typical transmon anharmonicity

- For a conventional transmon, (\alpha=\omega_{12}-\omega_{01}\approx-E_C/\hbar), and (alpha/2\pi) around (-200) to (-300) MHz is a common design range.
- Sign convention matters: some engineering tables quote the positive magnitude (E_C/h\) or (|\alpha|/2\pi), while the anchor uses negative anharmonicity.
- Tunable/fixed transmons, capacitively shunted flux qubits, fluxonium, and high-anharmonicity variants occupy different ranges; do not generalize to all superconducting qubits.
- “Typically” should be supported with representative processor parameter tables rather than Koch 2007 alone, which establishes theory more than a 2026 empirical distribution.
- Verdict: **verified as a representative conventional-transmon range with explicit sign convention**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4/5.** The small nonuniformity that makes a nonlinear oscillator addressable as a qubit is excellent hardware intuition.

### Lines 14–21 — Dilution-refrigerator temperature

- Superconducting processors commonly mount near a dilution refrigerator mixing chamber with base/operating temperatures of order 10 mK, often roughly 10–20 mK under low load.
- Base temperature, stage thermometer, chip temperature, and effective qubit temperature are distinct; wiring/control dissipation raises temperature during operation.
- Cooling power near 10 mK is limited and scales poorly with heat load, making the number an engineering constraint rather than merely environmental trivia.
- Some cryogenic electronics reside at higher stages, and not all superconducting quantum hardware uses identical thermal architecture.
- Verdict: **verified as an order-of-magnitude mixing-chamber temperature; distinguish physical/effective temperatures**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4/5.** Ten millikelvin is naturally dramatic, especially when tied to the tiny cooling-power budget.

### Lines 22–29 — Superconducting single-qubit pulse duration

- Microwave-driven transmon single-qubit gates in the 20–50 ns range are common, often using Gaussian/DRAG-like envelopes.
- This is not a hard platform range: faster gates face leakage/bandwidth/distortion, while slower pulses may improve spectral selectivity but accumulate decoherence.
- Virtual (Z) gates are frame updates with effectively zero pulse duration, so “single-qubit gates are microwave pulses” has an important exception.
- Error-per-gate and duration must be quoted together with amplitude calibration, simultaneous operation, and primitive-versus-Clifford convention.
- Vendor/device-specific primary tables should source the range.
- Verdict: **verified as representative (X/Y)-rotation timing; exclude virtual Z and avoid universality**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4/5.** Nanosecond control against microsecond lifetimes gives readers an immediate quality-factor ratio.

### Lines 30–37 — Superconducting two-qubit gate duration

- Tunable-coupler CZ/iSWAP/parametric gates can operate in the tens-of-nanoseconds to ~100 ns regime on selected systems.
- **Range/platform mismatch:** IBM-style cross-resonance/ECR gates have often been substantially longer—roughly hundreds of nanoseconds depending on generation—so 30–100 ns should not be presented as covering cross-resonance generally.
- Gate duration definitions may include echoed pulses, single-qubit wrappers, buffer time, coupler ramps, and dynamical-decoupling inserts; compare full scheduled instruction lengths.
- Faster is not automatically better because leakage, residual ZZ, spectator error, calibration sensitivity, and pulse bandwidth trade against decoherence.
- Split the table by gate family/vendor generation rather than forcing one range.
- Verdict: **plausible for fast tunable/parametric gates; incorrect or incomplete for cross-resonance as grouped**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4/5.** The speed–leakage/crosstalk tradeoff is more useful than a single stopwatch number.

### Lines 38–45 — Vendor attribution for tunable couplers and parametric drives

- “Tunable coupler” and “parametric drive” are not synonyms. A tunable coupler can be flux-pulsed adiabatically/nonadiabatically or parametrically modulated; parametric gates can also arise through modulating a qubit/coupler frequency.
- Google has prominently used tunable couplers/flux-activated CZ-family operations, but each processor generation’s pulse scheme should be named rather than labeled generically parametric.
- Rigetti and IQM architectures likewise require exact device-generation sources; vendor portfolios evolve and may use fixed/tunable couplers or resonator-mediated schemes.
- The parenthetical grammar suggests all three use one identical mechanism, which is unlikely and technologically uninformative.
- Verdict: **under-specified and potentially inaccurate vendor grouping; replace with a gate-family comparison table sourced per processor**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 3.5/5.** Vendor names add little unless readers learn how the coupling is actually switched.

### Lines 46–53 — 2026 superconducting coherence snapshot

- Device-wide medians near 100 μs and selected conventional-transmon (T_1/T_2) values in the stated hundreds-of-microseconds ranges are plausible, but the claim needs actual processor distributions.
- “Best-in-class devices” mixes isolated materials test structures, cavity devices, two-qubit prototypes, and full processor fleets. Define eligible architecture/scale.
- (T_2) again requires Ramsey versus echo/DD labeling, and medians must state time window because coherence drifts.
- Individual outliers beyond a range make “best-in-class 100–400” logically awkward: if outliers are valid devices, the range is not actually the best class.
- Reusing Chapter 18’s unsourced range does not independently verify it. Build one shared dated table instead of circular cross-reference.
- Verdict: **plausible representative summary, not verified as a 2026 device-wide/best-in-class dataset**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 3.5/5.** Distribution plots across a chip would tell a much richer story than champion ranges.

### Lines 54–61 — 2026 superconducting single-qubit fidelity

- Around 99.9% is common on mature superconducting processors, but “leading” devices often report 99.95%–99.99% class single-qubit RB values; one current primary prototype reports 99.98% simultaneous fidelity.
- Error per Clifford, primitive pulse, simultaneous RB, isolated RB, and average process fidelity are not interchangeable.
- Median across a large chip and best pair/qubit should be separate columns; 99.9% can be conservative as a fleet number and stale as a record number.
- Leakage and coherent/worst-case error are not captured by one average fidelity.
- Verdict: **reasonable broad operational figure, too low/vague as a 2026 leading-platform benchmark**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 3.5/5.** The number becomes interesting when converted into expected error opportunities per algorithm layer.

### Lines 62–69 — 2026 superconducting two-qubit fidelity

- Around 99.5% is plausible for strong contemporary processor-average/layered two-qubit performance, while selected pairs/prototypes have crossed 99.9%.
- “Occasionally” needs a dated count/source. Current official data show subsets of couplings below (10^{-3}) error and prototypes around 99.93%, but not necessarily full-chip simultaneous operation at that level.
- Gate type, leakage inclusion, spectator/crosstalk, RB protocol, and simultaneous layer size determine comparability.
- A best pair does not establish scalable yield; report distribution/median/worst-tail and calibration duration.
- Verdict: **broad split between ~99.5% fleet and >99.9% selected demonstrations is plausible; precise benchmark table required**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4/5.** The difference between champion pair and chip-wide yield is an important scaling tension.

### Lines 70–77 — Superconducting readout fidelity

- 98–99% single-shot assignment fidelity is common on many superconducting processors, while best current small devices can exceed 99.9% under selected conditions.
- Define average of (P(0|0)) and (P(1|1)), leakage handling, integration time, active reset, simultaneous multiplexed readout, and SPAM correction.
- Per-qubit isolated readout can be much better than simultaneous full-chip readout due to crosstalk/frequency collisions.
- Fidelity alone omits latency, QND character, reset, repeated-measurement consistency, and discrimination of leakage states—all important for QEC.
- Verdict: **verified as a common range, not a complete or best-in-class 2026 metric**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4/5.** Measurement’s speed–fidelity–QND tradeoff is more illuminating than assignment fidelity alone.

### Lines 78–85 — Rigetti Ankaa and IQM Garnet size characterization

- Rigetti’s Ankaa family and IQM’s Garnet are real superconducting processor/product names.
- The comment’s “a few tens of qubits” is not uniformly accurate: Ankaa systems are in the ~80-qubit class, while Garnet has been marketed in a smaller tens-of-qubits class. Verify exact current revisions/counts.
- Product accessibility, installed system versus cloud QPU, and generation suffix (Ankaa-2/3, etc.) should be stated; vendor lines change.
- Calling both “small” is relative and unhelpful unless contrasted to application/connectivity/yield.
- Verdict: **names verified broadly; shared size characterization is stale/inaccurate**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 3/5.** Product names without architecture or performance context read like a catalogue.

### Lines 86–93 — IBM Heron and Condor families

- Heron and Condor are genuine IBM processor families/generations. Heron prioritizes higher-quality modular-scale processors; Condor demonstrated 1,121 physical qubits.
- The comment’s “several hundred to approaching 1000” is wrong/stale for these names: Heron revisions are roughly 100–200-qubit class, while Condor exceeded 1,000 rather than approached it.
- Qubit count alone does not rank capability; IBM’s roadmap moved emphasis toward quality, modular coupling, and error-corrected logical operations after Condor.
- Distinguish announced, built, installed, and generally available systems.
- Verdict: **family names verified; implied count range needs correction and exact revision table**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 3.5/5.** The pivot from raw qubit count to quality/modularity is the interesting story.

### Lines 94–101 — Typical transmon (E_J/E_C)

- Conventional transmons operate in the (E_J/E_C\gg1) regime, and ratios around 50–100 are common, exponentially suppressing charge dispersion while retaining usable anharmonicity.
- Fixed versus flux-tunable devices have an effective (E_J) that varies with flux; quote maximum/sweet-spot ratio and operating range.
- Larger ratio reduces charge sensitivity but also reduces relative anharmonicity, creating a speed/leakage tradeoff.
- Koch et al. supplies the theoretical scaling; contemporary processor parameter tables should support “typically.”
- Verdict: **verified as a representative conventional-transmon design range**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4.5/5.** One dimensionless ratio controlling protection versus controllability is excellent design intuition.

### Lines 102–109 — Exponential suppression of transmon charge dispersion

- In the large-(E_J/E_C) transmon regime, charge dispersion has leading exponential dependence (e^{-\sqrt{8E_J/E_C}}), multiplied by level- and ratio-dependent algebraic prefactors.
- The anchor says generic “level shifts” scale exactly as the exponential; more precisely, the **charge dispersion amplitude/sensitivity to offset charge** has that leading asymptotic scaling.
- Charge noise dominated Cooper-pair-box dephasing near charge-sensitive operating points, though “dominant” should be historically/device scoped.
- **Markup defect:** Nested straight quotation marks around “Cooper-pair box” break the outer anchor quotation.
- Show the cost: increasing (E_J/E_C) also weakens relative anharmonicity, so exponential protection is purchased with leakage/control constraints.
- Verdict: **leading asymptotic verified; restore prefactor/sensitivity wording and repair quotation markup**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 5/5.** Exponential noise protection from a circuit-design ratio is one of the transmon’s most satisfying engineering insights.

### Lines 110–117 — IBM heavy-hex topology

- IBM’s heavy-hex connectivity graph places degree-three vertices and degree-two edge qubits in a hexagon-derived pattern, so maximum degree three is correct for the standard family.
- “Hexagonal lattice with extra qubits on each edge” is intuitive but should be paired with a diagram; graph-theoretic heavy-hex is not simply a honeycomb plus arbitrary subdivisions.
- IBM standardized heavily on heavy-hex across Falcon/Eagle/Heron/Condor-era processors to reduce frequency collisions/crosstalk, but future modular/qLDPC architectures introduce additional couplers and should not be forced under a timeless claim.
- Boundary sites can have lower degree; “degree 2 or 3 at every site” may fail at truncated boundaries or disabled couplers.
- Verdict: **verified for the named heavy-hex generations; scope in time/device and soften boundary universality**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4/5.** Sacrificing connectivity to improve calibratability presents a clear architecture tradeoff.

### Lines 118–125 — Google Sycamore/Willow connectivity

- Sycamore and Willow use two-dimensional rectangular/square-grid-like layouts with tunable couplers and interior connectivity up to four neighbors.
- “Degree 4” is not true for every qubit: boundary/corner sites have fewer neighbors, disabled couplers/qubits alter realized graphs, and Willow’s average degree is below four.
- Say “maximum/interior degree four” and distinguish fabricated processor graph from the active graph used in an experiment.
- Square-lattice compatibility is central to surface-code checks, while tunable coupling reduces residual interactions at the cost of control complexity.
- Verdict: **broad topology verified; correct universal degree wording**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4/5.** The direct fit between chip graph and surface-code checkerboard is a strong design narrative.

### Lines 126–133 — Rigetti and IQM connectivity generalization

- Rigetti’s older Aspen family used a distinctive octagonal connectivity/tiling, but newer Ankaa generations changed architecture/connectivity. “Rigetti uses” incorrectly turns one product family into a permanent vendor property.
- “IQM uses a square lattice with star-shaped subgraphs” is too unclear to verify: square grid and star connectivity describe different graph levels unless stars are resonator-mediated cells embedded in a lattice.
- Give an adjacency diagram and exact processor (Aspen-M, Ankaa, Garnet, etc.), number of qubits, maximum/average degree, and coupler type.
- Vendor topology is perishable and should be a dated table, not prose brand identity.
- **Markup defect:** Inner quotes around “Aspen” break the anchor’s outer straight quotation.
- Verdict: **Aspen historical fragment plausible; current vendor-wide Rigetti/IQM statement is stale/underdefined**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 3.5/5.** Connectivity pictures would be much more memorable than topology nicknames.

### Lines 134–141 — Fluxonium transition-frequency range

- Heavy fluxonium operated near half-flux sweet spots often has a low (omega_{01}/2\pi) in the hundreds-of-megahertz range, making 100–500 MHz representative for that design regime.
- Fluxonium is a family, not one frequency class: parameter choices and bias can move transitions substantially, and newer variants can operate in GHz ranges.
- Low frequency reduces dielectric-loss phase space and changes thermal population/control/readout challenges; the number should be tied to operating point.
- Cite contemporary devices in addition to the original Manucharyan paper.
- Verdict: **verified as a common heavy-fluxonium sweet-spot range; not universal**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4/5.** A qubit an order of magnitude lower in frequency than transmons naturally signals a different protection strategy.

### Lines 142–149 — Millisecond fluxonium (T_1)

- Millisecond-scale relaxation/coherence has been reported for carefully engineered individual fluxonium qubits, so the existence claim is sound.
- State exact (T_1), operating frequency/flux bias, device material/package, temperature, and whether the reported millisecond figure is median, maximum, or fitted over one interval.
- Individual-qubit lifetime does not imply processor-wide gate performance; readout, thermal population at low frequency, coupler loss, and fabrication yield may reduce system behavior.
- The institutional list in the comment is not evidence; cite the primary experiments and avoid corporate affiliation drift.
- Verdict: **verified as an existence result; source concrete devices and avoid scaling inference**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4.5/5.** Crossing a millisecond in a superconducting circuit is a striking payoff for fluxonium’s protection.

### Lines 150–157 — Fluxonium superinductor junction count

- Fluxonium’s original/some common superinductors use arrays of many Josephson junctions, often tens to hundreds, so “~100” is a reasonable schematic scale.
- Junction count is design-specific; array junction parameters, parasitic capacitance, self-resonances, phase slips, and total inductance matter more than one round number.
- Granular-aluminum/high-kinetic-inductance implementations can realize superinductance without a literal hundred-junction chain, so the statement should not define all fluxonium.
- Give a representative circuit and range, not one universal count.
- Verdict: **representative but not universal engineering detail**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4/5.** A hundred ordinary junctions acting as one extraordinary inductor is an appealing fabrication image.

### Lines 158–165 — Fluxonium processor scale and institutional examples

- Fluxonium multi-qubit processors have historically remained much smaller than leading transmon fleets, with demonstrations in single-digit/low-tens scales, so the broad comparison is plausible.
- “Processor” should require integrated controllable/readable multi-qubit operation, not merely fabricated qubits or a two-qubit gate prototype.
- Maryland/Yale groups have clear fluxonium research records; Atlantic Quantum and “others” need exact public processor demonstrations and dates, especially after corporate/team changes.
- A 2026 claim should list largest peer-reviewed array, operational qubits, connectivity, and simultaneous fidelities rather than an open-ended institutional roster.
- Verdict: **scale trend plausible; named-group and current-maximum claims unverified**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 3.5/5.** The quality-versus-scale tension is the meaningful comparison, not lab names.

### Lines 166–173 — Trapped-ion species list and vendor mapping

- (^{171}\mathrm{Yb}^+) and (^{40}\mathrm{Ca}^+) are widely used trapped-ion species; barium isotopes including (^{137}\mathrm{Ba}^+) are also studied/used in selected architectures.
- The list is not representative enough for “typically”: (^{43}\mathrm{Ca}^+), (^{88}\mathrm{Sr}^+), (^{9}\mathrm{Be}^+), and mixed-species coolant/data arrangements are important.
- **Likely vendor-mapping defect:** Quantinuum’s H-series is associated with ytterbium data ions (and barium in mixed-species roles in some architecture descriptions), not simply “Quantinuum uses Ca.” Calcium is prominent in other companies/labs such as Oxford Ionics/AQT configurations depending isotope.
- Different isotopes offer optical versus hyperfine qubits, clock transitions, cooling/readout wavelengths, and metastable lifetimes; the isotope superscript is not decorative.
- Replace the sentence with a dated vendor/species/encoding/coolant table from primary documentation.
- Verdict: **individual species plausible; “typical” selection and comment’s vendor mapping are incomplete/likely wrong**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4/5.** Species choice becomes engaging when tied to lasers, clock transitions, and cooling roles.

### Lines 174–181 — Trapped-ion clock-qubit coherence

- Hyperfine clock-state qubits can maintain coherence for seconds to minutes with magnetic-field-insensitive transitions, stable local oscillators, shielding, and dynamical decoupling.
- (T_2) must identify Ramsey/echo/DD sequence, ion count, oscillator reference, and whether phase is tracked relative to the same local oscillator.
- Ground-hyperfine population decay is usually far slower than observed phase coherence, so technical oscillator/field noise commonly limits (T_2); “not intrinsic decay” is a useful but device-specific summary.
- Laser/microwave phase noise, differential Stark shifts, collisions, and motional/control scheduling can matter in a running processor even when memory experiments last minutes.
- Verdict: **verified as best-case clock-qubit behavior; experimental protocol and processor relevance need specificity**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4.5/5.** Minutes of memory beside microsecond gates creates an impressive—but not complete—platform advantage.

### Lines 182–189 — Trapped-ion single-qubit gate duration

- Stimulated-Raman or microwave single-qubit rotations in roughly 1–10 μs are common on trapped-ion processors.
- Gate time depends on encoding, laser detuning/power, spontaneous-scattering budget, beam addressing, pulse shaping, crosstalk, and whether virtual/frame phase changes are included.
- Microwave/global operations and ultrafast-pulse demonstrations occupy different regimes; “typical” should be device/gate scoped.
- Duration alone is not throughput: ion transport, cooling, calibration, measurement, and classical latency can dominate a circuit schedule.
- Verdict: **verified as a representative addressed Raman-rotation range; not universal**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4/5.** The slower gate is meaningful only beside ions’ much longer memory and all-to-all connectivity.

### Lines 190–197 — Mølmer–Sørensen entangling-gate duration

- Around 100 μs is a reasonable representative scale for laser-driven Mølmer–Sørensen entangling gates, with demonstrations spanning tens to hundreds of microseconds or beyond.
- Time depends on motional-mode spectrum, detuning, ion separation/chain length, pulse shaping, laser power, mode cooling, and desired crosstalk/fidelity.
- Vendor public instruction duration may include transport, recooling, basis rotations, and scheduling differently from the physical interaction pulse.
- Avoid one exact-looking “~100 μs” as a cross-vendor constant; provide a range/table.
- Verdict: **representative but device- and compilation-dependent**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4/5.** Using shared motion as a temporary quantum bus is more memorable than the bare duration.

### Lines 198–205 — Trapped-ion single-qubit fidelity

- 99.99%-class single-qubit fidelities have been demonstrated on leading trapped-ion systems, making the headline plausible.
- Best small-system records, processor-wide averages, simultaneous/addressed gates, and long-term calibration stability should be separated.
- Error per primitive versus Clifford, SPAM correction, coherent drift, and leakage outside the qubit manifold affect comparisons.
- A platform-wide “around” value requires current primary benchmarking with confidence intervals, not vendor marketing alone.
- Verdict: **verified as an achievable leading level; insufficient as a normalized current-platform statistic**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 3.5/5.** Four nines matters when translated into how many sequential operations/calibration drift it tolerates.

### Lines 206–213 — Trapped-ion two-qubit fidelity and alleged >99.95% record

- 99.9%-class entangling fidelities are established in small/leading trapped-ion systems.
- Values above 99.95% have been reported in highly optimized small-ion demonstrations, but the record claim is perishable and must name species, ion count, gate protocol, benchmarking method, and publication date.
- Bell-state fidelity, process tomography, parity contrast, and randomized-benchmarking entangling fidelity are not equivalent record metrics.
- Scaling to long chains, many pairs, transport, and simultaneous operation generally lowers yield/stability relative to a best pair.
- Verdict: **broad benchmark plausible; “best published” requires exact current source and comparable metric**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4/5.** The small-chain record versus processor-wide challenge captures the platform’s central scaling tension.

### Lines 214–221 — MS-family native gates at IonQ and Quantinuum

- IonQ exposes an XX-type entangler derived from Mølmer–Sørensen interactions as a native operation in its hardware/compiler stack.
- Quantinuum exposes a (ZZ\)-phase/ZZMax-style native entangler in its software interface; it is implemented through trapped-ion spin–motion interactions and is locally equivalent/related to the MS family, but should not be called the exact same generator without basis/convention explanation.
- Public native gate sets can change or be compiler abstractions over calibrated physical pulses; cite the current API/device generation.
- Verify §8.12’s wording to prevent circular propagation of a vendor simplification.
- Verdict: **IonQ statement broadly verified; Quantinuum needs basis/native-interface nuance**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4/5.** One physical interaction appearing as different software-native generators is a useful hardware/software lesson.

### Lines 222–229 — Quantinuum/IonQ device names and qubit counts

- Quantinuum H-series, IonQ Forte, and IonQ Tempo are real product/device lines, but they do not share one static 30–60-qubit specification.
- Quantinuum H2 expanded to a mid-50s physical-qubit scale, while H1 is smaller. IonQ often advertises algorithmic qubits (#AQ), a performance metric, alongside physical trapped-ion capacity; these must not be treated as the same count.
- Forte/Tempo variants, availability dates, enterprise versus research systems, and enabled qubits change over time.
- “Currently operate” requires an as-of date and evidence of operational/customer availability rather than announced targets.
- Verdict: **names valid; range conflates generations and likely physical versus algorithmic qubit metrics**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 3.5/5.** A count is less informative than the distinction between resident ions, usable qubits, and algorithmic capability.

### Lines 230–237 — Oxford Ionics 100–256-ion scaling roadmap

- Oxford Ionics’ May 2025 company roadmap explicitly described 16–64-qubit “Foundation” systems and targeted 256+ physical-qubit “Enterprise-grade” systems; this supports 256 as a stated plan, not as a demonstrated per-trap operating capacity.
- “100–256 ions per trap” changes three things at once: ions versus qubits, one trap/QPU versus a modular system, and demonstrated hardware versus a sales roadmap. The cited company material instead describes tiled unit cells, junction transport, and a QCCD architecture.
- Since IonQ completed its acquisition of Oxford Ionics in September 2025, company identity and roadmap ownership are time-sensitive in a 2026 book.
- “And others” is not auditable. Name each project, architecture, target, date, and whether the number is trapped ions, physical qubits, simultaneously controlled qubits, or ordered product capacity.

- Verdict: **256+ is a verified company roadmap target; the quoted per-trap range and generalized present-tense implication are unsupported**.

### Lines 238–245 — Quantinuum H2 QCCD architecture

- Quantinuum’s current H2 documentation explicitly calls H2 a transport-based QCCD processor with a linear racetrack geometry, multiple gate zones, storage regions, and ion shuttling; the substantive claim is verified.
- The anchor is truncated at “uses the first,” so the fact-check record does not preserve the actual proposition. This is a ledger-quality defect even though the comment reconstructs it.
- “The first” would be risky if the manuscript means the first QCCD device: earlier Quantinuum/Honeywell H-series systems also used QCCD principles. If it means “the first architecture discussed,” rewrite the anchor.
- QCCD should be expanded once and explained as dynamic ion transport among specialized regions; “all-to-all” at the logical/compiler level is mediated by transport, not simultaneous direct interaction among every pair.
- Primary source: Quantinuum’s [H2 hardware guide](https://docs.quantinuum.com/systems/user_guide/hardware_user_guide/h2.html).
- Verdict: **verified architecture; malformed anchor and any historical “first” implication require correction**.
