- The base and coefficient depend on entanglement, Hamiltonian, phase, orientation, boundary conditions, and target error. A product state on a wide cylinder needs χ=1; the geometric cut count alone is not a lower bound of (2^w).
- The snake-path explanation is pedagogically useful, but note that long-range couplings in the 1D ordering also increase operator/MPO and sweep costs.
- Verdict: **correct generic exponential-width warning; χ∼2^w is only a heuristic worst-case-style shorthand**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4.5/5.** The cylinder-to-snake picture makes the dimensional curse tangible.

### Lines 225–231 — DMRG said to work for cylinder widths w≲8

- There is no stable universal width cutoff. Width eight has historically been challenging and common in demanding frustrated models, but modern studies may reach wider cylinders in favourable models, geometries, symmetries, and accuracy regimes; other sign-frustrated or highly entangled systems can become unreliable earlier.
- “Works” needs an observable and convergence standard. Energy may be well converged while competing phases, stripe periods, topological sectors, or correlation lengths remain bond-dimension sensitive.
- The cited application phrase “enough to address frustrated-magnet phase questions” should distinguish addressing from decisively resolving; finite-width extrapolation and metastability can dominate conclusions.
- Replace the hard threshold with “often widths of order 6–12 in demanding two-dimensional studies, highly problem-dependent,” backed by two representative benchmarks, or omit numbers.
- Verdict: **historically recognizable rule of thumb, too absolute and already method-/problem-dependent**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4/5.** A width number orients readers, but the scientific drama lies in why eight can still leave phases ambiguous.

### Lines 232–238 — Worst-case #P-hardness of two-dimensional PEPS contraction

- Schuch, Wolf, Verstraete, and Cirac prove that classical simulation/contraction tasks for general PEPS are #P-complete; the worst-case-hardness message is correct and stronger than merely “exponentially hard,” assuming standard complexity conjectures.
- “It is the partition function of a classical statistical-mechanics problem” is a useful correspondence but should not sound like every PEPS contraction literally has that single interpretation. General tensor-network contractions encompass partition functions, amplitudes, norms, and expectation values.
- #P-hard does not itself prove every instance takes exponential time, nor does it forbid efficient approximate contraction for structured/gapped/low-χ networks. Say “no general polynomial exact algorithm is expected.”
- Cite the precise #P-complete result and define whether norm/expectation contraction or arbitrary network contraction is meant.
- Verdict: **verified worst-case result, with standard complexity and instance-structure caveats**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4.5/5.** The method escaping one exponential only to meet another is an excellent conceptual turn.

### Lines 239–245 — Carleo–Troyer and neural-network quantum-state benchmark claims

- Carleo and Troyer’s *Science* 355, 602–606 (2017) paper is correctly identified as the work that prominently popularized neural-network variational quantum states, demonstrating high accuracy for prototypical interacting spin models in one and two dimensions.
- “Originated” would be too strong given earlier neural/autoregressive and variational-wavefunction history; the anchor’s “popularized” is appropriately safer.
- The added claim that NQS “matched—and on some reported benchmarks exceeded—tensor-network accuracy on 2D Heisenberg and fermionic systems” is not established by the 2017 citation alone and aggregates a heterogeneous later literature.
- Comparisons depend on equal parameter count versus equal compute, symmetry enforcement, sampling bias, optimization success, boundary conditions, sign structure, and availability of exact/controlled references. “Reported” usefully signals evidence rather than consensus, but named benchmark papers and metrics are still required.
- Verdict: **2017 popularization verified; broad superiority/comparability claim needs specific later sources and fair-comparison qualifiers**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4.5/5.** Neural wavefunctions provide novelty and optimism; benchmark discipline keeps the section from becoming trend advertising.

### Lines 246–252 — Pan, Chen, and Zhang Sycamore sampling simulation

- The relevant work by Feng Pan, Keyang Chen, and Pan Zhang reports one million uncorrelated samples for the 53-qubit, 20-cycle Sycamore circuit at approximate-state fidelity (F\approx0.0037), costing about 15 hours on 512 GPUs. “Hours-to-days on a GPU cluster” is therefore supported at that target fidelity.
- This should not be described as an exact replacement for Google’s sampling experiment. The target fidelity, XEB criterion, sample correlation status, and task definition are essential; different classical studies computed exact amplitudes for selected/correlated bitstrings rather than full-fidelity sampling.
- Dating is slippery: the preprint appeared in 2021 and later versions/publication may be 2022. Cite title/version rather than relying on “Pan, Chen, and Zhang 2022,” which can be confused with the distinct two-author Pan–Zhang 2022 big-batch PRL.
- “Dropped the believed cost” should say “demonstrated a lower-cost classical spoofing/sampling method at stated fidelity,” not imply the original Summit estimate was simply the same algorithm re-run faster.
- Verdict: **substantively verified once fidelity, hardware, task, and paper identity are stated**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 5/5.** The moving classical baseline is one of the chapter’s strongest stories; the fidelity detail makes it intellectually honest rather than less exciting.

### Lines 253–259 — NVIDIA H100 memory and bandwidth

- NVIDIA’s official H100 material supports the anchor’s deliberately broad “tens of GiB” and “TB/s-scale” wording. The SXM H100 was advertised with 80 GB HBM3 and over/about 3 TB/s bandwidth; current product tables also expose SKU/configuration differences, including 94-GB variants.
- The card heading says 80 **GiB**, while NVIDIA normally markets 80 **GB**. Those are not identical: 80 GB is about 74.5 GiB. Preserve vendor units or explicitly convert them.
- PCIe and SXM products, later HBM3e variants, and effective application bandwidth differ. The exact “3 TB/s” is a peak specification, not guaranteed sustained gate-kernel throughput.
- Since the anchor already says figures vary by SKU, update the card title to the same level of caution and cite a dated SKU datasheet.
- Verdict: **anchor verified; heading has a GB/GiB unit error and needs SKU/date precision**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4/5.** The bandwidth number gives hardware texture; unit discipline is especially important in a memory-scaling chapter.

### Lines 260–266 — cuStateVec, qsim, and Qulacs approaching memory-bandwidth peak

- The packages are plausibly among heavily optimized state-vector tools, and qsim/Qulacs CPU support is correct. cuStateVec is again an SDK/library rather than a fully parallel category match.
- “Approach memory-bandwidth peak” requires measured effective bandwidth, kernel/gate type, precision, device, problem size, and definition of bytes moved. Diagonal gates, permutations, fused gates, and communication-heavy distributed gates have different operational intensity.
- “At 30+ qubits” does not define the saturation threshold uniformly: a complex128 30-qubit state is 16 GiB and does not fit on every accelerator alongside workspace, while complex64 is 8 GiB. CPU NUMA effects and GPU capacity differ.
- Provide a roofline-style benchmark from each project or soften to “can become bandwidth-limited and attain a substantial fraction of peak on suitable local kernels.”
- Verdict: **credible qualitative claim, insufficiently benchmarked for the comparative/peak wording**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 3.5/5.** The package names matter less than the roofline insight; one measured kernel would be more engaging than another superlative.

### Lines 267–273 — Thirty-qubit fit and alleged thousandfold GPU speedups

- The memory arithmetic must name precision: 30 qubits occupy 16 GiB in complex128 or 8 GiB in complex64. “Fits in 16 GiB” is exact only as a bare complex128 allocation and leaves effectively no room for runtime state/workspace on a 16-GiB device.
- The anchor’s scepticism toward thousandfold claims is sound. For bandwidth-bound local kernels, speedup against an optimized CPU implementation is constrained largely by sustained bandwidth plus implementation/NUMA factors, not raw tensor-core FLOPS.
- “Roughly the bandwidth ratio” remains a model, not a benchmark. GPUs can gain from aggregate bandwidth and parallelism but lose to launch/transfer/communication overheads; fusion changes arithmetic intensity.
- Remove “three-orders-of-magnitude GPU speedup” from the heading unless an exact baseline is documented. Show one optimized-to-optimized comparison and label unoptimized-baseline marketing separately.
- Verdict: **good corrective principle; precision/capacity and benchmark definitions are still needed**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4.5/5.** Debunking thousandfold headlines with a bandwidth ratio is practical and pleasantly sharp.

### Lines 274–280 — Claimed 2021 Sunway and 2023 Frontier 42-qubit distributed simulations

- The Sunway citation appears conflated. The major 2021 new-Sunway Sycamore work scaled tensor-network contraction across roughly 42 million cores; “42” there is a core-count fragment, not evidently a 42-qubit dense distributed state-vector run. Other Sunway papers report 49-qubit/depth-limited or 53-qubit RCS tasks.
- I could not verify a primary 2023 “Frontier 42-qubit simulation” matching the wording. Contemporary reporting often estimated how Frontier would simulate or benchmark against quantum RCS; an estimate is not an executed distributed simulation.
- “Various Alibaba-Quantum and cuStateVec distributed runs” is too vague to audit and mixes an organization/project label with a software library. Each run needs qubits, circuit/depth, algorithm (state vector versus tensor network), precision/fidelity, node/GPU count, and achieved runtime.
- The communication-tax principle is correct for distributed state-vector gates that cross rank partitions, but tensor-network slicing has a different communication/computation profile. Do not use uncertain record anecdotes to prove a general systems fact that can be derived directly.
- Verdict: **communication claim sound; named chronology and 42-qubit attributions are unsupported or likely conflated**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 3.5/5.** A world-tour of supercomputers could be fun, but vague records become distracting trivia.

### Lines 281–287 — Quantum trajectories versus dense density matrices

- The anchor correctly rejects a universal break-even at (N\approx2^n). Bare state storage/work suggests (N2^n) versus (4^n), but trajectory simulation is embarrassingly parallel and stochastic, while density-matrix propagation has channel/Kraus and matrix-operation costs not captured by storage alone.
- The number of trajectories is set primarily by estimator variance, observable, time, confidence, and target statistical error—often scaling like (O(1/\epsilon^2)) for simple Monte Carlo estimates—not mechanically by qubit count.
- “Trajectories only option for (n>25)” in the heading is false if read literally. Tensor networks, low-rank density operators, purification, MPO methods, stochastic methods, problem-specific solvers, and smaller distributed dense matrices remain possible depending on structure and goal.
- Distinguish exact ensemble evolution from sampled unravelings, and note that different unravelings can have very different variance.
- Verdict: **anchor gives the right anti-rule; heading overstates trajectories as uniquely available and should be rewritten**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4.5/5.** The competing exponentials make a useful decision problem; emphasizing variance turns it into real scientific practice.

### Lines 288–294 — High-noise classical simulability and Aharonov–Ben-Or/Knill attribution

- Aharonov and Ben-Or’s 1996 *Polynomial Simulations of Decohered Quantum Computers* does show efficient classical simulation for parallel circuits above a sufficiently large constant decoherence rate in its specified model, while the sequential-QTM result differs. This supports a carefully model-bound high-noise statement.
- “Output converges toward easily sampled distributions” is intuitive but not a substitute for the theorem’s noise model and simulation guarantee. High local depolarization can wash out correlations, yet thresholds and algorithms depend on architecture, depth, locality, and error definition.
- Knill 2005 is a poor or opposite citation for this card: *Quantum computing with realistically noisy devices* presents a fault-tolerant architecture and evidence for reliable computation at comparatively high gate error rates. Error correction is precisely why constant physical noise below a fault-tolerance threshold need not make computation classically easy.
- Preserve the anchor’s crucial “uncorrected” qualifier, cite Aharonov–Ben-Or directly, and separate high-noise trivialization from fault-tolerance threshold results. Do not imply one universal depolarizing rate.
- Verdict: **restricted Aharonov–Ben-Or result is real; Knill 2005 is misapplied and the convergence gloss needs formal scope**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4.5/5.** The idea that too much noise restores classical ease is satisfying; juxtaposing it correctly with error correction would make the paradox even better.

### Lines 295–301 — Bremner–Montanaro–Shepherd and noisy IQP/RCS simulability

- Bremner, Montanaro, and Shepherd’s 2016/2017 IQP work is principally known for average-case hardness and approximate-sampling results, with noise-simulability statements under specific depolarizing-noise and anticoncentration assumptions. It does not by itself justify a generic combined statement about “IQP and random-circuit sampling” thresholds.
- Some noisy-IQP results are striking precisely because efficient approximation can occur for any fixed nonzero noise under a particular model, rather than at one simple universal threshold. Depth, whether noise is applied after each layer or only at output, knowledge of the rate, metric (ℓ1/total variation), and desired constant accuracy all matter.
- Random universal circuits and commuting IQP circuits are different ensembles with different hardness and noise analyses. Split them into separately cited statements instead of joining them by analogy.
- The year also needs bibliographic discipline: distinguish the 2016 PRL *Average-case complexity versus approximate simulation of commuting quantum computations* from the 2017 Quantum paper *Achieving quantum supremacy with sparse and noisy commuting quantum computations*.
- Verdict: **directionally plausible, but the citation and “thresholds” wording merge distinct theorems, models, and circuit families**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4/5.** A noise-driven phase change in simulability is fascinating; readers need to see which phase diagram they are actually looking at.

### Lines 302–308 — Stim and the provenance of surface-code threshold curves

- Stim is unquestionably prominent in modern circuit-level QEC simulation, particularly for fast detector sampling and integration with decoders. “The most widely used” is an empirical superlative for which no usage metric is supplied and which may vary by community and task.
- Stim generates syndrome/detector samples or error models; it does not by itself produce a physically universal “surface-code threshold.” Threshold curves also depend on the circuit, schedule, noise model, decoder, boundary conditions, logical observable, number of rounds, finite-size fitting, and sampling uncertainty.
- The statement that Chapter 19’s quoted curves come from such studies is a cross-file provenance claim. It should be proven by explicit citations attached to each Chapter 19 number; a generic reference to Stim cannot backfill them.
- Replace the superlative with “widely used,” name the decoder(s) and noise model for any reproduced curve, and make code/data seeds available if the book generated results itself.
- Verdict: **tool role credible; popularity superlative and Chapter 19 provenance remain unverified**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 3.5/5.** The practical pipeline could be compelling, but “tool produced curve” hides the scientific choices that make the curve interesting.

### Lines 309–315 — Original Sycamore runtime comparison

- This repeats the opening card and is verified as a report of Google’s 2019 claim: 53 functional qubits, 20-cycle random circuits, about 200 seconds for the sampling task, and an estimated roughly 10,000 years on Summit under the then-modelled classical approach.
- “Depth-20” should preferably be “20 cycles,” because circuit depth depends on whether single-qubit layers, entangling layers, and measurement are counted. The paper’s benchmark structure is more specific than generic depth.
- The 10,000-year figure was an estimate tied to a simulator/cost model, not an observed classical runtime or timeless lower bound. Later algorithms and hardware sharply reduced it, as the chapter correctly proceeds to discuss.
- If (T_Q) includes one million samples, clarify setup/calibration and sampling wall time versus the per-circuit quantum execution; keep task fidelity/XEB in the comparison.
- Verdict: **verified historical report with cycle/depth and estimate-status qualifications**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 5/5.** The famous contrast remains an excellent narrative baseline because the section then lets classical computing answer back.

### Lines 316–322 — Jiuzhang and Jiuzhang 2.0 photonic advantage experiments

- Verified at the stated high level: USTC’s 2020 Jiuzhang and 2021 Jiuzhang 2.0 experiments made quantum-computational-advantage claims using photonic Gaussian boson sampling.
- Say **Gaussian** boson sampling, not generic boson sampling. Jiuzhang used squeezed-state inputs, a static interferometer, and threshold detection; those details determine both hardness conjectures and classical competitors.
- The experiments and their claims should be distinguished: Jiuzhang reported up to 76 detected photon clicks; Jiuzhang 2.0 reported higher detected-photon regimes. Include modes, input states, detector model, sample count, validation method, and the classical estimator current at publication.
- “Analogous” should mean analogous sampling-based advantage claims, not the same task, programmability, verification, or complexity assumptions as Sycamore RCS.
- Verdict: **verified, but the sampling variant and limits of the analogy should be explicit**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4.5/5.** Moving from superconducting gates to a photonic interference machine broadens the story delightfully.

### Lines 323–329 — Zuchongzhi-series chronology and “67–105 qubit” heading

- The anchor’s generic statement is correct: successive USTC Zuchongzhi superconducting processors performed larger/deeper random-circuit-sampling experiments and renewed advantage claims.
- The heading is erroneous or conflated. Zuchongzhi 3.0 is a 105-qubit processor, but its most challenging reported experiment used 83 qubits and 32 cycles. The 67- and 70-qubit labels belong to Google’s later Sycamore RCS experiments, not a “67–105 qubit Zuchongzhi” range.
- Earlier USTC milestones also need clean naming: Zuchongzhi 2.1 is described as a 66-qubit device, while a prominent advantage experiment used 60 qubits and 24 cycles. Device qubit count must not be substituted for active benchmark qubits.
- The December 2024 preprint/publication chronology should be stated consistently; “2024” is reasonable for the initial report, but cite the final publication when available.
- Verdict: **series-level claim verified; heading mixes Google and USTC benchmarks and confuses chip capacity with active qubits**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4.5/5.** The international back-and-forth is engaging, but a compact timeline is essential to keep the many chip names pleasurable rather than bewildering.

### Lines 330–336 — Fifteen-hour Pan–Chen–Zhang simulation allegedly using a few thousand GPUs

- The 15-hour figure is supported for the 53-qubit, 20-cycle Sycamore sampling calculation at approximate fidelity (F\approx0.0037), but the reported cluster had **512 GPUs**, not “a few thousand GPUs.”
- The method contracts an approximate tensor-network state once to generate one million uncorrelated bitstrings. It is not simply an exact contraction of the complete output distribution, and fidelity/XEB must accompany the runtime.
- “Found a highly effective contraction order” is fair at a descriptive level, but the key contribution also includes reuse/batch sampling. Name the paper/version because it is easily confused with Pan and Zhang’s distinct big-batch exact-amplitude PRL.
- Correct the GPU count and specify GPU model, sample count, fidelity, and whether preprocessing/path-search time is included in the 15 hours.
- Verdict: **runtime broadly verified; GPU count is wrong and the approximation/task details are omitted**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 5/5.** This is exactly the classical countermove readers want to see; 512 GPUs is plenty dramatic without inflation.

### Lines 337–343 — Alleged Pan and Zhang 2023 extension to a 60-qubit Zuchongzhi benchmark

- Zuchongzhi’s 60-qubit, 24-cycle RCS advantage experiment is real, but its experimental paper is by Zhu *et al.*, not “Pan and Zhang 2023.” A later classical-simulation paper must be identified before attributing an extension.
- The readily identifiable 2023 Pan/Gu/Kuang/Liu/Zhang GPU tensor-network work benchmarks Sycamore verification and general GPU execution; its abstract does not establish this specific Zuchongzhi extension.
- “Zuchongzhi-class benchmarks” is too vague to verify: it could mean exact amplitudes for published bitstrings, low-fidelity spoofing, sample generation, or merely applying a cost estimator to the 60×24 network.
- Supply title, authors, arXiv/DOI, circuit instance, fidelity, hardware, and measured versus projected runtime. Until then, retain only a generic “follow-up classical work targeted Zuchongzhi circuits” if a source is found.
- Verdict: **unverified and likely bibliographically conflated**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 3.5/5.** A sequel should advance the plot, but an unnamed “extension” feels like connective tissue rather than evidence.

### Lines 344–350 — Sunway 304-second simulation and alleged 56-qubit circuit

- The 2021 new-Sunway paper does report scaling to about 42 million cores and a 304-second sampling time for the Google Sycamore task, alongside larger supported random-circuit shapes and extraordinary sustained mixed-/single-precision performance.
- The “56-qubit Sycamore-style circuit” description does not match the abstract’s 304-second claim, which is explicitly for Google Sycamore (53 active qubits). The paper separately discusses a (10\times10)-qubit, (1+40+1)-depth circuit as its simulatable frontier. The card appears to splice a qubit count from another benchmark into the Sycamore runtime.
- The 304 seconds is a classical tensor-network sampling workload under a chosen fidelity/precision and sample definition. “Within a small factor of the device’s wall-clock time” must compare equal sample counts, target fidelity, preprocessing, and total resource use, not seconds alone.
- Correct the circuit identity and retain the astounding resource contrast: 304 seconds on tens of millions of cores is not equivalent in cost or accessibility to 200 seconds on the QPU.
- Verdict: **42-million-core and 304-second figures verified; 56-qubit attribution is wrong and wall-clock parity needs task/resource qualification**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 5/5.** This is a superb climax to the classical chase, especially when “same seconds, radically different machine” is made explicit.

### Lines 351–356 — Gao–Anschuetz–Wang–Cirac–Lukin 2024 and noise-exploiting classical algorithms

- The named author combination corresponds to work on quantum advantages in learning/quantum correlations (with versions/publication chronology around 2021–2024), not an identifiable 2024 paper showing that recent device advantage benchmarks are classically matched by exploiting device noise.
- A distinct 2024 XEB critique by Xun Gao, Marcin Kalinowski, Chi-Ning Chou, Mikhail Lukin, Boaz Barak, and Soonwon Choi gives an efficient classical algorithm achieving a fraction of experimental XEB values and analyzes XEB/fidelity under noise. That may be the intended source, but it has different authors and a narrower conclusion.
- “Several recent advantage benchmarks can be matched” is substantially stronger than “an algorithm attains 5–12% of reported XEB values.” Matching sample quality, distributional distance, runtime, energy, and verification score are different standards.
- Identify each benchmark, metric, noise model, classical resource budget, and sense of “matched.” Do not use device noise as a universal explanation for every classical challenge to advantage experiments; many advances exploit tensor-network structure and batching independent of noise.
- Verdict: **citation appears wrong and the conclusion is overclaimed; likely conflates a learning paper with a separate XEB/noise analysis**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4.5/5.** Noise turning from hardware weakness into a classical algorithmic handle is a great final idea, but it needs exact intellectual ownership.

### Chapter 24 fact-check mirror — second-pass file verdict

- Every card in this 356-line mirror has now received a second-pass review, including arithmetic, attribution, evidentiary scope, improvement suggestions, doubts, and reader-experience assessment.
- Strongest defects: the Fugaku 48-qubit/1-PiB/130,000-node conflation; density-matrix “large server” and “edge” labels off by orders of magnitude; the Bravyi–Gosset benchmark/exponent conflations; Pashayan paper authorship error; H100 GB/GiB mismatch; uncertain Sunway/Frontier records; Knill 2005 cited in the wrong conceptual direction; Zuchongzhi mixed with Google’s 67/70-qubit labels; and wrong GPU/qubit counts in the Pan/Sunway closing chronology.
- Systemic issue: headings repeatedly assert more specific facts than their anchors, and many cards use “TBD” despite claims whose exact paper identity is essential. The mirror should treat task, precision/fidelity, hardware, achieved-versus-estimated status, and publication version as mandatory fields for simulation records.
- Systemic improvement: replace record-list prose with tables separating dense state vector, lossy/compressed state vector, tensor-network amplitude calculation, approximate sampling, and stabilizer/noise simulation. Most apparent contradictions disappear once representation and output task are explicit.
- Entertainment verdict: the chapter has excellent inherent drama—exponentials, ingenious structure, and a continuing quantum/classical race—but its enjoyment is repeatedly undercut by record numerology that does not survive provenance checks. Correct tables and a few worked resource calculations would raise both trust and narrative momentum.
- Overall verdict: **conceptually rich and unusually engaging, but factually high-risk in its numerical record chronology; major source-and-scope repair required before publication**.

## Second-pass review — `factcheck/part-10-practice-and-era/25-nisq-and-early-fault-tolerant-era.md`

### Lines 1–4 — File identity and extraction status

- The mirror target and extraction date are explicit, and the all-open status correctly warns that identification is not verification.
- “Extraction pass 2026-05” is already two months old relative to this review, which matters unusually much because this file uses a 2026 hardware snapshot. Add an `as_of` field per volatile card rather than relying on one file-level date.
- The title’s “Early Fault-Tolerant Era” should trigger a systematic distinction among NISQ physical qubits, error-detected logical demonstrations, logical memory, and universal fault-tolerant logical gates. The initial cards do not yet enforce that vocabulary.
- Verdict: **clear scaffold, but volatile claims need card-level dates and maturity categories**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 3.5/5.** Functional and easy to navigate; a one-line statement of what “early fault-tolerant” means would create anticipation.

### Lines 6–14 — Preskill’s coinage of “NISQ” and keynote chronology

- John Preskill is correctly credited with coining NISQ, and the article title, journal, volume, and article number are correct: *Quantum* 2, 79 (2018), *Quantum Computing in the NISQ era and beyond*.
- The keynote year is wrong or at least misleading. Preskill labels the work “Q2B 2017,” and contemporary records identify it as based on his December 2017 keynote at the inaugural Quantum Computing for Business conference. The article was submitted/posted in January 2018 and published in 2018.
- Preskill’s paper itself says he needed a name “for this talk” and made up NISQ, which is excellent primary evidence. Cite the paper DOI (`10.22331/q-2018-08-06-79`) and describe “a 2017 keynote and the 2018 article.”
- Preserve capitalization exactly as the published title uses it; do not silently turn the historical label into a precise hardware class, since Preskill’s later writing also stresses capability rather than raw count.
- Verdict: **coinage and article verified; keynote date should be 2017, not 2018**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4.5/5.** The origin story is concise and human; the “needed a name for this talk” detail would make it especially charming.

### Lines 15–22 — “Typical” NISQ two-qubit error rate of 10⁻³–10⁻²

- The range is a plausible broad historical order of magnitude for many deployed superconducting and trapped-ion systems, corresponding to 99–99.9% two-qubit fidelity. It is not a stable platform-independent definition of NISQ.
- Current examples already span or exceed the endpoints: IBM reports Heron r3 median two-qubit error around (1.17\times10^{-3}); Quantinuum’s H2 sheet gives typical (10^{-3}); component-level trapped-ion demonstrations report below (10^{-4}). Other devices/couplers can remain worse than (10^{-2}).
- “Per gate” must name metric and protocol. Randomized-benchmarking infidelity, cycle error, process infidelity, algorithmic error, crosstalk-aware simultaneous performance, leakage, and worst-edge error are not interchangeable.
- A median/best calibrated number does not describe a full chip or a circuit’s effective error. Give dated representative systems and a distribution or say “often of order (10^{-3}–10^{-2}), depending strongly on platform and benchmark.”
- Verdict: **reasonable orientation range, unsuitable as an uncited empirical invariant or NISQ definition**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4/5.** A compact error range helps, but one “one error per roughly 100–1,000 entangling gates before correlations/mitigation” intuition would make it matter.

### Lines 23–30 — Preskill’s original 50–100-qubit sketch

- Verified directly by the 2018 paper’s abstract: it describes quantum computers with 50–100 qubits as potentially surpassing then-current classical capabilities, and the body defines “intermediate scale” as roughly 50 to a few hundred qubits.
- “Original sketch was 50–100” slightly compresses two statements. The 50–100 interval characterizes a possible near-term advantage milestone in the abstract; his broader NISQ-size discussion extends to a few hundred.
- Quote/paraphrase both roles accurately rather than making 100 a hard upper boundary. The conceptual constraints—noise-limited circuit depth and lack of full error correction—matter more than the count.
- Verdict: **verified as an abstract-level milestone range, with broader body range worth noting**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4/5.** The historical yardstick is useful because readers can immediately see how raw counts outran the old sketch while capability did not automatically follow.

### Lines 31–38 — A 2026 NISQ “ceiling” of a few thousand qubits

- This is too category-free to verify. A few-thousand physical-qubit count may be claimed by neutral-atom arrays and annealing/special-purpose systems, while high-performing universal gate-model superconducting and trapped-ion QPUs remain mostly in the tens to low hundreds; demonstrated chip capacity, simultaneously controlled qubits, and cloud-available systems differ.
- IBM can truthfully say it demonstrated an 1,121-qubit Condor chip, while its current performance-focused Heron family is 133/156 qubits. That alone shows why “ceiling” is not one number.
- If annealers count, several-thousand-qubit systems predate 2026; if they do not, say “programmable gate-model” and decide whether analog neutral-atom processors count. “Some platforms” is too elastic to prevent apples-to-oranges comparison.
- Replace the sentence with a dated table: modality, processor/system, installed physical sites, controllably active qubits, connectivity, and error/performance measure. Explain that qubit count no longer defines the era.
- Verdict: **plausible only under selected counting conventions; presently vague and potentially misleading**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 3.5/5.** “A few thousand” sounds momentous but feels empty until the reader learns what those qubits can jointly do.

### Lines 39–47 — Pre-NISQ “few-qubit demos” dated roughly 1998–2015

- A historical periodization is necessarily interpretive, and the anchor’s caveats about annealers, special-purpose systems, and counting conventions are valuable.
- The bracket obscures substantial progression: gate-model demonstrations reached more than a literal handful before 2015, including 14-ion entanglement around 2011 and multi-qubit superconducting processors/algorithms. “Most” would require a survey, not anecdotes.
- Starting at 1998 omits foundational two-qubit demonstrations in the mid-1990s and may be chosen for landmark algorithms rather than hardware. Ending at 2015 similarly precedes the 50-qubit/NISQ transition but is not a clean boundary.
- Present this as a narrative phase, not a measured era: “from late-1990s few-qubit demonstrations through increasingly capable tens-of-qubits prototypes in the mid-2010s.” Add two or three milestones instead of asserting what “most” experiments did.
- Verdict: **usable rough narrative bracket, not a defensible quantitative taxonomy; existing caveat should be expanded**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4/5.** A timeline helps readers feel acceleration, and named milestones would make it much more alive.

### Lines 48–55 — Superconducting transmon count of roughly 100–1,000 per chip

- The range captures IBM’s span from 133/156-qubit Heron to the demonstrated 1,121-qubit Condor and Google’s 105-qubit Willow, but it should not be presented as typical across every named company.
- Rigetti’s deployed generations have commonly been below 100 qubits, so listing Rigetti beside a lower bound of approximately 100 makes the sentence internally misleading. IBM’s 1,121-qubit chip is also not the same as its highest-performing production architecture.
- “Per chip” needs physical definition: monolithic die, tiled module, multi-chip QPU, and system-level modular qubit counts can differ. Yield/operability and active qubits matter.
- Use named dated examples rather than a range, and distinguish scale demonstrations from performance-focused/available processors.
- Verdict: **range brackets selected leaders but is not representative of all named vendors and blurs chip maturity**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4/5.** Vendor names anchor the landscape; a three-row table would turn a fuzzy range into a satisfying comparison.

### Lines 56–63 — Superconducting one- and two-qubit fidelities

- Around 99.9% one-qubit and 99.5% two-qubit fidelity is a plausible coarse platform-level teaching value, but leading 2025–2026 systems report two-qubit errors closer to (10^{-3}) on selected aggregate metrics, while weaker edges/simultaneous operation can be worse.
- Fidelity figures cannot be divorced from protocol: isolated randomized benchmarking often looks better than simultaneous layer performance; leakage, readout, idling, and correlated errors may dominate algorithms.
- “Around” helps, but one number hides a distribution across qubits, couplers, calibration times, and gate families. Use median plus 10th/90th percentile or best/worst only when sourced.
- Avoid comparing vendor marketing numbers unless the benchmarking definitions align. IBM’s reported median Heron r3 error and Google’s RCS/cycle metrics are not automatically comparable.
- Verdict: **reasonable illustrative values, but too metric-free and somewhat pessimistic for current leading two-qubit gates**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 3.5/5.** Percentages alone are dry; converting them into expected error accumulation over a circuit layer would give them narrative force.

### Lines 64–71 — Superconducting gate and coherence times

- Tens to hundreds of nanoseconds is a sound broad scale for superconducting one-/two-qubit gates and measurement/reset may be longer. The statement should not imply all gate types occupy the same interval.
- (T_1,T_2=100–300\,\mu s) describes some strong current transmons but is not representative across IBM, Google, and Rigetti devices; many calibrated qubits or effective (T_2) values fall below 100 μs, while selected devices exceed the range.
- Coherence-to-gate-time ratios are more meaningful than either number alone, but still do not predict circuit depth under control error/crosstalk. Distinguish (T_2^*), Hahn-echo (T_2), and dynamical-decoupled measures.
- Provide per-platform dated medians and name gate type. If retaining a pedagogical range, widen it and label it “order of magnitude, device-dependent.”
- Verdict: **gate-time scale credible; coherence range is selectively optimistic and measurement definitions are absent**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4/5.** Nanoseconds versus microseconds gives a useful clock, especially if readers are invited to compute the misleadingly large naive gate budget.

### Lines 72–79 — Trapped-ion systems at roughly 30–100 physical qubits per trap

- The range covers prominent deployed examples such as Quantinuum H2 at 56 qubits and IonQ Forte Enterprise at 36 physical qubits. It is a reasonable snapshot of operational commercial machines, not a hard platform ceiling.
- Oxford Ionics advertised 16–64-qubit 2025 foundation systems and a 256+ 2026 roadmap/product ambition. A roadmap or system sold ahead of delivery should not be silently counted as demonstrated operation; its acquisition by IonQ also makes the three-company list historically time-sensitive.
- “Per trap” is imprecise: segmented traps can shuttle ions among zones, and the physically loaded ions, computational qubits, simultaneously usable qubits, and algorithmic/logical qubits differ.
- Use exact system models and status (“available,” “demonstrated,” “announced”) and explain all-to-all effective connectivity rather than making count the sole comparison.
- Verdict: **reasonable deployed-system bracket, but terminology and Oxford/IonQ status need dated clarification**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4/5.** The smaller count becomes interesting when paired with connectivity and quality; without that, it reads like a losing scoreboard.

### Lines 80–84 — Trapped-ion two-qubit fidelity and speed

- Quantinuum H2’s current data sheet gives typical two-qubit infidelity around (10^{-3}) (99.9% fidelity), while component/system demonstrations by Oxford Ionics/IonQ report 99.99% or better under particular protocols. Thus 99.7–99.9% is plausible for deployed-system orientation but omits the best recent result.
- Microseconds-to-milliseconds is a defensible broad trapped-ion entangling-gate scale; exact duration depends on ion species, mode spectrum, pulse scheme, chain/zone, transport, and whether cooling/reconfiguration is included.
- Relative to superconducting entangling gates of tens/hundreds of nanoseconds, the slowdown can span roughly one to four orders, as the anchor cautiously says. The extraction comment incorrectly paraphrases this as specifically “3–4 orders.”
- Compare full circuit throughput as well as primitive duration: parallelism, all-to-all connectivity, shuttling, measurement/reset, compilation SWAPs, and batching affect wall time.
- Verdict: **broadly sound with benchmark/status qualifiers; extraction comment misquotes the anchor’s range**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4.5/5.** The speed-versus-quality trade-off is inherently engaging and deserves a concrete same-circuit comparison.

### Lines 86–93 — Neutral-atom scale and 99.5% two-qubit fidelity

- Arrays from QuEra, Pasqal, and Atom Computing do occupy the hundreds-to-thousand-plus physical-atom regime; Atom Computing now advertises an AC1000 system with more than 1,200 physical qubits. Thus the stated upper bound of approximately 1,000 is already a rounded snapshot, not a ceiling.
- Atom count is especially slippery: trapped sites, successfully loaded atoms after rearrangement, computational qubits, atoms participating in a circuit, analog simulation sites, and error-corrected/logical qubits are different quantities.
- “Two-qubit fidelity reaching 99.5% on best devices” is likely stale and underspecified by 2026. Published/announced neutral-atom entangling-gate fidelities depend on whether they are isolated pairs, parallel gates across an array, native CZ/CZ-like gates, and inclusion of SPAM/leakage. Best-component results should not be attached to thousand-atom system scale without showing both were demonstrated together.
- Give dated per-vendor rows and distinguish analog programmable arrays from digital gate-model operation. State connectivity/reconfiguration and circuit depth alongside raw sites.
- Verdict: **scale broadly correct but rapidly stale; fidelity and simultaneous-system interpretation need exact sources**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4.5/5.** Rearranged atom arrays are visually and conceptually exciting; explaining why “1,000 atoms” is not automatically “1,000 circuit qubits” adds useful intrigue.

### Lines 94–101 — PsiQuantum and Xanadu photonic architectures

- PsiQuantum’s architecture is accurately associated with fusion-based quantum computation (FBQC), which builds large photonic resource states through entangling measurements and is closely related to measurement-based fault-tolerant computation. Calling it merely “measurement-based” loses the distinguishing fusion architecture.
- Xanadu is strongly associated with continuous-variable photonics and Gaussian boson sampling, while its fault-tolerant proposals/software also involve discrete logical encodings such as GKP and measurement-based photonic constructions. “Uses CV approaches” is true but incomplete as a company-wide architecture label.
- The two firms should not be presented as current NISQ processor peers in the same sense as cloud gate-model ion/superconducting systems. Their hardware maturity, computational models, and fault-tolerant roadmaps differ.
- Rewrite as separate bullets: PsiQuantum—fusion-based photonic FTQC; Xanadu—continuous-variable photonics/GBS with fault-tolerant photonic encoding research. Cite primary architecture papers, not only company pages.
- Verdict: **directionally correct but overcompressed and technologically category-blurring**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4/5.** Photons widen the platform panorama; one sentence on fusions versus quadrature modes would make the contrast memorable.

### Lines 102–109 — Barren-plateau variance claimed to scale exactly as 2⁻ⁿ

- McClean *et al.* 2018 verifies exponentially vanishing gradient variance for sufficiently expressive/random parameterized circuits whose relevant subcircuits form approximate 2-designs; the expectation is zero and variance is suppressed by inverse Hilbert-space dimension factors.
- “(∼2^{-n})” is an illustrative exponential, not a universal law. The paper’s formulas contain observable, generator, state-purity, and case-dependent factors, sometimes with denominators scaling like (2^{2n}) or other effective exponents after traces are evaluated.
- Later work shows strong dependence on global versus local cost, depth, initialization, locality, symmetries, entanglement, and noise. Shallow local-cost circuits can have only polynomially vanishing gradients; noise-induced plateaus obey different depth-dependent results.
- Say (mathrm{Var}(\partial_θ C)=O(b^{-n})) under the random/2-design assumptions, with (b>1), then give (2^{-n}) as a common schematic rather than equality.
- Verdict: **exponential phenomenon verified; exact (2^{-n}) scaling is overgeneralized and assumptions are missing**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4.5/5.** The landscape becoming exponentially flat is vivid; a small exception box would make the warning empowering rather than fatalistic.

### Lines 110–117 — VQE chemistry demonstrations around 50 spin-orbitals

- This claim cannot be assessed from qubit count alone. A molecular basis may begin with roughly one qubit per spin-orbital under Jordan–Wigner/parity-style encodings, but frozen cores, active-space selection, tapering, embedding, fragmentation, and compact encodings can reduce the hardware register drastically.
- “Hardware demonstrations up to roughly 50 spin-orbitals” needs a named molecule, basis, starting orbital count, active orbital/electron count, final qubits, ansatz, hardware, and whether optimization was performed on-device. Classical preprocessing of a 50-orbital problem followed by a tiny active-space VQE is not a 50-qubit chemistry demonstration.
- Demonstrating an energy for a classically tractable active space also differs from achieving chemical accuracy or quantum advantage. Report error against a controlled classical reference and total shot/runtime cost.
- Until a representative primary experiment is supplied, remove the numeric frontier or state only that active-space VQE demonstrations remain limited and classically benchmarkable.
- Verdict: **unsupported as stated; likely conflates parent spin-orbital count with active quantum register size**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 3.5/5.** Molecule and orbital numbers can fascinate, but only a concrete worked reduction lets readers understand what the hardware actually solved.

### Lines 118–125 — Virtual-distillation attribution and publication year

- The attribution to William J. Huggins and coauthors is correct. *Virtual Distillation for Quantum Error Mitigation* appeared in *Physical Review X* **11**, 041036 in **2021**, not 2022; the preprint dates to 2020.
- The technique estimates observables of (ρ^M/\mathrm{Tr}(ρ^M)) using measurements across (M) copies of a noisy state. It suppresses subdominant eigencomponents but cannot generally remove coherent bias in the dominant eigenvector.
- Huggins *et al.* was contemporaneous with closely related “exponential error suppression” work by Koczor, so avoid implying sole conceptual ownership if the chapter surveys origins.
- Mention the resource trade-off: multiple state copies, entangling/permutation measurements, and sampling overhead can themselves be noisy or expensive.
- Verdict: **attribution verified; likely reference year is wrong and practical limitations deserve one phrase**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4.5/5.** The idea of purifying a state only in the measured mathematics is genuinely clever and deserves a one-line mechanism.

### Lines 126–133 — Large variational demonstrations and classical reproductions in 2024–2025

- The anchor is cautiously worded and broadly consistent with the literature: large-qubit variational/dynamics demonstrations have often been followed or accompanied by tensor-network, stabilizer, perturbative, or other classical calculations of the same observables.
- The heading adds claims absent from the anchor—“hundreds of qubits” and “on a laptop.” Neither should be inferred from “large many-qubit” or “classical reproductions”; classical studies may use clusters, and prominent 127-qubit IBM work was Hamiltonian time evolution rather than a conventional optimized VQE.
- Name each paired experiment/reproduction and specify qubits, circuit depth, observable subset, approximation error, and classical hardware. Reproducing selected local observables is not equivalent to sampling the full quantum state.
- Dates should track initial preprints and final publications separately. “2024–2025 literature” can accidentally relabel 2023 experiments or later comments.
- Verdict: **plausible trend; extraction heading materially inflates hardware scale and laptop accessibility beyond the anchor**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4.5/5.** The scientific duel is compelling; side-by-side resource/result boxes would be far more fun than an allusive sentence.

### Lines 134–142 — Sycamore’s 53-qubit, 20-cycle, approximately 200-second result

- Verified against Arute *et al.*, *Nature* 574, 505–510 (2019), DOI `10.1038/s41586-019-1666-5`: 53 operational qubits and the reported roughly 200-second sampling task are historically correct.
- As in Chapter 24’s mirror, “depth-20” should be “20 cycles” unless the book defines its depth counting. The benchmark used a specific random-circuit layer pattern and XEB fidelity, not arbitrary generic depth 20.
- October 2019 is the publication month; distinguish that from experiment date if chronology becomes fine-grained.
- Avoid letting the 200 seconds imply setup/calibration or all verification was included. State sample count and target/observed fidelity beside runtime.
- Verdict: **verified historical headline with cycle/depth and task-boundary qualifications**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 5/5.** It remains a crisp landmark and works especially well when the classical responses immediately follow.

### Lines 143–151 — Google’s 10,000-year classical estimate

- Verified as Google’s contemporaneous estimate for simulating the specified Sycamore sampling task on Summit with the considered Schrödinger–Feynman approach. It was never a complexity-theoretic lower bound or an executed classical timing.
- “Leading supercomputer of the time” is acceptable but name Summit and date the estimate. Hardware ranking is less important than the algorithm, storage, fidelity, and output-task assumptions.
- Subsequent IBM storage analysis and tensor-network/sampling algorithms reduced estimates dramatically, so retain “estimated” and avoid treating later revisions as rebutting the experimental data itself.
- Verdict: **verified as a historical, model-dependent estimate; contestability must remain adjacent**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 5/5.** The spectacular number is narratively effective precisely because readers then watch it collapse under algorithmic progress.

### Lines 152–160 — IBM’s approximately 2.5-day secondary-storage counterestimate

- The attribution is broadly correct: Pednault *et al.*/IBM argued in 2019 that an ideal full-state simulation with sufficient disk/secondary storage could be completed in about 2.5 days on Summit, sharply revising Google’s 10,000-year framing.
- This was an estimate/proposal, not a reported completed 2.5-day run. It also targeted a full-state simulation and used enormous storage, while Google’s comparison involved a sampling/fidelity task; explain where the tasks and cost models align or differ.
- Cite the technical report/preprint title and version rather than an IBM blog alone. Include the projected disk footprint and I/O assumptions, which are the point of the method.
- “Brought the estimate down” can imply consensus replacement; say “IBM proposed an alternative simulation strategy and estimated approximately 2.5 days.”
- Verdict: **verified as a proposed estimate, not an executed classical reproduction**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 5/5.** Ten thousand years becoming days through storage engineering is one of the best examples of why advantage claims are moving targets.

### Lines 161–167 — Jiuzhang’s 76-click Gaussian-boson-sampling claim

- Verified at headline level: Zhong *et al.*, *Science* 370, 1460–1463 (2020), reported Gaussian boson sampling with up to 76 detected photon clicks and an estimated sampling-rate advantage of order (10^{14}) over the then-best classical strategy/supercomputer comparison.
- Use “detected photon clicks” rather than simply photons because threshold detectors do not resolve photon number; the distinction affects event interpretation and classical simulation.
- The factor is an estimated task- and comparator-dependent advantage, not a universal speedup or proof against all future classical algorithms. State the 100-mode interferometer, squeezed inputs, sample definition, and validation limits if space allows.
- December 2020 is correct for publication/announcement chronology.
- Verdict: **verified with detector and comparator qualifications**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4.5/5.** The shift from gates to a 100-mode optical maze is exhilarating; explaining “clicks” preserves both wonder and precision.

### Lines 168–174 — IBM Eagle’s 127-qubit kicked-Ising experiment

- Kim *et al.*, *Nature* 618, 500–505 (2023), DOI `10.1038/s41586-023-06096-3`, verifies the 127-qubit Eagle experiment and measurement of mitigated expectation values for Trotterized two-dimensional transverse-field/kicked-Ising dynamics at circuit volumes beyond brute-force exact state-vector computation.
- “Beyond exact statevector” is a memory/method statement, not beyond all classical methods. The circuit geometry, observable locality, and limited effective entanglement enabled subsequent tensor-network, PEPS, sparse-Pauli, and related classical reproductions.
- The original paper deliberately used classically verifiable subcases and then extrapolated into harder regimes. State which depths/observables were exact-checkable and which rested on cross-method consistency.
- “2023–2024” in the heading should distinguish the June 2023 experiment from later classical responses; it was not a multi-year series by default.
- Verdict: **experiment verified; classical-hardness wording must remain specifically ‘beyond brute-force state vector,’ not broad advantage**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 5/5.** This is an ideal case study in how “too large for one classical method” invites several smarter ones.

### Lines 175–182 — Alleged IBM shift from “advantage” to “utility”

- IBM explicitly promoted “quantum utility” in and around its 2023 Eagle paper as a more nuanced category for useful scientific exploration before a demonstrated quantum advantage. That communication framing is documented.
- “Subsequently shifted from advantage to utility” implies a clean reversal and chronology that needs quotations. IBM continued to discuss future quantum advantage while using utility for a different, weaker milestone; the concepts were not necessarily mutually exclusive replacements.
- The paper title itself is *Evidence for the utility of quantum computing before fault tolerance*. Later classical simulations challenged the strongest reading of utility but did not prove the hardware observations worthless.
- Rewrite neutrally: “IBM framed the experiment as quantum utility rather than a demonstrated end-to-end quantum advantage.” Cite IBM’s own definition and an independent critique.
- Verdict: **utility emphasis verified; ‘shifted from’ is interpretive corporate-narrative language, not yet proven**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4/5.** The vocabulary politics are revealing, though direct before/after wording would keep the analysis from sounding insinuative.

### Lines 183–190 — Quantum Volume definition

- Quantum Volume is not itself “the largest (n).” In the revised Cross *et al.* convention, the reported value is (V_Q=2^m), where (m) is the largest square random-model-circuit width/depth passing the heavy-output-generation criterion subject to device width.
- “Above-2/3 fidelity” is technically wrong. The threshold concerns heavy-output probability greater than (2/3), established with statistical confidence across an ensemble of circuits/shots. It is not state, process, or circuit fidelity.
- Random (m\times m) means width (m) and depth (m), not a literal matrix. Compilation and connectivity overhead are part of the system performance the benchmark captures.
- Define heavy outputs relative to the median ideal output probability and mention confidence/test protocol; otherwise the apparently simple (2/3) invites misinterpretation.
- Verdict: **materially imprecise definition: confuses exponent with QV and heavy-output probability with fidelity**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4/5.** A toy four-qubit heavy-output example would make this opaque benchmark surprisingly approachable.

### Lines 191–198 — Claimed best 2026 Quantum Volume range of 2¹⁴–2²⁰

- This range is already contradicted by vendor-reported results reviewed elsewhere in this ledger: Quantinuum announced H2 Quantum Volume (2^{25}=33{,}554{,}432). A “best devices” range capped at (2^{20}) is therefore stale/false by 2026.
- Vendor QV claims require the tested system version, date, compilation policy, error-detection/postselection or mitigation rules, circuit/sample counts, and whether results were independently reproduced.
- IBM’s reduced emphasis on QV does not mean the metric’s maximum froze; cross-vendor comparisons are further complicated by different architectures and reporting cadence.
- Either update to exact dated records or avoid a “best” interval. A historical timeline with QV exponent (m), not just (2^m), is more readable.
- Verdict: **contradicted by a reported (2^{25}) result; must be updated or removed**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 3.5/5.** Huge powers of two quickly become numbing; pairing (m=25) with what circuit actually passed restores meaning.

### Lines 199–206 — IonQ Algorithmic Qubits definition and benchmark suite

- IonQ did introduce #AQ as an application-oriented single-number metric derived from/adapted from QED-C benchmark circuits. Roughly, #AQ (N) requires selected structured circuit instances up to (N) qubits and about (N^2) entangling-gate depth/scale to meet benchmark-specific success criteria.
- It is more involved than “largest problem size at which a suite passes”: circuit families, eligible widths/depths, scoring, aggregation, mitigation, and pass rules matter. Cite IonQ’s formal specification/code at a pinned revision.
- The heading’s named suite “QFT, Grover, VQE on H₂O” is not present in the anchor and may not match the current #AQ subset. QED-C’s broader application benchmarks and IonQ’s AQ-selected tests should not be treated as identical.
- It is a vendor-proposed metric rather than an independent industry standard; report that provenance without either dismissing or endorsing it. Also verify whether IonQ still foregrounds #AQ in its 2026 roadmap.
- Verdict: **core attribution and structured-suite concept verified; exact suite/aggregation and current status need correction**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4/5.** Algorithms are more intuitive than random circuits, but the metric becomes interesting only when readers see how one score compresses unlike tasks.

### Lines 207–214 — Physical-qubit growth trend from 2018 to 2026

- The anchor says only “tens of percent per year,” whereas the heading upgrades this to approximately 1.5×/year. Those are not equivalent: 1.5× is 50% annual compound growth and would multiply counts by about 25.6 over eight years.
- No single series exists across modalities. Following each vendor’s flagship, maximum announced chip, best-quality available machine, neutral-atom site count, or annealer yields radically different growth curves and discontinuous architecture changes.
- Raw counts also suffer survivorship and cherry-picking: IBM’s maximum rose to 1,121 while its performance-led line moved back toward 100–156 qubits.
- Build a reproducible dataset with selection rule and CAGR; otherwise replace the quantified trend with “maximum reported physical counts rose substantially, unevenly across platforms.”
- Verdict: **general growth undeniable; 1.5×/year is an unsupported heading inflation and cross-platform aggregation is ill-defined**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 3.5/5.** A growth curve could be compelling; an uncited CAGR feels like industry-deck decoration.

### Lines 215–222 — Two-qubit-fidelity improvement over 2018–2026

- “Leading-platform error rates fell severalfold” is plausible but needs like-for-like time series. Comparing a 2018 full-system median to a 2026 isolated record gate manufactures progress by changing the benchmark.
- The heading’s endpoints—99.0 to 99.5% superconducting and 99.9% trapped-ion—are selective and already stale for some leaders: IBM Heron reports median error near (1.17\times10^{-3}) (~99.883%), and trapped-ion component claims exceed 99.99%.
- Parallel/simultaneous gate fidelity, leakage, crosstalk, duty cycle, and calibration stability determine scalable value. Best-pair fidelity can improve while usable circuit error remains less dramatic.
- Use one vendor/system family per trend and the same protocol, or say “published leading metrics improved substantially” without synthetic endpoints.
- Verdict: **directionally true but numerically under-specified, inconsistent with current leading figures, and vulnerable to benchmark switching**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4/5.** Error reduction is the real progress story; plotting error probability on a log scale would make “severalfold” tangible.

### Lines 223–230 — Quantum Volume’s rise and declining reporting

- The anchor’s cautious observation is defensible: QV rose rapidly among vendors that emphasized it, while some organizations shifted to other system-level metrics and stopped foregrounding QV.
- The heading again invents a stronger quantitative history—“roughly doubled per year on IBM systems, then plateaued”—that the anchor neither states nor sources. IBM’s historical QV increases were often stepwise and sometimes much faster than annual doubling.
- “Plateaued” differs from “stopped being reported.” Absence of a public score cannot be plotted as no technical improvement.
- Provide a dated vendor table and mark missing/not-reported values rather than interpolating a plateau. Discuss incentive/metric gaming and why vendors choose CLOPS, layer fidelity, AQ, logical error, or algorithmic benchmarks instead.
- Verdict: **anchor plausible; heading’s doubling/plateau narrative is unsupported and logically conflates missing data with stagnation**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4/5.** The rise and abandonment of benchmarks is a revealing industry story if told as sociology plus measurement, not a phantom trendline.

### Lines 231–238 — Conditional projection to 10⁴ qubits and 10⁻³ error around 2030

- The anchor properly begins with *if*, so it is a scenario rather than a prediction. The heading’s “Extrapolation to ~2030” makes it sound more forecast-like than the sentence warrants.
- Ten thousand physical qubits at (10^{-3}) two-qubit error do not by themselves guarantee a useful encoded system. Measurement/reset errors, leakage, correlations, cycle time, decoder latency, connectivity, yield, and logical-operation architecture matter.
- Small distance-(d) codes “outperform their physical constituents” only under a defined comparison: logical memory error per round versus physical idle/gate error over the same time, logical operation versus bare operation, or code-capacity benchmark. Below-threshold crossover has already been demonstrated at far fewer than 10,000 qubits, while application-scale advantage remains distant.
- Roadmaps are evidence of organizational intent, not verification of physical feasibility. Present several scenarios and resource estimates, not a single pseudo-trend.
- Verdict: **legitimate conditional scenario, but the asserted regime-to-code-performance connection is underdefined and not uniquely tied to 10⁴ qubits**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4/5.** A transparent “if/then” scenario engages readers; a sensitivity table would turn futurism into reasoning.

### Lines 239–246 — Surface-code logical-error scaling formula

- (p_L\sim A(p/p_{\mathrm{th}})^{(d+1)/2}) is a widely used below-threshold phenomenological/leading-order fit for odd-distance surface codes under specified stochastic circuit-level noise and decoder assumptions. The exponent reflects needing roughly ((d+1)/2) faults for a logical failure in the low-(p) regime.
- It is not “the threshold theorem” itself and cannot be derived solely by pointing to Chapter 19. (A) and (p_{\mathrm{th}}) depend on syndrome circuit, decoder, noise bias/correlation/leakage, boundaries, and whether error is per round or per logical operation.
- Near threshold, at small distance, or with correlated errors/error floors, the simple power law can fit poorly. Even/odd distance and phenomenological versus circuit-level models change conventions.
- Define all quantities and attach one representative fitted model; use the formula for intuition, not precise resource estimation without simulation.
- Verdict: **standard heuristic scaling, valid only under model/decoder/below-threshold qualifications**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4.5/5.** This formula is a superb lever: every two distance steps buy another factor, provided readers see the price and assumptions.

### Lines 247–252 — Google’s 2023 distance-3 versus distance-5 demonstration

- Google’s 2023 *Nature* paper did compare a 17-qubit distance-3 surface-code logical qubit with a 49-qubit distance-5 logical qubit and found the distance-5 code modestly better over the tested cycles. The year and distances are verified.
- Calling it straightforward “below-threshold operation” is too strong. The paper described a first experimental suppression with increasing code size and said the device was close to threshold; Google’s own 2023 blog anticipated *entering* the fault-tolerant regime with further improvements.
- The stronger repeated exponential-suppression/below-threshold evidence arrived with the 2024 Willow work at distances 3, 5, and 7 plus a distance-5 real-time-decoded memory. Thus “first claims” needs exact quotation and distinction between crossover evidence and sustained below-threshold scaling.
- Other code families/platforms had earlier fault-tolerant or break-even demonstrations, so “first” must be restricted to surface-code scaling under the defined criterion.
- Verdict: **experiment verified; ‘first below-threshold operation’ overstates the 2023 result and ignores the stronger 2024 milestone**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 5/5.** Bigger code finally becoming slightly better is a genuine turning point; the modest margin makes the later Willow jump more dramatic, not less.

### Lines 254–261 — Google’s 2024 distance-7 Willow result

- Verified: the preprint/report appeared online in December 2024 and the final *Nature* article, *Quantum error correction below the surface code threshold*, appeared in volume 638 (2025). It demonstrates distance-5 and distance-7 surface-code memories on Willow.
- Increasing distance by two suppressed logical error by Λ=(2.14\pm0.02), with the 101-qubit distance-7 memory reaching about 0.143% error per cycle. Thus (p_L(d=7)<p_L(d=5)) is correct and quantitatively stronger than the 2023 d=3/5 crossover.
- Cite both online-publication and issue years if calling it “Google 2024,” so readers do not think the 2025 bibliographic date is a contradiction.
- “Results” should specify memory experiment, repeated syndrome cycles, decoder, and per-cycle logical error; it is not yet arbitrary fault-tolerant computation at d=7.
- Verdict: **verified, with 2024-online/2025-print and logical-memory scope qualifications**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 5/5.** The clean suppression factor supplies the payoff that the earlier marginal crossover was building toward.

### Lines 262–269 — Quantinuum trapped-ion error-suppression scaling in 2024–2025

- Quantinuum/Microsoft reported strong logical-error suppression and multiple logical qubits on H-series trapped-ion hardware during this period, using small error-detecting/correcting codes distinct from Google’s surface code. The broad cross-platform point is credible.
- “Below threshold” is not present in the anchor and should not be imported by the heading without a threshold family and increasing-distance sequence. Error detection plus postselection, a logical-error ratio on fixed small codes, and asymptotic below-threshold scaling are different milestones.
- Name the code family, physical/logical qubit counts, logical operation or memory tested, acceptance/postselection rate, comparison baseline, and whether results used real-time correction. Marketing phrases such as “800× better” require the denominator and workload.
- The 2024–2025 range likely combines several papers/announcements; cite them separately rather than creating one continuous demonstration.
- Verdict: **broad attribution plausible, but code identity and the heading’s below-threshold interpretation remain unverified**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4.5/5.** A second hardware route keeps the story from becoming Google-only; contrasting code strategies would be genuinely illuminating.

### Lines 270–277 — Alleged distance-9 to distance-11 demonstrations in progress

- The anchor wisely says only that larger-distance demonstrations are anticipated and that plans are not demonstrations. The heading invents the specific d=9–11 “in progress” claim and therefore contradicts the card’s own epistemic caution.
- Google’s Willow paper includes surface-code memories through distance 7 and repetition-code studies at much larger distances, including fits across d=5–11 and experiments up to d=29. Repetition-code distance must not be relabelled as a d=9/11 surface-code demonstration.
- “In progress as of 2026” is hard to verify externally unless a lab publishes a dated experimental status; a roadmap can prove plans only.
- Delete the specific heading or cite an achieved d=9/d=11 surface-code result. Maintain separate rows for announced, underway (if officially documented), preprint, peer-reviewed, and independently reproduced.
- Verdict: **unsupported heading expansion; anchor itself states the correct plans-versus-results rule**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 3.5/5.** A future teaser is fine, but invented precision creates anticipation the evidence cannot satisfy.

### Lines 278–285 — Rotated surface-code patch count of 2d²−1 physical qubits

- For a standard unrotated-in-time rotated planar patch with (d^2) data qubits and (d^2-1) syndrome-measurement ancillas, the total (2d^2-1) count is correct.
- This is a patch-level memory layout, not full fault-tolerant overhead. Lattice surgery, routing space, magic-state factories, readout/reset ancillas, spare/yield qubits, boundaries, factories, and control infrastructure add large factors.
- Some layouts reuse ancillas, use subsystem/LDPC variants, change boundaries, or quote only data qubits; always label the convention.
- Verdict: **verified for the stated standard rotated-patch convention; not a complete logical-computer overhead formula**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4.5/5.** The simple quadratic count is gratifying and gives readers an immediate tool for checking roadmap claims.

### Lines 286–293 — Patch arithmetic at distances 7 and 21

- Exact application of (2d^2-1) gives 97 physical qubits at d=7 and 881 at d=21. “About 100” and “about 900” are correct; the heading’s “~1,000” is looser but not wrong as order of magnitude.
- These totals describe one idle logical patch with measurement ancillas. They do not include logical interactions or factory/routing overhead, and achieved Google d=7 used 101 qubits because experimental/layout details differ from the idealized 97 count.
- Keep exact and rounded values side by side so readers can distinguish formula from engineering realization.
- The extraction comment anticipates a Shor-distance claim that the anchor explicitly rejects in the next card; do not let adjacency turn d=21 into a recommendation.
- Verdict: **verified arithmetic, with ideal-patch versus system-overhead caveat**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4.5/5.** The jump from 97 to 881 makes distance costs tangible without requiring advanced coding theory.

### Lines 294–301 — No universal distance for cryptographically relevant Shor

- The anchor is correct: required code distance follows from the total logical failure budget, number/type of logical operations, physical error model, decoder, factory architecture, and target success probability. There is no universal d≈21 for RSA-2048.
- The heading and extraction comment misleadingly resurrect precisely the claim the anchor denies. A particular Gidney–Ekerå-style resource estimate may choose a distance near this value under one physical-error/factory model, but it cannot be generalized to “cryptographically relevant Shor.”
- Resource estimates often use different distances for data blocks and distillation levels and may dynamically schedule factories; a single d can be an oversimplification even within one architecture.
- Cite a full parameterized estimate and show sensitivity to physical error (p). Rename the card “Shor code distance is architecture- and error-budget-dependent.”
- Verdict: **anchor verified; heading/comment invert its meaning and should be corrected urgently**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4.5/5.** Showing why one seductive distance number dissolves under an error budget teaches readers how to judge roadmaps.

### Lines 302–309 — Small-scale magic-state-distillation demonstrations

- Small-scale logical magic-state distillation has indeed been experimentally demonstrated in this period. Quantinuum-related work/preprints describe distillation and repeat-until-success protocols on trapped-ion hardware, while a December 2024 neutral-atom preprint reports logical magic-state distillation on a neutral-atom computer.
- The exact Quantinuum chronology may begin with a 2023 preprint and later publication, so “demonstrated in 2024–2025” must distinguish experiment date, preprint, and journal date.
- “Distillation” is not established merely by preparing a non-Clifford state: report input/output logical error, acceptance probability, code, logical operations, whether output error improves over inputs, and statistical uncertainty.
- Emphasize scale. These are proof-of-principle protocols, not factories delivering the volumes/fidelities required by large algorithms.
- Verdict: **broad milestone verified, but named papers and quantitative distillation criteria are required**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 5/5.** Turning several imperfect magical resources into one better one is both technically central and narratively delightful.

### Lines 310–317 — Demanding workloads requiring 10⁹ or more T gates

- The anchor’s lower-bound-style “roughly (10^9) T gates upward” is plausible across prominent fault-tolerant RSA factoring and high-accuracy chemistry/materials estimates, but it is far too broad to act as one resource fact.
- Resource papers count T gates, Toffolis/CCZ states, arbitrary rotations, or spacetime volume differently. Converting among them depends on synthesis precision, catalysis, factories, and chosen universal gate set.
- RSA-2048 estimates and chemistry estimates must be separate rows with algorithm version, target error/precision, logical qubits, non-Clifford count, physical assumptions, and runtime. Algorithmic improvements can move figures by orders of magnitude.
- The heading’s upper endpoint (10^{12}) is absent from the anchor and should not be introduced without a source; “upward” could extend well beyond it for some chemistry targets.
- Verdict: **correct order-of-magnitude warning, not a verified universal 10⁹–10¹² band**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4/5.** Billion-gate scale conveys the gulf vividly; a factory-throughput calculation would make it more than a frightening integer.

### Lines 318–325 — Scenario of tens of logical qubits around 2030

- The anchor labels this “one scenario,” which is appropriately conditional. The heading turns it into “10–100 logical qubits” and “early-FT useful chemistry,” neither of which the anchor explicitly promises.
- Tens of modest-distance logical qubits could support demonstrations beyond today’s NISQ reach, but usefulness depends on logical error rate, gate set, circuit depth, non-Clifford throughput, connectivity, runtime, and classical competition—not count alone.
- Vendor roadmaps are not independent forecasts. Compare several dated roadmaps with academic resource analyses and track demonstrated milestones, while clearly marking aspirations.
- “Chemistry” needs a named algorithm/problem; many fault-tolerant quantum chemistry advantages require far more than tens of logical qubits and deep rotation/T budgets.
- Verdict: **reasonable explicitly conditional scenario; heading overstates numeric range and useful-chemistry consequence**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4/5.** Near-horizon scenarios help orientation, but a concrete small logical algorithm would inspire more than a round-number forecast.

### Lines 326–333 — Scenario of thousands of logical qubits around 2035–2040

- Again, the anchor is explicitly a scenario, not a forecast. Thousands of logical qubits sustaining at least (10^9) logical operations are broadly in the resource territory discussed for large-scale algorithms, but exact RSA-2048 needs depend on architecture and algorithm.
- The heading inserts (10^3–10^4) and “for RSA-2048 Shor” beyond the anchor. These may be compatible with selected estimates but require their own citations and should not be sold as an industry-consensus 2035–2040 arrival date.
- Logical operation count is not the same as T count, Toffoli count, circuit depth, or surface-code cycle count. Runtime depends heavily on parallel factories and cycle time.
- Separate “resources an algorithm might require” from “when hardware might supply them.” Combining two uncertain models gives false calendar precision.
- Verdict: **resource scale directionally plausible; date and RSA-specific heading are speculative additions**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4/5.** The long-range horizon is useful only if uncertainty bands become part of the story rather than fine print.

### Lines 334–340 — Post-quantum migration as a 10–15-year exercise

- The order of magnitude is well supported as a policy/engineering horizon: NIST finalized its first PQC standards in 2024, urges organizations to begin immediately, and its transition plan targets deprecation/removal of quantum-vulnerable algorithms by 2035, with high-risk systems earlier. That is roughly an eleven-year standards-transition window.
- It is not a universal duration for every organization. Small greenfield services may migrate faster; embedded systems, PKI, protocols, supply chains, long-lived devices, and regulated infrastructure can take longer.
