- Migration has already begun and includes discovery/inventory, crypto agility, interoperability testing, procurement, hybrid deployment, certificate/key lifecycle, and retirement—not merely swapping algorithms.
- Cite current NIST IR 8547 status and jurisdiction-specific mandates; avoid implying the timeline is predicted from quantum-hardware roadmaps. “Harvest now, decrypt later” makes delay risky even if cryptographically relevant machines arrive later.
- Verdict: **well-supported planning-scale estimate when framed as a broad programme, not a fixed duration**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4.5/5.** Connecting uncertain hardware timing to a slow, concrete migration programme gives the chapter welcome real-world urgency.

### Chapter 25 fact-check mirror — second-pass file verdict

- Every card in this 340-line mirror has now been reviewed at card granularity, with correctness, sourcing, uncertainty, improvement, and reader-experience notes.
- Strongest factual defects: the Q2B keynote dated 2018 instead of 2017; current QV ceiling capped at (2^{20}) despite a reported (2^{25}); Quantum Volume defined as (n) and its heavy-output threshold miscalled fidelity; the 2023 Google d=3/5 experiment overstated as unambiguous below-threshold operation; and numerous headings that add claims absent from or contradicted by their anchors.
- The mirror repeatedly confuses four statuses: demonstrated component record, full-system median, announced roadmap, and available user hardware. It also merges physical, active, algorithmic, and logical qubit counts. Those should be mandatory structured fields in every hardware card.
- Headings are a systemic integrity risk. They add “hundreds of qubits,” “on a laptop,” “1.5× per year,” “plateaued,” “d=9–11 in progress,” universal d=21 for Shor, and RSA/chemistry projections that the anchors do not say. Audit headings against anchors before any claim-level fact-check proceeds.
- Reader experience: the chapter’s era narrative, hardware trade-offs, advantage/classical-response duels, and QEC crossover form an excellent arc. Its entertainment suffers mainly when a stream of unsourced percentages and roadmap dates resembles a vendor slide. Named case studies, status labels, and uncertainty bands would make it both more vivid and more credible.
- Overall verdict: **strong conceptual and narrative architecture, but high volatility and extraction-heading drift create major factual risk; extensive dated-source normalization required**.

## Second-pass review — `factcheck/part-10-practice-and-era/26-practical-access-and-hands-on-work.md`

### Lines 1–4 — File identity and extraction status

- The mirror and open-verification status are clear, but a May 2026 extraction is already stale for cloud provider rosters, pricing, device availability, SDK APIs, and free-tier quotas.
- This practical chapter needs an explicit page-level “checked on YYYY-MM-DD” plus links to live provider matrices. Static prose should teach how to verify access, while tables generated from current data can carry ephemeral details.
- The title promises hands-on work, so review criteria should include reproducibility, cost safety, credential handling, queue behaviour, and API-version pinning—not only factual descriptions.
- Verdict: **good scaffold; unusually high update burden needs an explicit maintenance mechanism**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4/5.** Practical access naturally invites action; a dated “what you can run today” box would create immediate momentum.

### Lines 6–13 — Workstation state-vector capacity

- The anchor is syntactically incomplete (“handles up to about”), so the actual claim exists only in the comment. A fact-check card must quote the full book sentence before it can be verified.
- The comment’s “30–35 qubits in a few GB” is arithmetically false for ordinary dense complex128 state vectors: 30 qubits require 16 GiB, 33 require 128 GiB, and 35 require 512 GiB before simulator overhead. Complex64 halves those byte counts, not the exponent.
- A normal 16–64-GiB workstation commonly supports about 29–31 complex128 qubits comfortably; 33–35 describes high-memory workstations/servers and may be runtime-prohibitive even if storage fits.
- Give a precision/RAM table and reserve headroom for copies/workspace. State vector capacity is (n\le\lfloor\log_2(M/b)\rfloor), where (b) is bytes per complex amplitude.
- Verdict: **unverifiable truncated anchor; comment materially understates memory and inflates “few GB” capacity**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4.5/5.** A one-line memory calculator would be more useful and satisfying than a magic qubit ceiling.

### Lines 14–21 — Claim that a GPU simulator doubles qubit capacity

- GPU acceleration ordinarily improves throughput, not the exponential memory law. Capacity is set by available accelerator memory and precision; many GPUs have less memory than a workstation/server, so they can support fewer dense-state qubits.
- Even doubling available memory adds only **one qubit**, because (2^{n+1}=2\cdot2^n). “Doubles qubit capacity” would require squaring memory to go from, for example, 30 to 60 qubits and is physically implausible for dense state vectors.
- cuQuantum/cuStateVec and qsim are category-mixed: cuStateVec is an NVIDIA acceleration library; qsim has CPU/GPU paths/integrations. Multi-GPU/distributed configurations need explicit device count and interconnect.
- Replace with “can substantially reduce runtime for fitting states; maximum qubits follow device/aggregate memory and may be lower or higher than the CPU host.”
- Verdict: **false as written; conflates speedup with exponential state capacity**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 5/5.** The correction—twice the memory buys one qubit—is a memorable practical lesson and mild shock.

### Lines 22–29 — Practical Clifford/stabilizer simulation scale

- Gottesman–Knill verifies polynomial classical simulation of Clifford circuits; thousands of qubits is a conservative practical scale for standard tableau simulators, and specialized tools can reach much larger favourable QEC workloads.
- Practical capacity depends on tableau density, gate/measurement count, shots, noise model, detector sampling, and implementation. Qubit count alone is especially weak here because storage may be (O(n^2)) or exploit sparsity/frames.
- “Clifford-only” should include stabilizer inputs and Pauli measurements/errors under the supported model, while clearly excluding arbitrary T gates or non-stabilizer states.
- Cite both theorem and an implementation benchmark (for example CHP and Stim) rather than using theorem status to prove an empirical thousands-qubit claim.
- Verdict: **verified in theory; practical scale is conservative but workload-dependent**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4.5/5.** The contrast with 30-ish dense qubits is excellent and teaches that circuit structure outranks raw width.

### Lines 30–37 — IBM Quantum devices and access plans

- Qiskit Runtime remains IBM’s primary managed execution interface, and current Heron devices are in the 133/156-qubit family; older Eagle-family 127-qubit systems may still appear in fleets/legacy discussion. Device availability changes by plan and region.
- The anchor is truncated after “in the,” again preventing verification of its actual count range. The comment’s “~100–200” is plausible for performance-focused IBM systems but should not imply all IBM demonstrated chips or all available backends fall there.
- “Free tier” should use IBM’s current plan name, monthly execution-time allowance, eligibility, fair-use limits, and whether sessions/dynamic circuits are included. “Limited shots” may be wrong if quota is measured in quantum execution time rather than a simple shot pool.
- Paid access is not only “dedicated time”; plans can include pay-as-you-go usage, premium capacity, reservations, or organizational contracts. Link the live plan page and teach users to inspect backend status/pricing before submission.
- Verdict: **platform/interface broadly correct; truncated anchor and unverified quota/billing language make the practical advice unsafe**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4/5.** Readers want a concrete first run; a cost-safe current walkthrough would be far more engaging than plan taxonomy.

### Lines 38–45 — Amazon Braket provider roster and billing

- The single-SDK, multi-provider access model and on-demand per-task plus per-shot pricing are verified. Reservation mode instead charges by reserved duration, so the anchor should not imply one model covers all execution.
- The current official Braket roster includes gate QPUs from AQT, IonQ, IQM, and Rigetti plus QuEra’s analog Aquila. **Quantinuum is not in the current official AWS list**, so its inclusion is false; AQT and IQM are omitted.
- QuEra’s program model is analog Hamiltonian simulation, not the same gate-circuit submission path. A “single SDK” does not mean one portable circuit runs unchanged across every modality/provider.
- Prices, regions, device families, minimum shots, cancellation terms, and task batching change. Link the live pricing/device pages and show how to use the AWS cost calculator/budgets.
- Verdict: **access/billing model verified; vendor list is stale/wrong and modality portability is overstated**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4.5/5.** One doorway to several hardware species is exciting; the analog-versus-gate fork makes the doorway intellectually interesting too.

### Lines 46–53 — Azure Quantum provider roster and QDK positioning

- Microsoft’s April 2026 documentation verifies Azure Quantum access to IonQ, Pasqal, Quantinuum, and Rigetti, subject to region/account availability. The listed roster is therefore current at review time.
- The provider target table itself contains version/status inconsistencies (for example varying H2 qubit counts across targets), reinforcing the need to point readers to live target metadata rather than freeze counts in prose.
- Q# and the modern Quantum Development Kit are Microsoft’s first-party development path, but “on top” can imply they are required. Azure also accepts QIR and provider-specific formats and supports Qiskit-related workflows.
- Explain workspace/subscription/provider-plan setup, quotas, and region restrictions. A gateway existing does not guarantee a reader’s account can submit to every listed QPU.
- Verdict: **vendor list verified as of 2026-04-23; SDK and availability phrasing need nuance**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4/5.** The breadth is useful; a tiny decision tree by language and hardware would make it genuinely hands-on.

### Lines 54–61 — Google Quantum AI access restrictions

- Restricted/selective access has historically characterized Google’s superconducting QPUs; unlike IBM/AWS/Azure, there is no general public pay-per-shot Willow queue documented here. Research collaboration or approved programmes are plausible typical routes.
- “Typically need” is deliberately cautious but still needs a current official access page. Quantum Engine APIs, simulators, published datasets, Cirq/qsim, and actual QPU access should not be conflated.
- State whether the claim refers to Google Cloud Quantum Engine, Willow/Sycamore hardware, or external research programmes, and list any application route rather than leaving readers at a closed door.
- Verdict: **likely correct at a high level, but current official eligibility/process evidence is missing**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 3.5/5.** Honest restriction prevents frustration; offering public datasets/simulators as the alternative would preserve momentum.

### Lines 62–69 — Direct-vendor and aggregator access models

- The anchor’s main point is sound: reservations, subscriptions, contracts, per-shot/per-task billing, and aggregator-only routes vary significantly by vendor and product.
- QuEra Aquila remains available through Amazon Braket at review time, so “historically” understates that current route. Verify whether any direct commercial/research access also exists before saying “rather than directly.”
- Aggregators may transmit circuit/program metadata to third-party provider infrastructure, introduce regional availability and separate cloud charges, and expose different device capabilities than a direct contract.
- Replace anecdotal wording with a live matrix: device, modality, direct route, aggregator(s), geography, pricing disclosure, and reservation/on-demand support.
- Verdict: **verified general variability; QuEra example needs current rather than merely historical status and exclusivity proof**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 3.5/5.** Necessary procurement reality, though a matrix would be less tiring than prose full of commercial qualifiers.

### Lines 70–77 — Pricing opacity and paid experimentation

- The anchor is appropriately nonnumeric and largely correct. AWS publishes detailed per-task/per-shot and reservation prices, while other providers may expose plan-specific rates, credits, negotiated allocations, or no public list.
- “Serious experimentation typically” is a sociological generalization. Academic credits, hackathons, partner programmes, national facilities, queue-based free allocations, and institutional subscriptions can support serious work without the researcher directly paying.
- Define “serious” by shots, circuits, calibration windows, reservation needs, or reproducibility. Teach readers to cap cloud spend, estimate shots/tasks, account for failed tasks, and check refund policies.
- Verdict: **prudent warning, but avoid equating scientific seriousness with paid access**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4/5.** Cost realism is welcome; one worked $ estimate would be both useful and sobering.

### Lines 78–85 — Qiskit and Runtime Primitives as the IBM path

- Qiskit is IBM’s official primary SDK and is mature and extensively documented; those qualitative descriptions are fair, though “mature” should not imply API stability across major versions.
- Runtime SamplerV2 and EstimatorV2 are central abstractions for sampled distributions and expectation values, but “the right abstraction for most work” is advice, not a fact. Pulse/control work, backend characterization, dynamic circuits, and low-level experiments need other interfaces.
- Specify V2 primitives and current package/runtime versions; older tutorials using V1 APIs are a major practical failure mode. Estimator semantics and mitigation/resilience options should be demonstrated rather than assumed.
- Verdict: **official-tool claim verified; universal recommendation should be scoped and version-pinned**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4/5.** A clear default reduces choice paralysis; showing when to leave the default makes the advice feel expert rather than promotional.

### Lines 86–93 — PennyLane interfaces and multi-backend positioning

- PennyLane remains differentiation-first and multi-backend, with NumPy/autograd-style, JAX, and PyTorch workflows central to its interface design.
- The TensorFlow entry is stale as a recommendation: PennyLane 0.45 documentation warns that TensorFlow support is no longer maintained as of v0.44 and recommends JAX or PyTorch. Legacy functionality appearing in docs does not equal supported strategic integration.
- “Integrates with NumPy” should distinguish `pennylane.numpy`/Autograd from ordinary NumPy arrays, which do not automatically carry every differentiation behaviour.
- Hardware/backend support comes through plugins with independent version compatibility and maintenance status. Name tested versions and check plugin release cadence before promising portability.
- Verdict: **core positioning verified; TensorFlow must be labelled unmaintained and interface wording/versioning tightened**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4/5.** The differentiable-programming angle is appealing; a ten-line JAX QNode would make it concrete immediately.

### Lines 94–101 — tket/pytket as a multi-vendor compiler

- Verified at a high level: tket is Quantinuum’s optimizing quantum compiler/toolkit, and `pytket` exposes it in Python with extension packages for multiple ecosystems and hardware services.
- “Vendor-agnostic by design” is fair for compilation IR/passes but does not mean every backend is equally supported. Current docs list maintained Braket, IQM, QIR, Qiskit, Quantinuum, cuTensorNet, Qulacs, and qujax extensions while marking several older extensions unmaintained.
- A notable current migration: `pytket-quantinuum` v0.56 no longer handles submission to Quantinuum devices; users are directed to `qnexus`. Thus recommending “tket via pytket” for Quantinuum execution without qnexus is operationally stale.
- “Mature” is evaluative but reasonable; pin `pytket` and extension versions because their Python-version ranges and backend APIs differ.
- Verdict: **compiler/portability claim verified; current Quantinuum submission path and maintained-extension set need updating**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4/5.** Compiler portability is useful but abstract; a before/after two-qubit-gate count across targets would make it fun.

### Lines 102–109 — Microsoft Quantum Resource Estimator superlative

- Microsoft’s Quantum Resource Estimator is a substantial public tool for fault-tolerant resource forecasting, supports Q# workflows, and can be run locally without an Azure account according to current documentation.
- “The most widely used public tool” cannot be verified without usage data and unfairly excludes Qualtran, OpenFermion resource workflows, pyLIQTR, Azure/QDK alternatives, vendor estimators, and paper-specific code. “Gold standard” in the comment is similarly subjective and absent from the anchor.
- Resource estimators differ in layer: logical algorithm counts, synthesis, QEC/factory compilation, physical architecture, scheduling, and error budgets. No single tool is authoritative across all layers.
- Replace the popularity superlative with a capability description and include at least two independently developed alternatives. State supported QDK version and model assumptions.
- Verdict: **tool/capability credible; popularity/authority superlative unsupported**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 3.5/5.** Resource estimation can feel bureaucratic; comparing one algorithm under two qubit/error models would reveal its power.

### Lines 110–117 — Qiskit deprecations between versions 1.0 and 1.4

- The anchor is truncated after “between,” so it does not contain the version range the comment says appears in the book. This mirrors the earlier incomplete-anchor defect and prevents exact verification.
- Qiskit did deprecate and remove APIs throughout the 1.x transition and beyond; that general warning is incontrovertible but too vague to help a reader repair code.
- A 1.0-to-1.4 statement needs named APIs, deprecation and removal versions, migration replacements, and current supported version. Deprecation is not removal; examples should fail in CI against the book’s pinned environment before being labelled broken.
- Link the official migration/deprecation guides and supply a lockfile/requirements constraint rather than narrating churn abstractly.
- Verdict: **general phenomenon true; truncated anchor and unnamed APIs make the card non-verifiable and non-actionable**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 3/5.** Version churn is never charming, but a compact “old → new” table can at least remove anxiety.

### Lines 118–125 — Trapped-ion hardware choice summary

- Approximately 99.9% deployed-system two-qubit fidelity, all-to-all effective connectivity, tens of qubits, and slower primitive gates form a fair high-level description of current Quantinuum H2/IonQ-class systems.
- “Approaching 99.9%” is stale wording when Quantinuum’s current sheet lists typical 99.9% and Oxford Ionics/IonQ reports 99.99% component demonstrations. Keep system metrics separate from record gates.
- All-to-all may be mediated by ion motion/reconfiguration and does not imply every pair can gate simultaneously. Parallel entangling-operation limits and transport/cooling overhead matter.
- “Slow” is relative: primitive gates are slower than superconducting gates, but avoided SWAPs and higher fidelity may reduce total compiled circuit cost. Compare a workload, not just clocks.
- Verdict: **good orientation, but fidelity status and connectivity/throughput nuance need updating**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4.5/5.** This is a crisp engineering trade-off and becomes especially engaging with one compiled-circuit race.

### Lines 126–133 — IBM scale, public availability, heavy-hex, and fidelity

- IBM provides unusually broad public/cloud access to 100+-qubit superconducting systems, and Eagle/Heron families use sparse heavy-hex-derived connectivity. “Hundreds” is defensible for some fleets/modules but current performance-focused individual Heron QPUs are 133/156 qubits.
- “Largest scale” needs a comparison class. Neutral-atom analog systems and annealers expose more physical qubits; IBM demonstrated 433/1,121-qubit chips but does not foreground them as its best current user hardware.
- Two-qubit fidelity “around 99.5%” is too pessimistic for current Heron median reporting around 99.88%, while individual/system layer metrics vary. It may describe older Eagle generations.
- Replace the superlative with exact available backend examples and backend-reported calibration ranges, date-stamped. Mention queue/access-plan constraints.
- Verdict: **public-access and sparse-connectivity summary sound; scale superlative is ambiguous and fidelity is stale**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4/5.** The heavy-hex constraint gives readers a real mapping puzzle; a tiny topology diagram would outperform adjectives.

### Lines 134–141 — Neutral-atom scale and Hamiltonian-simulation strengths

- QuEra Aquila and Pasqal systems do expose hundreds-scale neutral-atom/Rydberg arrays or targets, with programmable/reconfigurable geometries. The platform is particularly natural for analog Hamiltonian simulation and optimization/physics problems expressible through Rydberg interactions.
- “Reconfigurable layouts” needs operational scope: atoms may be arranged before evolution and newer systems can move/reuse atoms, but not every arbitrary dynamic connectivity graph is available during a programme.
- Pasqal access/target names and qubit counts should come from the live Azure/provider table; QuEra Aquila’s Braket AHS model uses a different programme schema from gate circuits.
- “Strong” means architectural fit, not demonstrated quantum advantage on useful applications. Include constraints on geometry, blockade radius, controls, noise, and observable readout.
- Verdict: **verified high-level characterization with access/model and reconfiguration caveats**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4.5/5.** Drawing a Hamiltonian directly as an atom pattern is one of the chapter’s most appealing hands-on ideas.

### Lines 142–149 — D-Wave Advantage scale and computational model

- “Thousands of qubits” is verified. The current generally available Advantage2 system has more than 4,400 qubits and over 40,000 couplers on Zephyr topology; prior Advantage systems used a different topology/count.
- The product label “D-Wave Advantage” is now generation-ambiguous and should be updated to Advantage2 or presented historically with dates.
- The conceptual caveat is essential and correct: quantum annealing is not the universal gate model, so its qubits, connectivity, programme semantics, error model, and benchmark claims cannot be directly compared with circuit QPUs.
- Explain embedding overhead: a logical optimization variable may consume chains of physical annealing qubits, so 4,400 physical qubits do not imply a 4,400-variable dense problem.
- Verdict: **verified scale/model distinction; product generation is stale and embedding overhead should be explicit**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4.5/5.** The different model adds welcome variety; chain embedding is a concrete twist readers will remember.

### Lines 150–157 — Shot-count standard error

- The full anchor is truncated (“For a probability”), but the comment reconstructs the intended derivation. For (N) independent Bernoulli shots with probability (p), (mathrm{SE}(\hat p)=\sqrt{p(1-p)/N}).
- At (p\approx0.5), this is (0.5/\sqrt N); for (N=10^4), one standard error is 0.005. That arithmetic is correct.
- Calling 0.005 “precision” is ambiguous. A normal-approximation 95% margin is about 0.0098, and exact/binomial or Wilson intervals are better near 0/1 or for small (N).
- Hardware shots may not be IID due to drift, batching, correlations, readout bias, and circuit changes. Mitigation can increase variance; expectation values with outcomes ±1 use a related but different formula.
- Verdict: **verified IID-binomial derivation; restore the full anchor and define confidence/precision**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 5/5.** This is immediately useful and gives readers a satisfying reason why cloud runs consume so many shots.

### Lines 158–165 — Zenodo and reproducibility norms

- Many journals, funders, and conferences encourage or require code/data availability statements or deposits, and Zenodo is a common route because it issues persistent DOIs. The anchor wisely says policies vary.
- “A Zenodo record or companion repository” conflates archival and live-development roles. GitHub alone is not archival; a tagged release deposited to Zenodo or another trusted repository plus checksums/environment metadata is stronger.
- “Many venues” should be supported by representative policies rather than inferred from good practice. Sensitive/proprietary hardware calibration data may require documented exceptions.
- Add a reproducibility checklist: code commit, environment lockfile/container, raw and processed data, calibration snapshot, circuit/QASM/QIR, seeds, backend/job IDs, analysis script, licence, and persistent DOI.
- Verdict: **credible norm, but venue-policy evidence and archive-versus-repository distinction are needed**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4/5.** A practical reproducibility bundle gives readers a professional finish line and can feel empowering rather than administrative.

### Lines 166–173 — arXiv/quant-ph as the primary dissemination route

- arXiv `quant-ph` is unquestionably central to academic quantum-information/computing dissemination, and preprints often precede journal publication.
- “Most academic quantum-computing research” is a quantitative claim requiring bibliometric evidence and scope rules. Relevant work also appears under condensed matter, computer science, cryptography, high-energy theory, optimization, and publisher proceedings without a `quant-ph` cross-list.
- Corporate technical reports, patents, hardware announcements, and confidential/negative results are systematically underrepresented, so arXiv is not “almost everything.”
- Rephrase as “a large share of research is posted to arXiv, often in quant-ph, before peer review.” Teach readers to check version history, journal reference, comments, withdrawals, and follow-up criticism.
- Verdict: **cultural direction correct; majority/scope claim unmeasured and category too narrow**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4.5/5.** Showing how to follow a paper from v1 through critique to publication turns literature reading into detective work.

### Lines 174–180 — Advantage claims and classical-response checking

- The methodological advice is excellent: before repeating a clean quantum/classical separation, search for later classical algorithms, corrected cost models, changed fidelity targets, and independent reproductions.
- Sycamore and Jiuzhang are suitable examples, though their classical responses differ: RCS saw rapid tensor-network/storage/sampling advances; Gaussian boson sampling saw detector/noise-aware and approximate simulators under different metrics.
- The comment adds a “within 12–24 months” pattern not present in the anchor and not universally true. Some responses appeared within days or months; others evolved for years, and absence of a rebuttal is not evidence of hardness.
- Extend the checklist beyond dates: equal task, fidelity/distance metric, sample count, preprocessing, hardware cost/energy, projected versus executed time, public code/data, and best-known algorithm at citation date.
- Verdict: **verified and highly valuable review practice; avoid a fabricated universal response window**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 5/5.** Treating advantage as an evolving scientific contest is both accurate and intrinsically gripping.

### Chapter 26 fact-check mirror — second-pass file verdict

- Every card in this 180-line mirror has now received a granular second-pass review and reader-experience assessment.
- Strongest defects: “GPU acceleration doubles qubit capacity”; 30–35 dense complex128 qubits allegedly fitting in a few GB; Amazon Braket incorrectly listing Quantinuum while omitting AQT/IQM; PennyLane treating TensorFlow as maintained; stale `pytket` Quantinuum submission guidance; and several anchors truncated before their decisive number/version.
- Practical volatility is the systemic risk. Device rosters, prices, regions, quotas, SDKs, and API paths should be generated or linked from dated live sources, while durable prose teaches selection criteria and verification steps.
- A second systemic problem is recommendation language masquerading as fact (“right abstraction,” “most widely used,” “largest scale,” “mature”). These judgments can remain, but should be labelled editorial and supported by defined criteria.
- Reader experience is potentially excellent: memory calculators, cost estimates, same-circuit hardware comparisons, and reproducibility checklists would turn the chapter into an inviting laboratory guide. Static vendor catalogues and truncated claims currently interrupt that promise.
- Overall verdict: **high practical value and strong instincts, but several operationally dangerous current-state errors require correction before readers follow the instructions**.

## Second-pass review — `factcheck/part-11-applications/27-cryptography-and-security.md`

### Lines 1–4 — File identity and inherited verification status

- The mirror is unusually compact and says it was seeded from earlier ledger passes rather than from a fresh extraction. That provenance is useful, but it increases the risk that unextracted book claims remain outside the card set.
- Unlike the previous mirrors, it does not state globally whether verification is open or complete. Individual cards say “confirmed/updated,” yet current-state cryptographic standards can still change through errata and draft progress.
- Add extraction coverage statistics, last checked date, and explicit distinction between final standard, public draft, selected algorithm, and unpublished/internal drafting milestone.
- Verdict: **clear origin note, but coverage and status semantics are weaker than neighbouring mirrors**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 3.5/5.** Clean and short; a standards timeline would make the otherwise tabular material easier to enjoy.

### Lines 6–12 — ML-KEM-768 byte sizes

- FIPS 203 Table 3 verifies the values: ML-KEM-768 encapsulation/public key 1,184 bytes, ciphertext 1,088 bytes, and shared secret 32 bytes. The decapsulation/private key, omitted from the anchor, is 2,400 bytes.
- FIPS terminology is “encapsulation key” and “decapsulation key”; “public key” is familiar but the standard term should appear at least once.
- These are serialized algorithm-object lengths, not certificate, protocol-message, or implementation-memory sizes. TLS/PKI wrappers add framing and may combine classical/hybrid keys.
- NIST currently lists potential FIPS 203 errata, so cite table/version/date and monitor corrections, even though none identified here alter these sizes.
- Verdict: **confirmed**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4/5.** Concrete byte costs make migration real; comparing them with X25519/RSA handshake objects would add punch.

### Lines 13–19 — ML-DSA-65 public-key and signature sizes

- FIPS 204 Table 2 verifies 1,952-byte public keys and 3,309-byte signatures for ML-DSA-65; the private key is 4,032 bytes in the standard serialization.
- The correction from 3,293 to 3,309 is important and plausibly reflects draft-to-final changes. Record the exact draft/version that contained the old number rather than saying “likely,” which leaves the error genealogy uncertain.
- Signature length is fixed for the parameter set, but certificates/protocols add algorithm identifiers and framing. Seed-only storage options discussed by FIPS should not be confused with interoperable private-key encoding.
- NIST’s February 2026 planning note points to minor FIPS 204 errata; track them even though the table values remain authoritative now.
- Verdict: **confirmed current final-standard values; document the old-value source rather than speculate**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4/5.** The 16-byte draft/final discrepancy is a nice demonstration of why standards versioning matters.

### Lines 20–26 — SLH-DSA-SHA2-128s byte sizes

- FIPS 205 verifies a 32-byte public key and 7,856-byte signature for SLH-DSA-SHA2-128s; the compact public key versus large stateless hash-based signature is the intended trade-off.
- Include the 64-byte private-key size and distinguish the “s” small-signature parameter set from “f” fast variants. Performance and signature count, not just bytes, guide selection.
- As elsewhere, these are raw standardized object sizes, not complete certificate or network payloads.
- Verdict: **confirmed**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4.5/5.** The 32-byte/7.8-KiB asymmetry is striking and naturally invites explanation of the design trade-off.

### Lines 27–33 — Falcon/FN-DSA and alleged FIPS 206 draft status

- NIST did select Falcon for standardization and names the standardized algorithm FN-DSA (FFT over NTRU-Lattice-Based Digital Signature Algorithm), with FIPS 206 intended as its standard number.
- The anchor’s “renamed FN-DSA in NIST’s draft” is premature: as of this July 2026 check, NIST’s public material still speaks of the draft FIPS 206 **when it is released**, and no FIPS 206 initial-public-draft publication appears in NIST’s current catalogue.
- “IPD submitted August 2025” appears to describe an internal workflow/presentation milestone, not a public initial draft available for review. Internal submission is not a standards status readers can independently verify and should not be labelled IPD without a public document URL.
- Replace with: “Falcon was selected and will be standardized as FN-DSA in forthcoming FIPS 206; no public FIPS 206 draft was located as of 2026-07-21.” Update automatically when NIST publishes it.
- Verdict: **algorithm/name/standard number verified; claimed public-draft status is unsupported and misleading**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4/5.** The rename itself is mildly arcane; a status ladder makes the standards race comprehensible.

### Lines 34–40 — Finalization of FIPS 203, 204, and 205

- Verified from NIST: all three standards were finalized and published on 13 August 2024—FIPS 203 (ML-KEM), FIPS 204 (ML-DSA), and FIPS 205 (SLH-DSA).
- Calling all three “encryption standards” is common in NIST’s press headline but technically loose: FIPS 203 is a KEM and FIPS 204/205 are digital-signature standards, not message-encryption algorithms.
- Note current errata/planning notes and distinguish publication from protocol adoption/accreditation. A finalized primitive does not instantly update TLS, PKI, HSM validation, or every regulatory profile.
- Verdict: **confirmed date and identities; use precise KEM/signature terminology**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4.5/5.** A clear standards milestone gives the security chapter welcome concreteness and urgency.

### Lines 41–47 — HQC selection and future FIPS 207

- NIST selected HQC in March 2025 as an additional KEM to provide code-based mathematical diversity beyond ML-KEM; describing it as the outcome of the fourth round is correct.
- FIPS 207 is the planned standard number, but it remains forthcoming. A 2025 NIST presentation on “FIPS 207: HQC-KEM” and plans to convert the specification into FIPS format do not equal a public draft or final standard.
- “Fourth-round KEM” can be misread as fourth-ranked; say “selected after NIST’s fourth evaluation round.” Explain that ML-KEM remains the primary/general recommendation while HQC adds diversification.
- Record parameter-set and performance changes only from the eventual draft/final text, not submission packages or presentations.
- Verdict: **confirmed selection/date/planned number; retain forthcoming status explicitly**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4/5.** Mathematical diversity is a good plot point: standards bodies deliberately avoid a single cryptographic monoculture.

### Lines 48–54 — RSA-2048 physical-resource estimates

- The two cited estimates are accurately summarized. Gidney–Ekerå estimated about 20 million noisy physical qubits and roughly eight hours under its surface-code/hardware assumptions; Gidney’s May 2025 preprint estimates fewer than one million noisy qubits and less than one week.
- These are points on different space–time trade-offs, not a simple 20× improvement in every dimension. The 2025 result spends longer and adopts approximate residue arithmetic, yoked surface-code storage, magic-state cultivation, and explicit physical assumptions.
- “Resource bounds” is too theorem-like: these are architecture- and error-model-dependent estimates, not rigorous lower/upper bounds on all implementations.
- The field moved again in 2026 with modular-atomic and other proposals, so present these as dated influential estimates, not the current universal frontier. Keep Chapter 15/27 cross-references synchronized via a shared source table.
- Verdict: **verified as dated estimates; label assumptions, space–time trade-off, preprint status, and non-finality**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 5/5.** Twenty million in hours versus under a million in days beautifully demonstrates algorithm/architecture co-design and the moving threat model.

### Chapter 27 fact-check mirror — second-pass file verdict

- All seven cards in this 54-line mirror have now been reviewed against current primary standards/papers, including reader experience and improvement opportunities.
- The fixed FIPS object sizes, August 2024 finalization, HQC selection, and two RSA estimates are substantively correct.
- The strongest defect is standards-status inflation around FN-DSA/FIPS 206: an apparent internal August 2025 submission was described as a NIST draft despite no public FIPS 206 IPD being locatable as of 2026-07-21.
- The mirror should use a machine-readable standards-status table with `selected`, `internal drafting`, `public IPD`, `final`, `errata`, and `checked_at` fields. It also needs a full extraction coverage check because its compact inherited card set may omit smaller book claims.
- Reader experience is strongest when byte sizes expose engineering trade-offs and resource estimates show moving targets; acronyms without protocol comparisons or status ladders are the main entertainment drag.
- Overall verdict: **mostly accurate and refreshingly concise, with one important public-versus-internal draft-status correction and a need to prove extraction completeness**.

## Second-pass review — `factcheck/part-11-applications/28-scientific-computing-and-physical-simulation.md`

### Lines 1–4 — File identity, extraction date, and open verification status

- The filename/book-path pairing is clear, and the May 2026 extraction date usefully dates the mirror. This chapter contains unusually volatile resource estimates, however, so extraction date and claim-verification date must be separate fields.
- “Verification status: open” is honest but underspecified: it does not reveal extraction completeness, number of checked cards, or whether an open card is unsearched, disputed, or awaiting a primary source.
- Add a coverage count and per-card `checked_at`/status vocabulary. A final file verdict should never silently convert an incomplete extraction into an apparently complete factual audit.
- Verdict: **sound provenance shell, but insufficient state and coverage metadata**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 3.5/5.** The compact header stays out of the way; a one-line progress/status summary would make the research trail more satisfying to follow.

### Lines 6–12 — Feynman’s lecture and the publication date of “Simulating Physics with Computers”

- The famous paper appeared in the *International Journal of Theoretical Physics* in June 1982, so 1982 is the correct publication year.
- Calling it a “1982 lecture” blurs two events: the argument originated in Feynman’s May 1981 Physics of Computation conference contribution and was published in 1982. The prose should say “1981 lecture, published in 1982” or simply “1982 paper.”
- The historical thesis also deserves precision. Feynman did not merely observe that quantum systems are expensive on ordinary computers; he discussed universal simulation and proposed using quantum-mechanical computers for quantum probabilities. Avoid retroactively attributing today’s formal complexity claims to that text.
- Give the journal citation/DOI rather than a generic historical source, and distinguish the paper from Manin’s earlier related observation if the chapter makes a priority claim.
- Verdict: **core attribution right; lecture and publication dates are conflated**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 5/5.** This is a compelling origin scene, especially if the 1981 room and the 1982 publication are treated as a tiny chronology rather than collapsed into a date label.

### Lines 13–19 — Born–Oppenheimer mass-ratio justification

- The mass contrast is real: even a proton is about 1,836 electron masses, and ordinary nuclei are heavier still. “Thousands of times heavier” is therefore broadly serviceable for nuclei other than bare hydrogen.
- Mass alone does not make Born–Oppenheimer universally valid. The useful separation involves electronic and nuclear energy/time scales, with vibrational frequencies depending roughly on inverse square-root reduced mass as well as the potential-energy surface.
- “Nuclei move much more slowly” is intuitive but classical-sounding shorthand. The approximation factorizes electronic and nuclear motion parametrically; it can fail near degeneracies, avoided crossings, conical intersections, photochemical processes, and for especially light nuclei.
- Name these limits in one sentence so readers do not mistake a powerful approximation for a theorem following solely from a mass ratio.
- Verdict: **good first-order motivation, but incomplete as a justification and missing standard failure modes**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4.5/5.** The elephant-and-sparrow mass contrast is memorable; one vivid nonadiabatic counterexample would prevent the explanation from feeling too frictionless.

### Lines 26–31 — Jordan–Wigner Pauli-string weight

- In the standard Jordan–Wigner ordering, a creation or annihilation operator on mode (p) contains an (X/Y) endpoint preceded by a parity string of (Z) operators, so worst-case Pauli weight is (O(M)).
- Mapped hopping and interaction terms inherit ordering-dependent parity strings; cancellations can shorten particular products, so “local fermionic operator” must not imply a geometrically local qubit operator of universally maximal weight.
- The quoted anchor ends at “weight up to” and omits the claimed bound. This is another extraction defect: the mirror verifies a reconstruction in its source note rather than the actual preserved sentence.
- Orbital ordering matters greatly in practice. Put strongly coupled/local modes near one another, and distinguish Pauli weight from two-qubit gate count, routed depth, and measurement cost.
- Verdict: **asymptotic worst-case claim correct; anchor truncated and practical meaning needs qualification**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4.5/5.** The parity string is a satisfying visual mechanism; showing one mapped operator would be more engaging than giving only big-O notation.

### Lines 32–38 — Bravyi–Kitaev logarithmic operator support

- The standard Bravyi–Kitaev construction stores parity information in a binary-tree/Fenwick-tree-like data structure. A single fermionic operation touches (O(log M)) qubits rather than the Jordan–Wigner worst case (O(M)); this is supported by the foundational mapping literature.
- The exact Pauli support depends on the Bravyi–Kitaev variant, register size, index, and definitions of update, parity, and flip sets. Products forming Hamiltonian terms can carry different constant factors.
- “Achieves (O(log M)) Pauli weight” does not by itself establish (O(log M)) circuit depth on constrained hardware. Routing, basis changes, exponentiation strategy, and parallel scheduling remain separate costs.
- The anchor “A tree-structured mapping that achieves” is again incomplete and should include the bound it is meant to support.
- Verdict: **asymptotic mapping advantage verified; incomplete anchor and risk of translating support directly into depth**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4.5/5.** The binary-tree parity ledger is inherently elegant; a side-by-side path diagram would make the logarithm feel earned.

### Lines 153–159 — Hohenberg–Kohn theorem and the foundation of DFT

- Degenerate ground states and representability subtleties deserve a light caveat at this level. Practical Kohn–Sham DFT depends on approximate exchange-correlation functionals and is not made exact merely by invoking Hohenberg–Kohn.

- Verdict: **foundational statement essentially correct; incomplete anchor and likely overcompression of the theorem/practical-method distinction**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4.5/5.** Replacing a many-electron wavefunction with a three-dimensional density is a wonderful conceptual reveal; the unknown-functional catch keeps the reveal intellectually honest.

- Verdict: **verified landmark attribution; qualify priority and emphasize the reduced 1+1D few-qubit encoding**.
