### Lines 228–234 — Claimed resources for useful 3+1D SU(3) lattice QCD

- Full 3+1-dimensional SU(3) lattice gauge theory with dynamical fermions, controlled continuum/volume limits, and real-time observables is unquestionably a formidable quantum-resource target.
- The comment’s “(10^7+) logical qubits and (10^{20}) T gates” is not supported by a named resource study. Existing algorithm papers often give symbolic scaling in volume, evolution time, precision, gauge-field truncation, and encoding; inserting “useful” physical parameters is highly scenario-dependent.
- Define lattice spacing/volume, quark flavors/masses, gauge truncation, observable, real versus Euclidean time, state preparation, target precision, algorithm, and error correction. Logical-qubit and T-count figures without these inputs are not reproducible.
- The anchor sensibly says only “enormous figures,” while the comment manufactures precision. Either cite the exact calculation or retain qualitative language.
- Verdict: **qualitative difficulty certain; quoted (10^7/10^{20}) resource pair is unsupported and too model-dependent to stand alone**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4.5/5.** The jump from four ions to collider-relevant QCD is dramatic; a parameterized scale ladder would be more gripping than two unexplained giant numbers.

### Lines 235–241 — Carleman-linearization efficiency and the (R<1) condition

- The cited 2021 nonlinear-differential-equation algorithm analyzes dissipative quadratic systems via Carleman linearization and obtains efficient scaling under a condition commonly expressed as (R<1), balancing nonlinearity/initial magnitude against linear dissipation.
- Calling (R) merely “roughly the strength of nonlinearity relative to dissipation” is acceptable intuition but not enough for a theorem claim. Its exact definition includes norms and problem parameters and may depend on rescaling/assumptions.
- “Provably efficient only” risks converting a sufficient condition for this analysis/algorithm into a universal impossibility statement. The paper proves efficiency in the dissipative regime; it does not prove that every quantum algorithm is inefficient whenever (R\ge1).
- Give the exact definition, sparsity/oracle/output assumptions, truncation error, time dependence, and what “solution” means—typically a quantum state or observable rather than all grid values.
- Verdict: **specific sufficient condition is broadly verified; “only” overstates it as a necessary barrier and (R) needs its formal definition**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4.5/5.** A clean red line at (R=1) is memorable, but presenting it as an algorithmic convergence frontier rather than a law of nature makes the story sharper.

### Lines 242–247 — Attribution of the 2021 Carleman algorithm

- The author chain Liu–Kolden–Krovi–Loureiro–Trivisa–Childs and year 2021 correspond to the dissipative nonlinear differential-equation work; retaining all authors avoids the ambiguity of a generic “Liu et al.”
- The card gives no title, venue/identifier, or citations for “subsequent refinements.” That last phrase is a separate plural factual claim and must be expanded into named papers with what each refinement changes.
- Separate the original algorithm’s assumptions from later changes in nonlinearity order, dissipativity, convergence, time dependence, or complexity. Otherwise improvements may be silently attributed backward.
- Verdict: **original attribution appears correct; the refinement lineage is unverified and bibliographically incomplete**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 3.5/5.** An author list alone is inert; a one-sentence “what changed next” sequence would turn it into intellectual progress.

### Lines 248–254 — Condition number of a three-dimensional Poisson discretization

- For a regular three-dimensional grid with (n) points per dimension and (N=n^3) total unknowns, the standard second-difference Laplacian has condition number (O(n^2)=O(N^{2/3})) under common boundary/scaling conventions. The source note’s derivation is sound.
- The anchor truncates before the condition number. It also fails to define whether (N) is total grid points or points per dimension—a distinction that changes the displayed exponent.
- A growing condition number can erase a naive exponential-in-dimension linear-system advantage, but total complexity also depends on sparsity, state preparation, preconditioning, desired observable, and output/readout. It does not categorically “eliminate exponential speedup” in every formulation.
- Mention that effective preconditioners must themselves be efficiently implementable in the quantum access model; importing a powerful classical preconditioner is not free.
- Verdict: **(O(N^{2/3})) verified for (N) total points on a standard 3D grid; anchor/variable definition and speedup conclusion need qualification**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4.5/5.** The condition number quietly eating the promised speedup is an excellent cautionary twist; a three-line scaling calculation makes it satisfying.

### Lines 255–261 — CCSD(T) as a “gold standard” and (N^7) scaling

- Conventional canonical CCSD(T) has leading (O(N^7)) computational scaling under common orbital-count assumptions, with substantial storage and lower-order costs. The parenthetical-triples correction is the source of the seventh-power step.
- “Gold standard” is established community shorthand for many closed-shell, single-reference, weak-to-moderately correlated molecules, but it is praise with a domain, not a guarantee. Bond breaking, transition metals, open shells, near degeneracy, relativistic effects, and basis incompleteness can defeat it.
- Modern local, density-fitted, explicitly correlated, and reduced-scaling variants change practical scaling/accuracy trade-offs; distinguish canonical formal scaling from implementation behavior.
- The anchor is truncated immediately before the exponent, so the card fails to quote the very fact its comment verifies.
- Verdict: **canonical (N^7) and scoped reputation are correct; preserve failure regimes and repair the anchor**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4/5.** “Gold standard with a seventh-power bill” is an effective contrast; one failure case would keep the metallurgy from sounding magical.

### Lines 262–268 — DMRG accuracy and cylinder-width limits

- DMRG is exceptionally effective for one-dimensional gapped systems with modest entanglement, but “essentially exact in 1D” still depends on bond dimension, system size, gap/criticality, boundary conditions, and convergence checks.
- Width 8–12 is a recognizable practical range for demanding two-dimensional fermionic/correlated models on cylinders, not a universal limit. Accessible width depends exponentially on entanglement across the cut and varies with model, geometry, doping, symmetry exploitation, precision, and computational resources.
- The anchor truncates before the width and the comment gives no benchmark. Some spin models reach wider cylinders; some frustrated fermion problems remain difficult at narrower ones.
- Phrase this as a representative current range for a named model such as doped Hubbard, with bond dimensions and truncation errors, rather than as a property of DMRG itself.
- Verdict: **qualitative geometry limitation correct; 8–12 is a model- and resource-dependent benchmark, not a general ceiling**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4.5/5.** The cylinder getting exponentially harder as it widens is highly visual; an entanglement cut diagram would make the limit intuitive.

### Lines 269–275 — Ten-to-twenty-year quantum-advantage forecast for chemistry

- QPE on roughly 100–1,000 logical qubits is a plausible scale in selected strongly correlated chemistry proposals, but logical-qubit count alone omits the far larger constraints of non-Clifford throughput, state preparation, runtime, physical qubits, and error-correction cycle quality.
- “Credibly within 10–20 years” is a forecast, not a fact-checkable technical result. It needs an identified forecaster, forecast date, probability/confidence, hardware assumptions, and success criterion; otherwise the horizon simply rolls forward.
- “Quantum advantage” must specify the molecule/observable/accuracy and best classical competitor. Scientific usefulness, runtime advantage, cost advantage, and an uncheckable calculation are different thresholds.
- Keep scenario forecasts in a dated box or table and pair optimistic/base/pessimistic cases with falsifiable milestones.
- Verdict: **resource scale plausible in selected studies; timeline and advantage claim are speculative and should be labeled explicitly as such**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4/5.** Timelines create urgency, but an unsupported decade range feels promotional; milestone-based scenarios invite readers to track reality.

### Lines 276–282 — Thousand-qubit fault-tolerant prerequisite for the doped Hubbard phase diagram

- Solving scientifically decisive regions of the doped two-dimensional Hubbard model beyond reliable classical methods is a credible quantum-computing target, but “~(10^3) qubits” cannot be assessed without saying logical or physical, lattice size, encoding, algorithm, precision, observable, and runtime.
- Register count for a (L\times L) spinful lattice is already tied to roughly (2L^2) fermionic modes before ancillas/reductions, yet useful thermodynamic extrapolation requires several sizes and control of finite-size, temperature, and boundary effects.
- A fault-tolerant device with 1,000 logical qubits is not automatically capable of the needed depth or state preparation. DMRG is only one comparator; AFQMC, tensor networks, diagrammatic methods, DMFT/embeddings, and analog simulators define the moving classical/experimental frontier.
- The one-word anchor “contingent on” is unusable and preserves none of the claimed resource statement.
- Verdict: **scientific target valid; the thousand-qubit threshold is an unsupported shorthand and the extraction is effectively missing**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4.5/5.** The race to settle a famous phase diagram is strong narrative material; specify the lattice and observable so readers know what “solve” means.

### Chapter 28 fact-check mirror — second-pass file verdict

- Every card in this 299-line mirror has now received a granular second-pass review, including factual confidence, hidden assumptions, improvement ideas, doubts, and reader-experience assessment.
- The strongest concrete errors are: combining the CAS(54e,54o) and CAS(113e,76o) FeMoco benchmarks into “roughly 54 electrons in 54–76 orbitals”; attributing roughly (10^{11}) T gates to Reiher 2017 instead of the original estimate near (5\times10^{13}); and converting 10–40 spin-orbitals into 20–80 qubits.
- Other high-risk claims are unsupported numerical folklore: a universal Bravyi–Kitaev crossover near 20–30 orbitals, 50-orbital VQE requiring (10^9)–(10^{12}) shots without scenarios, thousand-site Hubbard experiments, (10^7)-logical-qubit/(10^{20})-T QCD estimates, and 10–20-year advantage forecasts.
- Extraction quality is a systemic defect. Numerous anchors stop immediately before the number, exponent, noun, or resource being checked; one anchor is only “contingent on.” The comments then reconstruct stronger claims that the ledger cannot trace back to book prose.
- The chapter’s conceptual spine is excellent: Feynman to electronic structure, FeMoco, Hubbard physics, embedding, optimal simulation, field theory, nonlinear PDEs, and honest classical baselines. Its reader experience is strongest when a physical system and a cost model form a concrete story, and weakest when author-year lists or giant numbers appear without normalized assumptions.
- Replace resource prose with dated scenario tables, distinguish query/gate/depth/runtime currencies, identify spatial versus spin orbitals everywhere, and use a strict extraction validator that rejects incomplete sentence fragments.
- Overall verdict: **rich, unusually compelling applications material, but its fact-check mirror exposes several material unit/attribution errors and pervasive non-reproducible resource estimates that require correction before publication**.

## Second-pass review — `factcheck/part-11-applications/29-optimization-finance-and-industrial.md`

### Lines 1–4 — File identity and open verification status

- The mirror/path and May 2026 extraction provenance are clear, but optimization, finance, solver capability, and hardware claims age quickly; extraction date and last-verification date need separate fields.
- “Verification still OPEN” gives no card count, coverage percentage, or reason codes. In a chapter full of marketing-sensitive comparisons, an open item should distinguish missing source, conflicting evidence, volatile snapshot, and non-falsifiable forecast.
- Add extraction completeness checks and require benchmark cards to name instance sets, hardware/software versions, clocks, budgets, and comparison rules.
- Verdict: **usable shell, but status metadata is too weak for volatile industrial claims**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 3.5/5.** The terse header is unobtrusive; a compact benchmark/source dashboard would make the audit itself easier to follow.

### Lines 6–12 — Goemans–Williamson 0.8786 approximation guarantee

- Goemans and Williamson’s semidefinite-programming algorithm guarantees an expected Max-Cut value at least (alpha_{GW}\approx0.878567) times optimum for general weighted graphs with nonnegative weights; rounding to 0.8786 is correct.
- Say “approximation guarantee/ratio” rather than implying every run returns exactly that fraction. Random hyperplane rounding is probabilistic and can be repeated or derandomized.
- Scope matters: variants with signed weights, constraints, or different objective normalization may not inherit the same statement. The algorithm is polynomial-time in the usual theoretical model, while SDP scale can be practically demanding.
- Cite the original 1995 journal paper and define approximation ratio against the optimal cut value.
- Verdict: **verified, with routine scope and probabilistic-rounding qualifications**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4.5/5.** A mysterious constant emerging from geometry is inherently appealing; one sentence about cutting an SDP sphere with a random hyperplane would make 0.8786 memorable.

### Lines 13–19 — Conditional optimality under the Unique Games Conjecture

- Assuming the Unique Games Conjecture, the Goemans–Williamson constant is the optimal polynomial-time approximation threshold for Max-Cut, via the Khot–Kindler–Mossel–O’Donnell hardness result. The broad conditional claim is correct.
- “Modulo” is too casual and may obscure that UGC remains unproved. Say “assuming the Unique Games Conjecture” and distinguish NP-hardness beyond (16/17) from UGC-conditional hardness beyond (alpha_{GW}).
- Complexity statements also require the usual (P\ne NP)/randomization conventions and an arbitrarily small additive (epsilon) around the hardness threshold.
- Cite both the algorithm and conditional-hardness theorem rather than making one parenthesis carry an entire frontier.
- Verdict: **verified conditional result; hypothesis and epsilon-level formulation should be explicit**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4/5.** The fact that a geometric algorithm may sit exactly at a conjectured hardness wall is fascinating; unpacking the conjectural status prevents the parenthesis from feeling cryptic.

### Lines 20–26 — “Routine” branch-and-cut solutions of TSPs with tens of thousands of cities

- Specialized exact TSP software such as Concorde has solved very large structured instances, but that does not establish that generic Gurobi, CPLEX, and HiGHS “routinely” solve arbitrary tens-of-thousands-city TSPs.
- TSP formulations create (O(n^2)) edge variables and exponentially many subtour constraints handled by separation/cuts. Runtime depends enormously on geometry, instance family, formulation, cuts, heuristics, hardware, gap target, and whether the task is exact proof or merely a good tour.
- HiGHS is a general open-source LP/MIP solver and should not be presented as interchangeable with a purpose-built TSP branch-and-cut code without benchmarks. “Solve” must distinguish feasible, near-optimal, and optimality-certified.
- Replace “routinely” with named benchmark records or a table of TSPLIB/world instances, solver/version, city count, wall time, machine, and final gap.
- Verdict: **overstated and weakly sourced; exceptional specialized records do not prove routine generic-MIP capability**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4.5/5.** Huge city tours are intuitive and competitive; naming one famous solved instance would be far more vivid than a vendor list.

### Lines 27–33 — D-Wave Advantage2 qubit count and topology

- This card conflates two product generations. D-Wave’s current Advantage2 specification lists 4,400+ qubits, 40,000+ couplers, and 20-way **Zephyr** connectivity; a current system-specific page reports 4,514 working qubits.
- **Pegasus** topology with degree/connectivity 15 belongs to the earlier Advantage system. Early roadmap material anticipated Advantage2 with more than 7,000 qubits, but still with Zephyr/degree 20; a roadmap target is not a deployed 2026-era specification.
- Working-qubit counts vary with calibration/yield, so cite a dated product specification or solver identity/graph ID. Also distinguish native physical qubits from the far smaller number of logical problem variables after minor embedding.
- Replace the sentence wholesale rather than adjusting one number: it combines an old target count with the old product’s topology.
- Verdict: **materially false product-generation mash-up: count, topology, and degree do not describe one Advantage2 system**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4/5.** Native-versus-embedded scale is a useful reality check, but incorrect hardware genealogy turns it into confusion.

### Lines 34–40 — “Roughly 100 logical-quality qubits” on a 2026 gate-model device

- “Logical-quality qubit” is not a standard measurable category. A qubit is physical, encoded/logical under a stated code, or described by benchmarked fidelity/lifetime; blending these concepts makes the number unfalsifiable.
- Current devices may have hundreds or thousands of physical qubits and demonstrations involving varying numbers of logical qubits, but there is no general-purpose 100-logical-qubit machine with a universally defined fault-tolerant depth implied by this sentence.
- The parenthesis “more raw qubits, but depths limited by decoherence” sounds like NISQ physical qubits, contradicting the “logical” label. Error-corrected logical depth is limited by logical error rate, decoding, cycle time, and available gates, not simply physical decoherence.
- Replace with dated rows for physical-qubit systems and separately for logical-qubit demonstrations, including code, distance, logical error per cycle/gate, gate set, and longest demonstrated computation.
- Verdict: **category error and unsupported snapshot; the sentence mixes physical NISQ scale with logical-qubit language**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 3.5/5.** A clean annealer-versus-gate-model comparison could orient readers; a synthetic “logical-quality” unit instead feels slippery.

### Lines 41–47 — Industrial QUBOs allegedly “routinely” containing (10^4)–(10^7) variables

- Industrial optimization models can certainly reach this range or larger, but “QUBO” size is formulation-dependent: discretization, one-hot/binary encodings, slack variables, penalty construction, decomposition, and preprocessing can inflate or reduce variables by orders of magnitude.
- “Practitioners want to solve” and “routinely” are not measurable populations. The card provides no sectors, datasets, variable-count distribution, density, constraint structure, or required solution quality.
- Raw variable count is a poor difficulty metric. Interaction-graph density/treewidth, coefficient precision/dynamic range, degeneracy, constraints, and exploitable structure determine both classical and quantum performance; sparse million-variable problems may be easier than dense thousand-variable ones.
- Use named public industrial cases and preserve original formulation, QUBO conversion, nonzero quadratic terms, solver baseline, time budget, and gap. Do not imply these sizes can be embedded directly on annealers.
- Verdict: **plausible existence claim but unsupported as a routine industry-wide scale and misleading without structure/encoding context**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4/5.** The enormous scale gap is striking; a real factory, routing, or scheduling instance would replace abstraction with stakes.

### Lines 48–54 — QAOA’s (p\to\infty) connection to adiabatic evolution

- Alternating exponentials of cost and mixer Hamiltonians can approximate a discretized adiabatic path as the number of layers grows, so QAOA can represent schedules converging toward adiabatic evolution under suitable controllability and gap/runtime conditions.
- “Ground state is reached in the limit” needs initial-ground-state preparation, a path whose relevant spectral gap does not close too severely, sufficiently slow total evolution, and a Trotter schedule whose discretization error vanishes. Merely increasing (p) with arbitrary optimized angles proves none of these.
- This is an expressibility/existence statement, not an efficient optimization guarantee: finding the required parameters may be hard, and (p) may scale impractically with size/gap/precision.
- Cite the adiabatic-QAOA connection and specify whether the statement concerns standard transverse-field mixer and unconstrained binary optimization or a generalized alternating-operator ansatz.
- Verdict: **valid existence intuition with explicit assumptions; must not be read as efficient convergence of trained finite-(p) QAOA**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4.5/5.** Watching a smooth adiabatic path crystallize into alternating pulses is elegant; the parameter-finding caveat supplies the necessary sting.

### Lines 55–61 — Farhi–Goldstone–Gutmann (p=1) ratio on 3-regular Max-Cut

- The original 2014 QAOA preprint states that level (p=1) on 3-regular graphs always yields a cut at least 0.6924 times optimum; the number, graph family, authors, and year are verified.
- This is a worst-case guarantee with analytically selected angles, not a typical empirical score and not superiority over simple classical algorithms. Random cutting already gives expected ratio at least 1/2, while stronger classical guarantees exist.
- Preserve assumptions about unweighted 3-regular graphs and finite-size cycles. “Proved” is fair, but readers should know the guarantee concerns expectation value/sampling rather than deterministic production in one shot.
- Verdict: **verified**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4.5/5.** A precise first-layer guarantee anchors QAOA in mathematics; comparing 0.6924 with random and Goemans–Williamson makes its position instantly legible.

### Lines 62–68 — (p=2) QAOA guarantee of 0.7559

- Wurtz and Love derived a worst-case lower bound of 0.7559 for (p=2) QAOA on unweighted 3-regular Max-Cut, with worst cases lacking short cycles under the analysis; the numerical claim is verified.
- “Pushed (p=2) ... to 0.7559” can sound like an experimental optimization record. Say explicitly that it is an analytic performance guarantee at fixed parameters.
- The result remains below the general Goemans–Williamson guarantee, though graph-family restrictions and computational cost complicate simplistic comparisons.
- Add authors/year and avoid implying monotonic guaranteed improvement for every finite graph/parameter-training procedure merely because the best achievable value is nondecreasing when layers can be neutralized.
- Verdict: **verified analytic bound; wording should identify guarantee, graph scope, and source**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4.5/5.** The step from 0.6924 to 0.7559 gives the depth ladder momentum; a tiny ratio table would make the progression satisfying.

### Lines 69–75 — “No fixed-(p) proof beats Goemans–Williamson”

- This is a time-sensitive negative literature claim and requires a dated systematic search, precise quantifiers, and definition of “natural family.” The mirror provides none.
- Fixed-(p) QAOA can perform very well or exactly on specially constructed/bounded-local structures, while comparisons to Goemans–Williamson may use worst-case guarantees, instance-specific expected ratios, or restricted graph ensembles. These are not interchangeable.
- Work on fixed-angle conjectures suggests conditional regimes where deeper constant-(p) QAOA guarantees might exceed the general 0.8786 number on 3-regular graphs; conjectural and proved results must be separated.
- Recast as “we found no unconditional theorem as of [date] under [search scope]” and list the closest positive/negative results. Avoid asserting an exhaustive global absence without a review protocol.
- Verdict: **plausible but not verified; ill-defined negative claim vulnerable to newer and conditional results**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4/5.** An open race against 0.8786 is engaging, but readers need a finish line with rules rather than an unsourced absence statement.

### Lines 76–82 — Claimed 2018–2025 wall-clock consensus against hardware QAOA

- Published comparisons commonly find current hardware QAOA uncompetitive with inexpensive classical heuristics at useful sizes, so the chapter’s skeptical direction is reasonable.
- The sentence nevertheless compresses eight years, several unnamed institutions, heterogeneous devices, simulators, graph families, depths, optimizers, queue/calibration overheads, and solution-quality metrics into “generally.” It is not reproducible evidence.
- Wall-clock comparisons must declare whether compilation, parameter training, shots, network/queue latency, and classical preprocessing are included. Simulated annealing and tabu search also require tuned budgets and implementation/hardware disclosure.
- Create a benchmark table with one row per paper and matched instance/quality/time conditions. Separate “quantum processing unit time” from end-to-end time and avoid institutional name-dropping without citations.
- Verdict: **likely correct qualitative snapshot, but unsupported as a literature-wide empirical conclusion**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4.5/5.** A fair head-to-head race is inherently compelling; an anonymous consensus summary denies readers the race details.

### Lines 83–89 — McClean et al. 2018 barren-plateau result

- McClean et al. showed concentration of gradients around zero with exponentially small variance for a broad class of sufficiently random parameterized circuits approximating unitary 2-design behavior; the foundational attribution/year and core phenomenon are correct.
- “Wide variational ansatz” is imprecise. Random initialization alone is not enough; circuit ensemble/expressibility, depth, cost locality, and placement of the differentiated gate matter. Later work identifies shallow, noise-induced, and cost-dependent plateaus under other conditions.
- QAOA’s local structured ansatz can avoid some original Haar-random assumptions at small depth, but is not generally immune; depth, graph/problem, parameter initialization, concentration, and noise can still impair trainability.
- State that it is gradient **variance** (and typical resolvability) that shrinks exponentially, rather than asserting every individual gradient is identically zero.
- Verdict: **verified foundational result, but applicability conditions and QAOA caveat need more precision**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4.5/5.** A landscape flattening as Hilbert space grows is memorable; a visual ridge fading into measurement noise would make the danger intuitive.

### Lines 90–96 — Bravyi–Kliesch–Koenig–Tang and RQAOA

- The cited 2020 work by Bravyi, Kliesch, Koenig, and Tang studies recursive QAOA for Max-(k)-Cut/graph coloring, including classical simulation of level-1 QAOA/RQAOA and large numerical comparisons.
- The abstract supports strong empirical competitiveness of level-1 RQAOA on generated 3-colorable regular-graph ensembles, while also stressing that level-1 versions are efficiently classically simulable. The card’s blanket “proved it beats (p=1) QAOA on certain instance families” needs an exact theorem number/family before it can be accepted.
- Distinguish analytical separation, numerical ensemble average, and comparison with generic SDP rounding. “Provably” must identify approximation ratio and quantifiers, not merely cite a paper containing other proofs.
- Also say that recursion adds classical elimination steps and repeated circuit solves, so final quality cannot be credited solely to one quantum state.
- Verdict: **paper/authors/topic verified; claimed theorem is too vague and may overstate numerical evidence**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4.5/5.** Recursively freezing correlations gives QAOA a strategic plot twist; the efficient classical simulation is an equally interesting counter-twist.

### Lines 97–104 — Illustrative 50-qubit, (10^{-3})-error, (p=3) QAOA viability

- A two-qubit error near (10^{-3}) is attainable in selected best-reported calibrations, but it is not a generic 50-qubit device parameter. Simultaneous operation, crosstalk, connectivity, drift, leakage, measurement, and compilation change effective circuit error.
- QAOA (p=3) gate count/depth depends on graph degree, edge coloring/parallel scheduling, native (ZZ) implementation, routing/SWAPs, and mixer gates. Qubit count plus one average error rate cannot establish “edge of viability.”
- Multiplying independent gate fidelities is at best a rough sanity check and does not predict approximation quality after coherent error, noise bias, parameter training, and mitigation. Define viability as a measurable success probability or approximation ratio against a classical baseline.
- Label all device numbers explicitly illustrative and avoid “best current reports” without device, benchmark protocol, date, and simultaneous-gate data.
- Verdict: **useful pedagogical scenario but not a verified hardware-performance claim; insufficient error/circuit model**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4.5/5.** A concrete error-budget calculation is engaging, provided readers see the graph turn into gates rather than receiving a verdict from one fidelity number.

### Lines 120–126 — D-Wave commercial annealers since 2011

- D-Wave’s first commercial 128-qubit system was purchased by Lockheed Martin in 2011, and Chimera was used in that first commercial annealer; the historical date is defensible.
- “Has built since” could refer to prototypes, public demonstrations, sales, installation, or cloud availability, which began at different times. Say “sold its first commercial system in 2011” for the clearest verifiable milestone.
- Early D-Wave devices prompted substantial debate over quantum behavior and speedup; commercial sale should not be equated with demonstrated computational advantage.
- Verdict: **verified if phrased as first commercial sale/system, with milestone semantics clarified**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4/5.** A 2011 starting gun gives the annealing story chronology; the distinction between selling hardware and proving advantage adds useful tension.

### Lines 127–133 — Chimera → Pegasus → Zephyr hardware genealogy

- The topology sequence and nominal degrees are broadly right: Chimera uses (K_{4,4}) cells with degree 6, Pegasus raises nominal degree to 15, and Zephyr to 20; Advantage uses Pegasus and Advantage2 uses Zephyr.
- The product/count parenthesis is wrong: D-Wave 2X had up to roughly 1,152 fabricated qubits on a C12 Chimera graph, whereas the 2,048-qubit Chimera generation was D-Wave 2000Q/C16. “2X and earlier, 2048 qubits” reverses the chronology.
- Advantage is properly “5,000+”/Pegasus. Advantage2 is no longer merely a prototype in the current snapshot; deployed specifications list 4,400+ qubits, although earlier prototypes and roadmap targets had different counts.
- Distinguish nominal fabricated graph from working graph after yield/calibration and cite each generation independently.
- Verdict: **topology/degree progression correct; Chimera product count and present Advantage2 status are materially stale/misassigned**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4.5/5.** The three named graph generations form a satisfying evolution; accurate product milestones would make the family tree easy to retain.

### Lines 134–140 — Claimed (K_N) embedding cost (O(N^2)) on Chimera but (O(N\log N)) on Pegasus

- The Chimera (O(N^2)) physical-qubit scaling for embedding a growing clique is consistent with bounded native degree and chain embeddings.
- The claimed Pegasus (O(N\log N)) scaling is implausible and conflicts with the same bounded-degree constraint. A (K_N) minor has (Theta(N^2)) logical adjacencies; a host graph of constant maximum degree requires (Omega(N^2)) host vertices/edges up to constants. Pegasus improves constants and maximum clique size, not the asymptotic order to (N\log N).
- Official examples show a C16/2,048-qubit Chimera system natively clique-embedding only around 64–65 variables; Pegasus similarly uses chains and quadratic-scale hardware for dense cliques.
- Cite an explicit embedding theorem/construction for both topologies and separate physical-qubit count from embedding-algorithm runtime. The current asymptotic contrast should be corrected, not merely caveated.
- Verdict: **material mathematical error: bounded-degree Pegasus cannot generally embed (K_N) with only (O(N\log N)) physical qubits; scaling remains quadratic up to improved constants**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 5/5.** The simple edge-count lower bound is a crisp “marketing meets graph theory” moment and would teach more than the incorrect formula.

### Lines 141–147 — No demonstrated annealing scaling advantage over simulated annealing

- Careful benchmark literature has repeatedly failed to establish a robust application-relevant asymptotic scaling advantage for earlier D-Wave optimization experiments over well-tuned classical methods, so the skeptical historical summary is defensible.
- The absolute “have not shown” is time-sensitive and comparator-specific. Simulated annealing is only one baseline; spin-vector Monte Carlo, cluster algorithms, parallel tempering, isoenergetic cluster moves, tensor networks, GPUs, and specialized hardware may change conclusions.
- Scaling claims require a growing instance family, fixed success/quality criterion, optimized time-to-solution including programming/readout, confidence intervals, and enough size range to distinguish exponents from prefactors/crossovers.
- Newer claims about quantum dynamics or sampling are not automatically optimization speedups. Date and scope the conclusion to the benchmark class reviewed.
- Verdict: **reasonable dated consensus for studied optimization instances, but too broad without benchmark scope and current-search date**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4.5/5.** The long-running speedup detective story is engaging; naming the successive classical challengers would give it characters and motion.

### Lines 148–154 — King et al. and constant-factor gains on planted spin glasses

- Planted-solution spin-glass benchmarks have been used to probe D-Wave performance, and papers/reporting have discussed large constant-factor advantages without a convincingly different fitted scaling exponent over accessible sizes.
- The card attributes this specifically to “King et al. 2018” but supplies no title/device/problem class or actual factors. Multiple King-led and related papers exist, and a 2015 planted-solutions paper already used this benchmark family; bibliographic identity needs repair.
- A constant-factor speedup is meaningful only against a named implementation/hardware and at matched success probability, precision, preprocessing, and energy target. It is not portable to arbitrary problems or larger sizes.
- “No established difference” should include fit intervals and alternative scaling models; limited ranges notoriously make exponential and stretched/polynomial fits hard to distinguish.
- Verdict: **nuanced conclusion plausible, but attribution/year and quantitative benchmark are insufficiently specified to verify**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4.5/5.** Prefactor versus exponent is a crucial and surprisingly subtle contest; a log-scale plot would let readers see why the verdict remains cautious.

### Lines 155–161 — Simulated bifurcation and alleged (10^5)-variable millisecond solves

- Goto, Tatsumura, and Dixon introduced simulated bifurcation in 2019, but the contemporaneous FPGA implementation source located describes dense 2,048/4,096-spin machines and matrix-vector throughput—not a generic 100,000-variable QUBO solved in milliseconds.
- Later simulated-bifurcation systems may reach much larger sparse/structured instances, but year, hardware, interaction density, iteration count, objective quality, and whether timing excludes data transfer/setup must follow the exact result.
- “Solving” needs optimality versus heuristic energy/target distinction. For a dense (10^5) QUBO, merely reading (Theta(10^{10})) coefficients makes a millisecond end-to-end claim physically suspect unless structure/compression is assumed.
- The anchor’s caveat about instance class, quality target, and hardware is good; the mirror supplies none of them. Do not attach the headline to the 2019 paper without a precise table/figure.
- Verdict: **algorithm attribution verified; 100,000-variable millisecond performance is unsupported and likely conflates later or structured benchmarks with the 2019 implementation**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 5/5.** Classical oscillators racing quantum annealers is delightful; input-size arithmetic gives readers the tools to interrogate spectacular throughput claims.

### Lines 162–168 — Coherent Ising machines versus D-Wave

- Optical coherent Ising machines from Stanford/NTT collaborations have been benchmarked against D-Wave systems and classical algorithms, with favorable time/quality results on selected instance families.
- “Match or beat” is too underspecified: CIM delay-line pulse count, coupling implementation, measurement/control electronics, and problem mapping differ from D-Wave’s native graph, while benchmark papers have debated scaling, effective classical descriptions, and fair timing.
- “Same instance sizes” does not ensure matched connectivity, coefficient precision, success target, preprocessing, or energy use. State whether the comparison is time-to-target, best energy, success probability, or scaling fit.
- The phrase “classically coherent regime” needs careful physical explanation; optical coherence does not by itself settle every taxonomy or computational-resource question.
- Verdict: **existence of favorable benchmark comparisons credible; broad platform ranking is not verified without named studies and matched metrics**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 5/5.** Networks of light pulses competing with superconducting loops make excellent industrial-science storytelling; benchmark rules must remain visible.

### Lines 169–175 — Named banks with five-plus-year quantum teams

- Goldman Sachs, JPMorgan Chase, HSBC, BBVA, and Mizuho have all publicly participated in quantum-computing research, pilots, partnerships, or publications, but those facts do not automatically establish dedicated internal “teams” continuously operating for five-plus years at the snapshot date.
- Team formation dates, headcount, dedicated versus distributed roles, and organizational continuity are usually not public and can change. A press release about a partnership is weaker evidence than job records, research publications, or an institutional program page.
- Review each bank separately with the earliest dated evidence and phrase conservatively—“has publicly worked on quantum projects since at least…”—unless a primary source explicitly documents a dedicated team.
- This company-roster sentence is volatile and adds little technical value unless it supports a measurable investment/adoption argument.
- Verdict: **broad institutional involvement credible; continuous dedicated-team duration is unverified for the named set**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 3.5/5.** A logo roll-call is mildly impressive but corporate; one concrete experiment per bank would be more human and informative.

### Lines 176–182 — Classical continuous Markowitz solve times

- With a positive-semidefinite covariance matrix and linear constraints, the basic continuous mean–variance problem is a convex quadratic program and is efficiently solvable; integrality, cardinality, transaction costs, lots, and nonlinear risk constraints change the class.
- “Fractions of a second at (N\sim10^3)–(10^4)” is hardware-, sparsity-, conditioning-, tolerance-, formulation-, and solver-dependent. The mirror comment’s word “microseconds” is much stronger than the anchor and is almost certainly an accidental escalation.
- Dense covariance storage/factorization costs differ radically from sparse/factor-model structure, and repeated warm-started frontier solves differ from a cold solve.
- Supply a reproducible benchmark matrix and solver/version or remove the timing while retaining the robust polynomial/convex baseline.
- Verdict: **convexity/efficient solvability verified; timing unsupported, and the comment incorrectly upgrades fractions of a second to microseconds**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4/5.** The classical baseline is essential but dry; contrasting the continuous solve with one realistic cardinality constraint creates a useful plot turn.

### Lines 183–189 — No matched quantum wall-clock win for portfolio optimization

- The cautious conclusion is plausible: published portfolio pilots generally emphasize formulation and feasibility rather than a robust end-to-end wall-clock/quality advantage over strong MIQP or specialized classical solvers.
- This is another time-sensitive negative claim. “Better portfolios” requires a common objective and constraints; “less wall-clock” requires inclusion rules for embedding, compilation, tuning, queueing, reads, postprocessing, and classical solver optimality gaps.
- The named institutional pilots must be cited and classified as hardware, simulator, annealer, gate-model, or hybrid. Avoid treating absence in a casual search as proof of absence.
- Use “we found no demonstration under the following search/matching criteria as of [date]” and maintain a benchmark registry.
- Verdict: **likely fair snapshot, but not proven without a systematic dated search and matched-condition definition**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4.5/5.** A sober scoreboard is refreshing; showing the strongest quantum pilot beside the classical result would make the conclusion earned.

### Lines 190–196 — Classical Monte Carlo (O(M^{-1/2})) convergence

- For independent samples of a finite-variance random variable, the standard error of the sample mean scales as (sigma/\sqrt{M}); equivalently (O(1/\epsilon^2)) samples achieve additive root-mean-square error (epsilon) up to variance/confidence factors.
- The claim needs finite variance and a definition of error/confidence. Correlated Markov-chain samples replace (M) with effective sample size, while variance reduction, quasi-Monte Carlo, multilevel Monte Carlo, and problem smoothness can improve practical or asymptotic behavior.
- Do not describe (1/\sqrt M) as a lower bound for every classical integration algorithm; it is the baseline for ordinary i.i.d. Monte Carlo under broad assumptions.
- Verdict: **verified standard baseline with independence/variance and competing-method qualifications**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4/5.** The square-root law is clear; showing that one extra decimal digit costs roughly 100× samples gives it immediate force.

### Lines 197–203 — QAE’s quadratic query advantage

- Canonical amplitude estimation achieves additive error (epsilon) using (O(1/\epsilon)) coherent applications of the state-preparation/oracle machinery, versus (O(1/\epsilon^2)) i.i.d. samples for ordinary Monte Carlo; the query-complexity advantage is genuine.
- This is a query comparison, not automatically a runtime advantage. QAE requires coherent controlled operations/inverses or alternative iterative variants, and every query may contain expensive path generation, arithmetic, payoff evaluation, and uncomputation.
- Classical baselines include variance reduction, quasi-/randomized quasi-Monte Carlo, multilevel methods, GPUs, and analytic structure. Confidence and variance/range normalization must be matched.
- Say which QAE variant and error guarantee is meant; modern maximum-likelihood/iterative methods trade ancillas and depth without making state preparation free.
- Verdict: **verified quadratic oracle/query scaling; end-to-end speedup remains conditional**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 5/5.** Halving the exponent is the finance section’s clean quantum promise; counting the machinery inside one query keeps the promise intellectually exciting rather than magical.

### Lines 204–210 — Stamatopoulos et al. 2019 and alleged (10^7) T-gate estimate

- Stamatopoulos et al. 2019 did establish a gate-based QAE methodology for vanilla, multi-asset, and path-dependent option pricing, with explicit state/operator circuits, simulations, and a small IBM hardware demonstration.
- The located paper’s abstract and framing do not establish the mirror comment’s “European call at (10^{-3}) needs ~(10^7) T gates.” The work predates many full fault-tolerant accounting conventions and discusses circuit constructions rather than presenting that headline T-resource result.
- A T count must identify discretization qubits, QAE variant/iterations, arithmetic synthesis, rotation precision, state loading, payoff approximation, success/error allocation, and whether oracle repetitions are included. The anchor itself mentions only unspecified “circuit-resource estimates.”
- Locate the exact table/equation or attribute the (10^7) figure to the later paper that derived it. Do not infer “well into fault tolerance” from an unverified reconstructed number.
- Verdict: **framework attribution verified; specific (10^7)-T estimate is unsupported and likely misattributed**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4.5/5.** Following a clean quadratic theorem into a brutal compiled circuit bill is excellent storytelling—if the bill has a traceable receipt.

### Lines 211–217 — Claim that most option-pricing papers quietly assume QRAM-style loading

- State preparation is a genuine bottleneck in QAE finance: the algorithm needs a coherent distribution/path generator and reversible payoff calculation, and arbitrary amplitude loading can erase the query advantage.
- “Most” is an unmeasured literature-frequency claim, “quietly” imputes presentation behavior, and “QRAM-style” conflates explicit QRAM data access with algorithmic distribution loading from a known stochastic model. Stamatopoulos et al. explicitly emphasize input-state/operator circuits, which cuts against the blanket rhetoric.
- Audit a defined corpus and classify exact amplitude loading, Grover–Rudolph/integrable distributions, reversible pseudorandom/path generation, variational loading, QRAM/database access, and excluded loading cost.
- Criticize the precise access/cost assumption paper by paper rather than borrowing the dequantization narrative from quantum machine learning.
- Verdict: **important methodological concern, but the majority/quiet/QRAM characterization is unsupported and overgeneralized**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4.5/5.** “Who loads the probability distribution?” is exactly the right skeptical question; a taxonomy is more illuminating than a literary accusation.

### Lines 218–224 — Claimed QAE crossover only near (epsilon\sim10^{-4})

- There is no universal precision crossover. It depends on derivative/model, dimension/path count, variance reduction, classical hardware, quantum cycle/gate times, oracle depth, state preparation, error correction, target confidence, and whether many related prices/Greeks are amortized.
- “Reasonable analyses” supplies no sources or parameter sets, and “most pricing applications need” is a separate empirical finance claim requiring evidence about quoting, hedging, XVA/risk, regulatory, and calibration workflows.
- Absolute price error (10^{-4}), relative error, normalized amplitude error, basis points, and currency units are not interchangeable. QAE rescales payoff into an amplitude, so (epsilon) needs units and normalization.
- Present explicit crossover scenarios with sensitivity analysis; do not collapse them to a portable threshold.
- Verdict: **unsupported pseudo-consensus; (10^{-4}) has no meaning without normalization and full classical/quantum cost models**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 4.5/5.** A crossover plot could be one of the chapter’s most useful visuals; a floating epsilon is merely technical-looking.

### Lines 240–246 — Vehicle-routing QUBO arithmetic and hardware feasibility

- The stated product (VCT\sim10\times100\times100=100{,}000) binary assignment variables is arithmetically correct for that particular time-indexed encoding before auxiliary/slack variables.
- Calling those values “realistic” requires a specific logistics model; alternative arc-, route-, set-partitioning-, and decomposition formulations have very different variable counts and constraint structures.
- The claim that a 100,000-variable QUBO is “at the edge” of current D-Wave hardware **after minor embedding** is false for direct QPU use: Advantage2 has roughly 4,400 physical qubits, and dense logical variables consume chains, so even 100,000 native independent variables cannot fit, much less an embedded interacting QUBO.
- D-Wave hybrid solvers may accept far larger models by classical decomposition, but that is not QPU ingestion and must be labeled separately. The gate-model conclusion is directionally obvious but also needs depth/connectivity rather than qubit count alone.
- Verdict: **variable arithmetic correct for one encoding; direct-annealer feasibility is wrong by orders of magnitude and conflates hybrid service input with QPU embedding**.
- **Reader entertainment/readability: 5/5.** The formulation explosion is a strong reality check; comparing 100,000 logical variables with 4,400 pre-embedding physical qubits makes the mismatch unforgettable.

### Lines 247–253 — Volkswagen’s 2017–2020 quantum pilots

- Volkswagen publicly announced Beijing traffic work with D-Wave in 2017 (describing earlier 2016 work), presented a Lisbon traffic-management concept in 2018, and ran a nine-bus Lisbon pilot during Web Summit 2019. Those traffic milestones are supported by Volkswagen’s own releases.
- The card additionally bundles Wolfsburg paint-shop sequencing and Barcelona traffic simulation without sources. The 2018 release says Barcelona was the intended first test location, whereas the documented live 2019 pilot was Lisbon; “simulation in Barcelona” needs independent confirmation.

### Lines 254–260 — Scale of the Volkswagen Beijing taxi demonstration

- Volkswagen’s 2017 release says the work used data from **10,000 public taxis** in Beijing, not merely “a few thousand vehicles.”
- Using records from 10,000 taxis is not necessarily the same as simultaneously optimizing 10,000 independently represented vehicles on the QPU. The exact QUBO decomposition, number of selected routes/traffic segments, logical variables, and QPU subproblems must be reported.

### Lines 261–267 — BMW/AWS/Quantinuum and Daimler/IBM partnerships

- BMW’s 2021 Quantum Computing Challenge with AWS explicitly included pre-production vehicle-configuration optimization and offered Amazon Braket access. Daimler/Mercedes-Benz and IBM have publicly explored quantum chemistry/materials, especially battery materials.
- The BMW sentence conflates distinct partners/events: AWS hosted/supported a challenge; any Honeywell/Quantinuum project needs its own source and scope. “Which options to bundle” is a loose gloss of pre-production vehicle configuration and may misstate the actual optimization variables.
